children.translated_text: // <s>Śrīḥ</s> (Auspiciousness) //
<s>Alaṅkārasarvasvam</s> (The Essence of All Ornaments)
Having bowed to the supreme <s>Vāc</s> (Speech), the <s>Devī</s> (Goddess) of threefold form,
The purport of the master's <s>alaṅkāra</s>-<s>sūtras</s> (aphorisms on ornamentation) is stated through commentary. [<s>Ruyyaka</s>'s <s>Alaṃkārasarvasva</s> 0]
[Commentary on <s>Ruyyaka</s>'s <s>Alaṃkārasarvasva</s> 0/1:]
<s>Śrī Jayaratha</s>'s <s>Alaṅkāravimarśinī</s>

children.text:
maṅgalakāmanayā granthakṛnnijeṣṭadevatāpraṇāmapuraḥsaramabhidheyaṃ tātparvaṃ caikenaiva vākyena parāmṛśati-namaskṛtyeti /
parāṃ vāṅmayādhidevatāṃ parākhyāṃ śabdabrahmaṇo 'pṛthagbhūtāṃ śaktiṃ parāṃ vācaṃ devīṃ trividhavigrahāṃ bahirullilāsayiṣayā paśyantīmadhyamāvaikharīrūpeṇa prakāratrayeṇādhiṣṭitaśarīrāṃ namaskṛtya nirvighnacikīrṣitagranthasamātpaye tāṃ prati kāyavāṅmanobhiḥ prahvībhūya nijālaṅkārasūtrāṇāṃ vṛttyā tātparyamucyata iti maṅgalānvayayojanā /

children.translated_text: And here, the elaboration of the characteristics described therein:
'You yourselves are <s>vimarśa</s> (reflective awareness) in form, the ultimate <s>camatkṛti</s> (aesthetic rapture);
That itself is the essence of all things — it is called the supreme <s>Vāc</s> (Speech).

With the desire for auspiciousness, the author of the treatise, prefacing with a salutation to his chosen deity, touches upon the subject matter and purport in a single sentence — 'having bowed' etc.
The supreme <s>Vāc</s> (Speech) — the deity presiding over the verbal domain, the power called <s>Parā</s> (the Supreme), inseparable from <s>Śabdabrahman</s> (the Absolute as Word), the supreme Speech, the <s>Devī</s> (Goddess) of threefold form — whose body is constituted by three modes, namely <s>Paśyantī</s>, <s>Madhyamā</s>, and <s>Vaikharī</s>, manifesting outward through desire to play — having bowed to her, having prostrated through body, speech, and mind toward her for the unobstructed completion of the intended treatise, the purport of his own <s>alaṅkāra</s>-<s>sūtras</s> is stated through commentary — this is the construal of the auspicious invocation.
Known as <s>Nāda</s> (primal sound), it abides in all beings in the form of the individual soul;
Without beginning or end, that itself is the subtle, imperishable <s>Vāc</s> (Speech).
Without beginning or end, <s>Brahman</s> is the imperishable reality of sound;
From which the creation of the world proceeds through transformation into the form of meaning.
<s>Vaikharī</s> is the production of audible sound; <s>Madhyamā</s> is within the domain of recollection;
<s>Paśyantī</s> illuminates meaning; the subtle one is <s>Brahman</s> alone.'

children.text: ityādiśāstroktikrameṇa sarvatra sadoditāyāḥ sūkṣmāyāḥ parāyāḥ śabdabrahmaṇaḥ śakterbahirunmiṣantyāḥ prathamo vivartaḥ paśyantī nāma /

children.translated_text: And thus it has been said:
'<s>Paśyantī</s> is undifferentiated, with sequence entirely withdrawn;
Self-luminous within, it is the subtle, imperishable <s>Vāc</s> (Speech).'

Thus, in accordance with the progression taught in the <s>śāstras</s> (authoritative treatises), the first transformation of the subtle supreme <s>Śabdabrahman</s> (Word-Absolute), the power that is ever-present everywhere, as it manifests outward, is called <s>Paśyantī</s>.

children.text:
iti /
asyārthaḥ-avibhāgā sthānakāraṇaprayantaprakāreṇa varṇānāṃ vibhāgahīnā ata eva saṃhṛtakramā tathaivāntaḥsvarūpajyotiḥ svayaṃprakāśā svasyātmano rūpaṃ jyotiśca sarvatra hi sarvavidhāyinī śaktireveti vāntaḥsūkṣmabījādaṅkuramiva bahirunmiṣantī kiñciducchūnā parāyā madhyamāyāścāvasthāṃ taṭasthā paśyatīti paśyantītyucyate /

children.translated_text: Then, beyond that:
'That which is in the form of internal conception, following the sequential pattern,
Transcending the activity of <s>prāṇa</s> (vital breath), <s>Madhyamā</s> (Middle) speech proceeds.'

Thus.
The meaning of this: 'undifferentiated' — devoid of the differentiation of phonemes by way of place, instrument, and effort of articulation; hence 'with sequence withdrawn'; likewise 'internally self-luminous' — self-illuminating, its own nature being light; and everywhere indeed the all-creating power itself — or, sprouting outward from the subtle seed within, like a shoot from a seed, somewhat swollen, standing at the boundary between the states of <s>Parā</s> (Supreme) and <s>Madhyamā</s> (Middle), she 'sees' and hence is called <s>Paśyantī</s> (the Seer).

children.text:
etatkathayāmīti vimarśarūpā antaḥsaṃkalparūpā prāṇavṛttimatikramya śrotragrāhyavarṇā bhivyaktirahitā kramarūpānupātinī bhānanasikavarṇoccāraṇakrameṇa dvitīyo vivarto madhyamārūpojāte /
madhyamā kila dvayorvāgvivartayoḥ paśyantīvaikharīsaṃjñayormadhye vartanānmadhyametyucyate /

children.translated_text: And subsequently:
'When the breath is opened at the places of articulation, having assumed the form of phonemes,
<s>Vaikharī</s> speech of speakers is grounded in the activity of <s>prāṇa</s> (vital breath).'

'I shall speak this' — being of the nature of <s>vimarśa</s> (reflective awareness), in the form of internal conception, transcending the activity of <s>prāṇa</s>, devoid of the manifestation of phonemes perceptible to the ear, following the sequential pattern — following the sequence of labial, nasal, and other phoneme-articulation — the second transformation in the form of <s>Madhyamā</s> arises.
Indeed, <s>Madhyamā</s> is so called because it exists in the middle between the two transformations of speech known as <s>Paśyantī</s> and <s>Vaikharī</s>.

children.text:
iti lakṣaṇātsthānakaraṇaprayatnakramavyajyamānaḥ śrotragrāhyadundubhivīṇādinādaparicayo gadgadāvyaktagakārādivilāsasamuñcayapadavākyātmakastṛtīyo vivarto vaikharītyucyate /
viśiṣṭaṃ khamākāśaṃ mukharūpaṃ rāti gṛhṇātīti vikharaḥ prāṇavāyusaṃcāraviśiṣṭo varṇoccārastenābhivyaktā vaikharīti /
vikhare śarīre bhavā vaikharīti vā kicit /
siddho maṅgalārthaḥ /
tathā cātra pūrvārdha eva punarāvṛttyābhidheyapadārthānvayayojanā-yathā parāṃ vācamuttamakāvyarūpatayā kāvyātmadhvanisaṃjñām abhidhātātparyalakṣaṇottīrṇāmutkṛṣṭām /
devīm 'divu krīṭāvijigīṣādyutistutivyavahāramodamadakāntisvapnagatiṣu' iti yathāyathaṃ dhāvtarthānāmanusmaraṇāt śaktimatāṃ kavīnāṃ śrotṛṇāṃ ca svabhāvātsvecchayā samucchalantīṃ krīḍantīm /
tathā devīṃ dyotamānāṃ dyotanadhvananayoḥ śabdaṃ tatsaṃkīrtitaṃ cārthamupasarjanīkṛtya varnāmānām /
tathā devīṃ dyotamānāṃ dyotanaghvananayoḥ paryāyatvād dhvanisaṃjñām /
tathā devīṃ stutyāṃ sarvaiḥ kāvyātmatvādabhivandyām /
tathā devīṃ vyavaharantī sarvatra pracarititāṃ na tu kvāpi skhalitām /
tathā devīṃ dyotamānāṃ śrutimātreṇaiva paramānandadāyinīm /
tathā devīṃ mādyantīṃ kaveḥ sahṛdayasya ca yathāyathaṃ karaṇāvabodhaghābhyāṃ kamapyahaṅkāraṃ janayantīm /
tathā devīṃ kamanīyāṃ sarvairabhilaṣaṇīyām /
tpividhavigrahāṃ trividhastriprakāro vigraho vyatirekeṇa grāho vyatirekamūlaḥ pramākaraṇaprakāro yasyāstām /
tathā hi 'gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ' ityādivākyeṣu ghoṣasya yacchaityapāvanatvādikaṃ pratīyate tatra nābhidhā /
gaṅgādiśabdānāṃ śaityādyarthasyāvācakatvāt /
na tātparyātmā /
tātparyaśaktyā hyādhārādheyabhaghāvāvagamārthaṃ parasparamanvayamātra eva kṣīṇatvāt /
na lakṣaṇā /
mukhyārthabādhādihetutritayābhāvāt /
tasmādabhidhātātparyalakṣaṇāvyatiriktacaturthakakṣyānikṣitpo vyañjanavyāpira ityādi so 'yamevāgre vimṛṣyati /
atha cavyaṅgayasya śabdārthobhayamūlatvena prasiddhastrividho viśeṣaṇānāṃ vigrāho viśeṣaṇānāṃ bhedānāṃ graho yasyā iti vā /
etādṛśīṃ tāṃ namaskṛtya maṅgalācaraṇarūpatvena manāguddiśya na tu sūtravṛttibhyāṃ tātparyakathanādilakṣaṇaparīkṣāvistāreṇa nirṇīya nijālaṅkārasūtrāṇāṃ vṛttyā tātparyamucyata iti /
asyābhiprāyaḥ-tathā ca dhvanermanāguddeśamātrameva karoti 'iha hi tāvadbhāmaha-'ityādinā /
tadevattāvadāstām /
nijeti /
parakīyāṇāṃ sūtrāṇāṃ sūtraṇāṃ tātparyakathanānavabodho 'pi syāditi bhāvaḥ /
tathā na kaiścidapi parairīddaṃśi sūtrāṇi kṛtānītyapi dhvanitam /
tātparyamiti /
saṃkṣitpārthaprakāśanamityarthaḥ /
anyathā hi kathanāpi granthena pāraṃ na yāyāt /

children.translated_text: Now, [an objection]:
'In the opening statement, the subject matter and purpose should be stated
In order to establish the listener's engagement, inclination, and confidence.'

According to this definition, the third transformation, manifested through the sequence of place, instrument, and effort of articulation, familiar as sounds perceptible to the ear like drums, <s>vīṇā</s>, and other instruments, comprising the display of indistinct sounds like stammering and unclear 'ga' sounds and the like, and consisting of words and sentences, is called <s>Vaikharī</s>.
The distinguished space — the mouth-form of <s>ākāśa</s> (ether) — 'rāti' (takes/receives), hence '<s>vikhara</s>' — the <s>prāṇa</s> (vital breath) moving through the distinguished [space] manifests phoneme-articulation, and that which is manifested by it is <s>Vaikharī</s>.
Or alternatively, that which exists in the body (<s>vikhara</s>) is <s>Vaikharī</s>.
Thus the meaning of the auspicious invocation is established.
And here, through repetition, the construal connecting the subject matter with the first half [of the verse] only: 'the supreme <s>Vāc</s>' means the supreme in the form of excellent poetry, that is, designated as <s>dhvani</s> (suggestion) which is the soul of poetry, transcending <s>abhidhā</s> (denotation), <s>tātparya</s> (intention), and <s>lakṣaṇā</s> (indication), the most exalted.
'<s>Devī</s>' — remembering the various root-meanings from '<s>divu</s>' — playing, conquering, shining, praising, transacting, rejoicing, intoxicating, desiring, sleeping, going — she who spontaneously surges forth by her own will from the nature of powerful poets and listeners, who plays.
Likewise '<s>Devī</s>' means shining — since <s>dyotana</s> (illumination) and <s>dhvanana</s> (suggestion) are synonyms — she who makes subsidiary both the word and the meaning proclaimed by it, manifesting names.
Likewise '<s>Devī</s>' means shining — since <s>dyotana</s> and <s>dhvanana</s> are synonymous, she is designated as <s>dhvani</s>.
Likewise '<s>Devī</s>' means praiseworthy — worthy of veneration by all, being the soul of poetry.
Likewise '<s>Devī</s>' means transacting — current everywhere, never stumbling anywhere.
Likewise '<s>Devī</s>' means shining — bestowing supreme bliss by mere hearing.
Likewise '<s>Devī</s>' means intoxicating — generating for the poet and the <s>sahṛdaya</s> (connoisseur) respectively, through composition and apprehension, an indescribable sense of self.
Likewise '<s>Devī</s>' means desirable — wished for by all.
'Of threefold form' — threefold, i.e., of three kinds, is the <s>vigraha</s> (apprehension through exclusion), the mode of cognition based on exclusion — possessing that.
Thus indeed, in sentences like 'the cowherd settlement is on the <s>Gaṅgā</s>,' whatever coolness, purity, etc. of the settlement is apprehended — there, <s>abhidhā</s> (denotation) [does not account for it],
since words like '<s>Gaṅgā</s>' etc. do not denote meanings like coolness.
Nor is it the function of <s>tātparya</s> (purport),
for the power of purport is exhausted in merely effecting the syntactic connection for understanding the relation of container and contained.
Nor is it <s>lakṣaṇā</s> (indication),
due to the absence of the three causes such as obstruction of primary meaning.
Therefore, the operation of <s>vyañjana</s> (suggestion), stationed in a fourth level distinct from <s>abhidhā</s>, <s>tātparya</s>, and <s>lakṣaṇā</s> — this and more he examines hereafter.
Now, since the suggested meaning is well known as threefold — rooted in word, meaning, or both — 'of threefold form' can also mean: she whose apprehension (<s>graha</s>) of distinctions (<s>vigraha</s>) of qualifications, i.e., of varieties, is [threefold].
Having bowed to her of such nature — having invoked her by way of auspicious practice, merely indicating briefly, but not determining through detailed examination of definitions etc. through the <s>sūtras</s> and commentary — the purport of his own <s>alaṅkāra</s>-<s>sūtras</s> is stated through commentary.
The intention of this: and thus he makes only a brief indication of <s>dhvani</s>, through 'iha hi tāvad bhāmaha-' etc.
Let that remain aside for now.
'His own' — the implication is that even the statement of the purport of others' <s>sūtras</s> (aphorisms/compositions) might not be understood.
Also implied thereby is that no one else has composed <s>sūtras</s> of this kind.
'Purport' — meaning: a concise illumination of the meaning.
Otherwise, indeed, one could never reach the end through any treatise whatsoever.

children.text:
iti nītyā śrotṛpravṛttyartha sarvatraivādivākye 'bhidheyaprayojanādyabhidhīyatte /
tacceha noktamiti kathamatra śrotṝṇāṃ pravṛttiḥ syāt /
maivam /
alaṅkārā hyatrābhidheyāḥ /
teṣāmatra sākṣādevābhidhānāt /
tadabhidhāyakaṃ cedamalaṅkārasarvasvākhyaṃ prakaraṇamityabhidhānābhidheyayorniyamagarbhīkāreṇārthākṣitpo vācyavācakabhāvalakṣaṇaḥ saṃbandhaḥ /
nahyevaṃvidhametabhidhāyakaṃ prakaraṇāntaramasti /
tasyānviṣyamāṇasyāpyupalambhayogyasyānupalambhāt /
ata evātrānyālaṅkāragranthavailakṣaṇyoddhoṣaṇāya 'tātparyamucyate'ityādyuktam /
abhidheyāścātrālaṅkārāḥ kāvyālaṅkārā na laukikā ityeteṣāṃ kāvyopaskṛtidvāreṇa pāramparyeṇa-
children.translated_text: And the <s>alaṅkāras</s> that are the subject matter here are poetic ornaments, not worldly ones — and through the medium of their enhancement of poetry, indirectly —
'Poetry serves fame, wealth, worldly knowledge, the warding off of the inauspicious,
Immediate delight, and instruction in the manner of a beloved — '

According to this principle, the subject matter, purpose, etc. are always stated in the opening sentence everywhere, for the sake of the listener's engagement.
But that has not been stated here — so how will the listeners' engagement arise?
Not so.
For here, the <s>alaṅkāras</s> (figures of speech) are the subject matter,
since they are directly stated here.
And this treatise called <s>Alaṅkārasarvasva</s> (Essence of All Ornaments) is their expositor — thus, through the internalization of the necessary connection between the exposition and what is expounded, the connection is that of the expressed and the expression, characterized by the relation of signifier and signified.
For there is no other such treatise that expounds these.
Because even when sought, no other capable of being found is found.
For this very reason, to proclaim the distinctiveness from other treatises on ornamentation, 'the purport is stated' etc. has been said.

children.text:
ityādyuktanītyā tadavinābhāvasvabhāvatvādarthākṣitpasarvapuruṣārthasiddhirūpā caturvargāvātpiḥ prayojanam /
tayośca sādhyasādhanabhāvalakṣaṇaḥ saṃbandhaḥ /
iti sthitamevādivākyasya śrotṛśravaṇaśraddhāvirbhāvanibandhanatvam /
children.translated_text:
According to the principle stated thus and others, because [the ornaments] are by nature inseparable from [poetry], the purpose is the attainment of all human goals in the form of the four aims of life (<s>caturvarga</s>), which is a full fruition of meaning. And between these two, the connection is that of means and end.
Thus it is established that the opening statement serves as the basis for arousing the listener's faith in hearing.
[Commentary on <s>Ruyyaka</s>'s <s>Alaṃkārasarvasva</s> 0/2:]

children.text:
nanu yadīhālaṅkārā abhidheyāstarhi tadalaṅkaryo 'pya-bhidheyaḥ /
'alaṅkārā alaṅkāryāpekṣāḥ' iti nītyā sa evaiṣāṃ ko nāma yadupaskārakatvenaitatsvarūpamabhidhīyata ityāśaṅkya tadavataraṇikāmeva vaktumupakramate-
ihetyādinā /
children.translated_text:
Now, if the <s>alaṅkāras</s> are the subject matter here, then the object they ornament (<s>alaṅkārya</s>) must also be stated as a subject.
According to the principle that '<s>alaṅkāras</s> are dependent on the <s>alaṅkārya</s> (the thing to be ornamented),' who indeed is that [object] by whose enhancement their very nature is defined? — anticipating this objection, he begins to state the introduction to that topic with 'iha' (here) etc.
START Introduction

children.text:
iha hi tāvad bhāmahodbhaṭaprabhṛtayaścirantanālaṅkārakārāḥ pratīyamānamarthe vācyopaskārakatayālaṅkārapakṣanikṣitpaṃ manyante /
tathāhi-paryāyoktāprastutapraśaṃsāsamāsoktyākṣepavyājastutyupameyopamānanvayādau vastumātraṃ gamyamānaṃ vācyopaskārakatvena 'svasiddhaye parākṣepaḥparārthe svasamarpaṇam' iti yathāyogaṃ dvividhayā bhaṅgyā pratipāditaṃ taiḥ /
rudraṭenāpi bhāvālaṅkāro dvidhoktaḥ /
rūpakadīpakāpahnutitulyayogitādāvupamādyalaṅkāro vācyopaskārakatvenoktaḥ /
utprekṣā tu svayameva pratīyamānā kathitā /
rasavatpreyaḥprabhṛtau tu rasabhāvādirvācyaśobhāhetutvenoktaḥ /
taditthaṃ trividhamapi pratīyamānamalaṅkāratayā khyāpitameva / [RuAss_Bhū.1]
children.translated_text:
Here, indeed, the ancient <s>alaṅkārikas</s> (rhetoricians) such as <s>Bhāmaha</s>, <s>Udbhaṭa</s>, and others consider the apprehended meaning, by virtue of its being an embellishment of the expressed, as falling within the province of <s>alaṅkāra</s> (figures of speech).
Thus — in <s>paryāyokta</s> (circumlocution), <s>aprastutapraśaṃsā</s> (praise of the irrelevant), <s>samāsokti</s> (condensed expression), <s>ākṣepa</s> (objection), <s>vyājastuti</s> (ironic praise), <s>upameyopamā</s> (reciprocal simile), <s>anvaya</s> (connection), etc., the mere factual content that is apprehended, being an embellishment of the expressed, was presented by them in a twofold manner: 'the invocation of another for one's own establishment' and 'the offering of oneself for another's purpose.'
<s>Rudraṭa</s> also stated <s>bhāvālaṅkāra</s> (figure of emotion) as twofold.
<s>Rūpaka</s> (metaphor), <s>dīpaka</s> (illumination), <s>apahṇuti</s> (concealment), <s>tulyayogitā</s> (equal conjunction), etc. — <s>upamā</s> (simile) and related figures were stated as embellishments of the expressed.
But <s>utprekṣā</s> (poetic fancy) was described as itself being apprehended.
In <s>rasavat</s> (rasa-bearing), <s>preyaḥ</s> (charming), etc., <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic relish), <s>bhāva</s> (emotion), etc. were stated as causes of the beauty of the expressed.
Thus, the apprehended element in all three forms has been proclaimed as belonging to the category of <s>alaṅkāra</s>. [<s>Ruyyaka</s>'s <s>Alaṃkārasarvasva</s>, Introduction 1]
[Commentary on <s>Ruyyaka</s>'s <s>Alaṃkārasarvasva</s>, Introduction 1:]

kvacicca svayamanupapadyamānaḥ sanpratīyamāna evārthe svaṃ samarpayati /
tena yatra yādṛtkatra tādṛgeva yojyamityarthaḥ /
children.translated_text:
By the word 'and others' (<s>prabhṛti</s>), <s>Daṇḍin</s> and others are meant.
The word 'tāvat' indicates the absence of disagreement [at this stage].
'Ancient' etc.
The implication is that these did not perceive the doctrine of the <s>Dhvanikāra</s> (the author of the <s>Dhvani</s> theory).
'Apprehended' — although established through self-experience as distinct from the expressed.
'Meaning' — in the sense of being the ultimate resting place, characterized by supreme desirability.
'As an embellishment of the expressed' — for embellishment of the expressed is the very essence of <s>alaṅkāras</s>.
'Within the province of <s>alaṅkāra</s>' — included within the totality of figures, not something distinct from them.
'Consider' — they consider it to be so, but it does not actually exist thus. For mere opinion does not change the nature of things — this is the implication.
He demonstrates this very point with 'thus' etc.
The construction is: 'the mere factual content that is apprehended, being an embellishment of the expressed, was presented by them.'
'Mere factual content' — but not <s>alaṅkāras</s> and <s>rasa</s>.
'For one's own establishment' — in cases like 'the spears enter,' the spears invoke (<s>ākṣipanti</s>) the men connected with them for the sake of establishing their own entry, since without those [men], the entry [of spears] is impossible.
In 'the cowherd settlement is on the <s>Gaṅgā</s>,' however, the word '<s>Gaṅgā</s>' surrenders itself for the sake of establishing elsewhere — on the bank — the location-status of the settlement, since it itself cannot be the location of a settlement.
'As appropriate' — for in some cases, the expressed meaning invokes the apprehended meaning for its own establishment. In other cases, being itself impossible, it surrenders itself to the very apprehended meaning. Therefore, wherever whichever [mode] is applicable, that alone should be applied — this is the meaning.
[Commentary on <s>Ruyyaka</s>'s <s>Alaṃkārasarvasva</s>, Introduction 1a:]
Among these, <s>paryāyokta</s> (circumlocution), for example:
'He brought down <s>Laṅkā</s>, he crossed this ocean, he brought the medicine-forest for the healing of <s>Saumitri</s> (<s>Lakṣmaṇa</s>) —

children.text: iti smāraṃ smāraṃ tvadarivalabhīcitralikhitaṃ hanūmantaṃ dantairdaśati kupito rākṣasagaṇaḥ //
children.translated_text: Remembering and remembering thus, the painting of <s>Hanumān</s> on the arches of your enemy's palace — the <s>Rākṣasa</s> host angrily bites it with their teeth.'

children.text:
'atra rākṣasagaṇavṛttānto vācyaḥ san svasiddhaye paraṃ kāraṇarūpamaripalāyanādyākṣipati /
tatpalāyanādyantareṇa rākṣasavṛttāntasyāsaṃgateḥ /

children.translated_text: Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 6a: Having thus defined the two <s>alaṅkāras</s> (poetic ornaments) that depend solely on consonants, he now defines <s>yamaka</s> (rhyming repetition) which depends on both vowels and consonants — beginning with 'svara' etc.

children.text: 'prāṇā yena samarpitāstava valādyena tvamutthāpitaḥ skandhe yasya ciraṃ sthito 'si vidadhe yaste saparyāmapi /
children.translated_text: <s>Sūtra</s> 7: The repetition of a combination of vowels and consonants is <s>yamaka</s> (rhyming repetition). // <s>RuAss</s>_7 // Here there are briefly three varieties: sometimes the repeated elements have different meanings, sometimes they have the same meaning, and sometimes one is meaningless while the other is meaningful. For example — 'Whoever sees those charming eyes, in him beauty is born; in the other eyes of that person, beauty indeed is not born.' // This illustrates the case of meaningfulness. The rest should be understood similarly.

children.text: tasyāsya smitamātrakeṇa janayanprāṇāpahārakriyāṃ bhrātaḥ pratyupakāriṇāṃ dhuri paraṃ vetālalīlāyase' //
children.translated_text: Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 7: The word 'ekasya' (of one) etc. is meant as an <s>upalakṣaṇa</s> (indicative expression). Therefore the meaningfulness and meaninglessness of many <s>yamakas</s> is established and included. But in the reading 'sometimes meaningful, sometimes meaningless,' only two distinctions would be stated first, and there would be no third variety. Therefore the text specifying the distinctions as it stands is preferable. 'In brief' means: since it would obstruct the relishing of <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic sentiment), which is the soul of <s>kāvya</s> (poetry), if elaborated, it is not suitable to expand upon — therefore, unlike the ancient <s>alaṅkāra</s> treatises, it is defined without subdividing. The same should be understood regarding <s>citra</s> (pictorial poetry) as well. 'Other' means: the two varieties. Among these, the meaningless variety is illustrated as: 'In spring, with swarms of bees and waters, he bestowed upon the lotus pond a beauty resembling the goddess of the ocean, with the brilliance of manifest <s>rāga</s> (colour/passion).' Here 'tarāga' is meaningless. For the combination of meaninglessness and meaningfulness: '<s>sāhāraṃ sāhāraṃ sāhāraṃ</s>, to the ascetic the true sustenance; <s>saṃtāṇaṃ saṃtāṇaṃ saṃtāṇaṃ</s>, the succession of delusion.' Here '<s>sajjasāhāram</s>' is meaningless; the others are meaningful, so there is no fault. // This does not occur without positional restriction. As stated: 'A word with multiple meanings or a syllable repeated with positional restriction is <s>yamaka</s>.' For this very reason, calling it <s>yamaka</s> because of positional restriction is an etymologically apt designation. And this positional restriction is intentional, not inherent. For example: 'He bore the world's splendour, with bees defeated, the pride of proud women conquered, minds fragrant with flowers, having warded off the flooding of lotuses, with the hue of blossomed copper.' Here the <s>yamaka</s> arrangement in two syllables establishes the positional fixity. Or alternatively: 'May <s>Kārtikeya</s> destroy your fear and affliction — he by whom the moon was conquered, who in the month of <s>Kārtika</s>; the lord of the one whose tusk was uprooted, master of the <s>gaṇas</s> — what other is there for counting?' Here also, with two meanings and two <s>yamakas</s>, the positional restriction is twofold, so there is no deficiency in this <s>alaṅkāra</s>.

Here, the account of the <s>Rākṣasa</s> host, being the expressed content, invokes for its own establishment the causal element of the enemy's flight and such — since the account of the <s>Rākṣasas</s> would be incoherent without that flight and the like.

children.text: atra vetālacaritamaprastutaṃ prakaraṇādivaśena svayamanupapadyamānaṃ sat prastute kṛtaghnavṛttānte svaṃ samarpayati /

children.translated_text: Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 8: 'Praruḍha' means: [repetition that is] manifest as such through convention. For example: 'Born in that lineage, the purest of the pure in mind, the king <s>Dilīpa</s>, the moon among kings, like the moon in the ocean of milk.' Here 'moon' [is repeated], but since the moon has a twofold birth — from the eye of <s>Atri</s> and from the milk ocean — this is not established [tautology], as such a convention is not recognized in poetic tradition. 'They say' refers to the <s>Ākṣapāda</s> [Naiyāyika] school. 'Except in restatement' means...

<s>Sūtra</s> 9-10: 'But when there is a difference in purport, it is <s>lāṭānuprāsa</s> (a type of repetition).' // <s>RuAss</s>_9 // <s>Tātparya</s> (purport) means having another as its primary reference. It is the purport that differs, not the form of word and meaning. For example: 'Then qualities are born when they are grasped by the <s>sahṛdayas</s> (connoisseurs); the rays of the sun...' ['Then qualities are born when they are perceived by the sensitive; the rays of the sun that followed the lotuses...'] Here the <s>upameya</s> (object of comparison) being obscured by the <s>ṣaṭpada</s> (bee) is imagined.
Thus there are five <s>alaṅkāras</s> (ornaments) in the domain of repetition. // <s>RuAss</s>_10 // This has been explained through direct statement.

<s>Sūtra</s> 8: "Established repetition of word and meaning is a fault." // <s>RuAss</s>_8 // The word 'praruḍha' (established) is used to distinguish it from the varieties to be described later. As they say: 'Repetition of word and meaning is <s>punarukta</s> (tautology), except in the case of <s>anuvāda</s> (restatement).'

children.text: atra bodhisattve nāyakavyavahāre na saṃbhavatīti svasiddhyarthaṃ nāyakatvamākṣipati /

children.translated_text: Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 9-10a: We say, how much [is there to discuss]? Here, since the word '<s>abja</s>' (lotus) also has no repetition, one should consider whether it is only <s>lāṭānuprāsa</s>. For here, since both words for 'eye' (<s>nayana</s>) rest in the expressed meaning, there is no difference in purport due to the absence of having another as primary reference. That indeed is its life. Otherwise it would merely be <s>anuprāsa</s> (alliteration), not an <s>alaṅkāra</s>. Even if the word '<s>nayana</s>' alone rests in its own meaning...

children.text: 'kiṃ bhaṇimo bhaṇṇai kitti adha kiṃ vā imeṇa bhaṇieṇa /
children.translated_text: <s>Sūtra</s> 11: When the arrangement of phonemes produces shapes like swords etc., it is <s>citra</s> (pictorial poetry). // <s>RuAss</s>_11 // In the context of repetition, <s>citra</s> refers to the repetition of phonemes arranged in specific positions forming patterns. Although the written letters have specific configurations such as sword-shapes etc., nevertheless, since in common usage they are perceived as identical with the sounds apprehended in the space of hearing, this is a verbal <s>alaṅkāra</s>. The word 'ādi' (etc.)...

children.text: bhaṇṇihisi tahavi ahavā bhaṇāmi kiṃ vā ṇa bhaṇiosi' //
children.translated_text: Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 11: 'Of phonemes' etc. — Since at the time of pronunciation there is no actual existence of sword-shapes etc. formed by phonemes arranged in specific positions, there is no perception of repetition here — so objecting 'what is the basis of this <s>alaṅkāra</s>?', he answers with 'although' etc. Through the non-difference between the ink-dot-formed written letters and the sounds perceived through hearing, this is a figurative verbal <s>alaṅkāra</s> — this is the purport. The word 'ādi'...

Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 9-10: 'Having another as primary reference' means: when one [element] rests in the expressed meaning, the other rests in the suggested or implied meaning — this is the meaning. 'Differs' means: at the conclusion. For at the outset, like the word, the meaning too appears as one. Therefore he says — 'not the form of word and meaning.' And thus this is not a mere <s>anuvāda</s> (restatement) as an <s>alaṅkāra</s> when both rest in the expressed meaning. For the absence of a fault alone does not...

children.text: ('kiṃ bhaṇamo bhaṇyate kiyadivātha kiṃ vānena bhaṇitena /
children.translated_text: <s>Sūtra</s> 12: When there is similarity of properties between <s>upamāna</s> (standard of comparison) and <s>upameya</s> (object of comparison), with equality of identity and difference, it is <s>upamā</s> (simile). // <s>RuAss</s>_12 // This is the section on <s>arthālaṅkāra</s> (sense-ornaments). The mention of '<s>upamāna</s> and <s>upameya</s>' is to exclude cases where these are not recognized. In similarity there are three varieties: predominance of difference, as in <s>vyatireka</s> (contrast) etc.; predominance of identity, as in <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor) etc.; and equality of both, as in this [<s>upamā</s>]. As they say: 'Where...'

children.text: bhaṇiṣyate tathāpyathavā bhaṇāmi kiṃvā na bhaṇito 'si') //
children.translated_text: Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 12: '<s>Upamāna</s>' etc. — 'Artha' means: since after the determination of verbal <s>alaṅkāras</s> the occasion has arrived — this is the meaning. Now, since similarity can only exist between <s>upamāna</s> and <s>upameya</s>, not between cause and effect etc., what is the point of mentioning them? — anticipating this objection, he says '<s>upamāna</s>' etc. Therein, the non-recognition of the <s>upamāna</s> is explained by the ancient scholars through difference of gender etc. For example: 'Harsh, biting, impurity-bestowing are the wicked...'

children.text:
atra vakṣyamāṇaviṣayo bhaṇananiṣedho vācyaḥ san vaktumevopakrāntasya niṣedhānupapatteḥ svayamaviśrāmyan svātmasamarpaṇena tvāṃ prati mariṣyāmi athavā mriye yadvā mṛtā yāvadahamiti vidhitrayamarthānataramākṣipati /
yattvatrānyaiḥ 'vācyor'thaḥ svasiddhayer'thāntaramākṣipati'ityuktaṃ tadayuktameva /
tathātve hi niṣedha eva paryavasitaḥ syānna niṣedhābhāsa ityākṣepālaṅkāra eva na syāt /
'āmukhāvabhāsamāno hi niṣedha' ākṣepalakṣaṇam /
na ca vidhiniṣedhayorvirodhātsādhyasādhanabhāvo yuktaḥ /

children.translated_text: Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 12b: 'Even there' means: even though the ancient scholars have specified distinctions like completeness etc. — this is the meaning. 'Of the common property' means: a property depends on something else, and its applicability to both this and that constitutes its commonness. And that alone is the basis of <s>upamā</s> (simile) etc. And this is fourfold, as the <s>Mahābhāṣya</s> states 'the fourfold application of words' — through properties such as genus, quality, action, and substance...

Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 12c: There, the genus-nature etc. of the property-bearer is illustrated as: 'As if from the desert path the shade of dense gardens, from the forest fire a pool of snow-waters, from the effect of poison the nectar, from increasing madness the natural state — having rescued from separation, when shall I obtain your devotion, O <s>Śaṅkara</s>, the incomparable <s>rasa</s> (sentiment)?' Here the <s>upamānas</s> — shade, pool, nectar, natural state — have the nature of genus, quality, substance, and action respectively.

children.text: guṇadosā dosaguṇā ehiṃ kaā ṇahu kaā tehiṃ' //
children.translated_text: Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 12d: And for the properties: 'O <s>Vaidehī</s>, behold the foam-white ocean divided by my bridge, like the clear autumn sky with the Milky Way revealed, displaying its beautiful stars.' Here 'divided' has the nature of action; <s>Rāma</s>'s bridge and the Milky Way have the nature of substance; foam and stars have the nature of genus; and clarity has the nature of quality — being subordinated to the substance-natured sky and ocean...

Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 12a: To explain the equality of identity and difference, he shows the distribution of similarity according to subject divisions — with 'sādharmya' (similarity of properties) etc. And through these three varieties alone, the entire class of <s>alaṅkāras</s> based on similarity is encompassed. Thus, by 'like <s>vyatireka</s>' etc., <s>sahokti</s> (co-expression) and similar figures are included; by 'like <s>rūpaka</s>' etc., <s>pariṇāma</s> (transformation), <s>utprekṣā</s> (poetic fancy) and others are included. However, <s>rūpaka</s>...

Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 12e: 'In single form' means: at once. As will be stated: 'When the common property is presented with a single mention at the outset, it is <s>upamā</s>.' 'Separate mention' means: repeatedly. As will be stated: 'Even with repeated mention through the relation of thing and counter-thing, it is that very [<s>upamā</s>].' This should also be connected with 'of the common property.' To show the twofoldness even in the thing-counter-thing relation, he says...

children.text: guṇadoṣā doṣaguṇā ebhiḥ kṛtā na khaluḥ kṛtāstaiḥ') //
children.translated_text: Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 12f: 'Of necklace and body-paint' — the supplement is 'of their forms.' And here one should not, by demonstrating that the reflection-original relation pertains to another domain, suspect <s>upamā</s> through sentence-meaning implication, and propose a fourth variety called 'equality of qualities.' For inasmuch as the essential nature of <s>upamā</s> is based on a common property, and that property is here twofold — as stated or unstated — and in the stated case, its three...

children.text:
atra cirantanānāṃ nindā vācyā satī svayamanupapadyamānā stutāvātmānamarpayati /
tadgatatvena vastudarśitāyā nindāyā asaṃbhavāt /
evamadyatanānāmapi stutirnindāyāmātmānamarpayati /
tasyā api viparītatayā tadgatatvenāsaṃbhavāt /
yatpunaratrānyaiḥ svasiddhaye parākṣepo vyākhyātastadupekṣyameva /
yato 'tra cirantanānāṃ syutyākṣepeṇa eva paryavasitaḥ syāditi naitadyuktam /
kiṃ ca lakṣaṇāyāmapi svasiddhaye parākṣepo na yuktaḥ /
tathātve hilakṣaṇāyāḥ svarūpahāniḥ syāt /
vācyalakṣaṇasyaiva svasya siddhatvānmukhyārthabādhābhāvāt /
na caikadā ekasya bādhaḥ siddhiśceti vaktuṃ yuktam /
vipratiṣiddhaṃ hyetat /
vācyasyaiva yadyatrasiddhistadabhidhaiva syānna lakṣaṇā /
tasyā hi mukhyārthabādha eva jīvitam /
'kuntāḥ praviśanti' ityādau ca kuntānāṃ svayaṃ praveṣṭumasaṃbhavānmukhyārthabādha eveti parasya kuntavadrūpasya lakṣyasyaivārthasya prādhānyam /
ataśca lakṣaṇāyāṃ bādhitaḥ sanmukhyo 'rthaḥ paratra lakṣya eva svaṃ samarpayatītyeva yuktam /
nanu yadyevaṃ tatparyāyoktādau vācyasidhyarthaṃ parasya lakṣyasyākṣepaḥ pratīyata yatītyeva yuktam /
nanu yadyevaṃ tatparyāyoktādau vācyasidhyarthaḥ paratra lakṣya eva svaṃ samarpayatītyeva yuktam /
nanu yadyevaṃ tatparyāyoktādau vācyasidhyarthaṃ parasya lakṣyasyākṣepaḥ pratīyata iti tatra kiṃ pratipattavyam /
idaṃ pratipattavyam-atra hi lakṣaṇāyā eva nāvakāśaḥ /
tatra hi kathamahaṃ syāmiti vācyaṃ sat kāryaṃ tadavinābhāvātparaṃ kāraṇamākṣipatītyākṣepeṇaiva siddhestasyā anupayogaḥ /
'gauranubandhyaḥ'ityatra yathā kathaṃ me śruticoditamanubandhanaṃ syāditi jātyā vyaktyavinābhāvādvyaktirākṣipyate natu lakṣyate tathaivātrāpi kārcakāraṇayorjñeyam /
evaṃ samāsoktāvapi nāyakavyavahārastadavinābhāvitvādeva nāyakatvamākṣipatītcatrāpi lakṣaṇāmūlatvaṃ nāśāṅkanīyam /
anthakṛtā punaretañcirantanamatānuvādaparatayoktam /
asmābhistu prasaṅgādvastu paryālocitamityalaṃ bahunā /
children.translated_text: Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 12g: Now, since the necklace and the waterfall lack the quality of being applicable to both, how can there be a common property? — to this we reply: The commonness of this property is its very life. And that occurs when the property is singular. But here the property is not actually singular. For the property of beauty etc. that resides in the face is not the very same one in the moon etc., since its actual continuity is impossible. Rather, one of the same kind...

Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 12h: This is abundantly found in literature. For example: 'The graceful women resembling lightning, with rainbow, with varied beauty; for the concert, the drums struck with deep, resonant sound; with gem-paved floors, lofty, touching the clouds — the palaces there equal you with those very qualities.' Here, lightning, women, etc. serve the function of establishing the distinctiveness of the cloud and the palace...

Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 12i: And this <s>upamā</s> occurs as accumulated upon both — upon those that are relevant and those that are not relevant. Sequentially, for example: 'In her voice, as if nectar were flowing, in her well-born speech; even though nurtured by another, with harsh sound, like a lute being struck by an outsider.' Here, in relation to the lady, the birds raised by others and the lute are irrelevant, and their commonality in harsh sound is accumulated. And...

Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 12j: Sequentially, for example: 'Bow to the navel-lotus of <s>Hari</s>, who is delightful as the canvas of the sky; in whom <s>Vidhī</s> (<s>Brahmā</s>) sits covered by bees, like a blemish on the moon.' ['Bow to the navel-lotus of <s>Hari</s>, who is charming as the expanse of the sky; where <s>Brahmā</s>, his body covered by six-footed bees, appears like a spot on the moon.'] Here the covering of the <s>upameya</s> by bees is imagined. 'Bent down...'

<s>Sūtra</s> 13: When one and the same thing serves as both <s>upamāna</s> (standard) and <s>upameya</s> (object of comparison), it is <s>ananvaya</s> (non-correlation). // <s>RuAss</s>_13 // The earlier form is followed from the standpoint of the expressed meaning. The conjunction of contradictory properties in one entity is for the purpose of excluding a second companion. Therefore the term <s>ananvaya</s> (absence of correlation) also applies here. For example: '<s>Arjuna</s> in battle is famous in prowess like <s>Arjuna</s> himself; <s>Bhīma</s> too among enemies is terrible like <s>Bhīma</s> himself...'

children.text: atra dvayoḥ parasparamupamānopameyatvaṃ vācyaṃ sat svayamanupapadyamānamupamānāntaravihalakṣaṇe paratra vastvantare sva samarpayati /

children.translated_text: Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 13a: 'The earlier form' means: of the nature of being based on similarity — this is the meaning. Let there indeed be a verbal cognition of similarity here. Just as in 'the face is like the moon' etc., so here too the <s>upamāna-upameya</s> relationship is established through expressed meaning. Therefore he says 'from the standpoint of the expressed meaning' — not from the standpoint of the actual reality. For in reality, since a single entity cannot simultaneously possess both established and to-be-established properties, the <s>upamāna-upameya</s> [relation]...

Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 13b: Thus, the exclusion of a second companion is indeed the validating evidence for its status as an <s>alaṅkāra</s>. Otherwise it would not be an <s>alaṅkāra</s>. For example: 'While protecting the people by his command alone, this old age with grey hair near the ears has come upon me; like the embryonic form, so this teacher's great partiality still instructs me even today.' Here, just as the embryonic form...

<s>Sūtra</s> 14: When two things alternately serve as that [<s>upamāna</s> and <s>upameya</s>], it is <s>upameyopamā</s> (mutual simile). // <s>RuAss</s>_14 // The word 'tat' refers back to the <s>upamāna-upameya</s> relationship. <s>Paryāya</s> (alternation) means the absence of simultaneity. Therefore here there is a division of sentences. And this is twofold: through the commonness of the property and through thing-counter-thing mention. In the first case: 'The sky is like water, water is like the sky; the swan is like the moon, the moon is like the swan...'

Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 13: 'Of one and the same' etc. — Now, since the <s>alaṅkāras</s> based on similarity are being defined, and since similarity by its nature requires two terms, and in the case of one entity there is no such [duality], how can this figure which does not depend on it be discussed here? — anticipating this objection, he says 'from the standpoint of the expressed meaning' etc.

children.text:
atraikasyaivopamānopameyabhāvo vācyaḥ sandvitīyamabrahmacajāryabhāve paratra vastvantare svaṃ samarpayati /
ādiśabdaḥ prakāre /
tenāniṣṭavidhyābhāsākṣepādergrahaṇam /

children.translated_text: Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 14a: 'In commonness' — and this has been stated with reference to the twofold division of the property as stated or unstated. In the stated case, although commonness exists, since it is followed by a single mention here, the apprehension of it is clear — this is the purport. In the unstated case, the commonness is real. Following which, 'the sky is like water' etc. was cited as illustration. Of the property when unstated...

children.text: 'bhavatu viditaṃ vyarthālāpairalaṃ priya gamyatāṃ tanurapi na te doṣo 'smākaṃ vivistu parāṅmukhaḥ /
children.translated_text: <s>Sūtra</s> 15: The remembrance of another thing due to the experience of something similar is <s>smaraṇa</s> (recollection). // <s>RuAss</s>_15 // The 'other thing' is indeed something similar. Since there is no invariable concomitance, it is not inference. For example: 'Seeing the child of surpassing divine and demonic power, of exactly similar form, I remember <s>Raghunandana</s> (<s>Rāma</s>), the son of <s>Kuśika</s>, bearing his bow at the destruction of the enemies of sacrifice.' But recollection without similarity is not this <s>alaṅkāra</s>...

children.text: tava yadi tathā ruḍhaṃ prema prapannamimāṃ daśāṃ prakṛtitarale kā no vrīḍā gate hatajīvite' //
children.translated_text: Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 15: 'Similar' — 'another thing' refers to what is remembered. 'Indeed similar' — because similarity subsists in both. Therefore, the positing of similarity between the remembered and the experienced, or between the experienced and the remembered, constitutes this <s>alaṅkāra</s>. As stated: 'Just as the cognition of similarity produced by what is seen pertains to what is remembered, so too does it pertain to what is seen when produced by what is remembered...'

Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 14: 'Of two' etc. — 'Two' refers to <s>upamāna</s> and <s>upameya</s>, not to the number two [in the numerical sense]. Therefore: 'The face of the beloved, the lotus, and the moon — formerly there was a mutual <s>upamāna</s>-relationship among them; now, stricken by old age, frost, and <s>Rāhu</s> respectively, another mutual disrelish has arisen.' Here the <s>upamāna-upameya</s> relationship of all three is established as a component of this very [figure]. The word 'tat'...

children.text:
atra kāntaprasthānavidhirvācyaḥ sanniṣeddhamevopakrāntatya vidhānānupapatteḥ svayamaviśrāntaḥ svasamarpaṇena niṣedhamākṣipati /
evaṃ dvividhayā bhaṅgyā gamyamānaṃ vastumātraṃ vācyoparaskārakamevotyuktam /
evamapi pratīyamānasyārthasya viviktaviṣayāntaropālambhādalaṅkārāntarbhāvo na sidhyatītyāśaṅkyāha-rudraṭenetyādi /
dvidheti /
guṇībhūtāguṇībhūtavastuviṣayatvenetyarthaḥ /

children.translated_text: Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 15/1: He shows yet another counter-example — with 'of the <s>preyolaṅkāra</s>' etc. The word 'tu' (however) is used in the sense of 'and.' A cause other than similarity means a cause such as <s>saṃskāra</s> (latent impression) etc. 'Even there' means: even when the situation is thus. When the <s>vibhāva</s> (determinant) etc. are implied, the relation is with [the statement that] the domain of <s>preyolaṅkāra</s> is recollection aroused by a cause other than similarity. Therein, when the <s>vibhāva</s> etc. are implied...

<s>Sūtra</s> 16: When identity predominates, with <s>āropa</s> (superimposition) and without negation of the object of superimposition, it is <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor). // <s>RuAss</s>_16 // Because of the predominance of identity, difference still truly exists. <s>Āropa</s> (superimposition) is the imposition of one thing upon another. Since it is supported by both object and superimposed entity, when the object is negated, it becomes <s>apahnutti</s> (concealment). Otherwise, through the imposition of the form of the superimposed upon the object which possesses form, it is <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor). In similarity, this is fully subsumed.

Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 16: 'Now' — since after the <s>alaṅkāras</s> based on the equality of similarity, difference, and identity, it is appropriate to define what has identity as predominant, the occasion has arrived — this is the meaning. Therein, first he defines <s>rūpaka</s> — with 'when identity predominates' etc. 'Truly' means: not in cognition. 'Exists' — because predominance and non-predominance are relational terms. 'The imposition of one thing upon another is <s>āropa</s>' — ...

The <s>preyolaṅkāra</s> (ornament of love), however, has as its domain a recollection aroused by a cause other than similarity. For example, 'Ah, even in anger the face is lovely.' Even there, when <s>vibhāva</s> (determinant) etc. are implied, in cases where only the literal word conveys the meaning: 'Here the discourse...' etc. 'Those who saw you then in battle, with spears striking the forehead, the front part reddened by copious streams of blood, [remembering] others...'

Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 16a: 'Otherwise' means: without negation. Thus the difference between <s>apahnutti</s> (concealment) and <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor) is also stated by this. 'They say' refers to <s>Daṇḍin</s> and others. Therefore, since similarity actually exists, its threefold nature animated by the three types of division should also be known. For example: 'The conch of <s>Kandarpā</s>'s (Cupid's) ear, marked with streams of <s>dāna</s>-fluid (ichor), darkened with clusters of collyrium-black, the cheek-pillow of <s>Rati</s> (Love); the bird-nest of the sky...'

This [<s>rūpaka</s>] is threefold: without parts, with parts, and indirect. The first is twofold: simple and garland-<s>rūpaka</s>. The second is twofold: pertaining to the entire entity and varying in one part. The third, being based on <s>śliṣṭa</s> (double-meaning) words, is twofold, and each being either simple or garland-form, is fourfold. Thus there are eight varieties of <s>rūpaka</s>. Others however...

Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 16/1: The word 'ca' (and) indicates aggregation of distinctions relative to other <s>alaṅkāras</s>. The word 'tu' (but) indicates the domain. 'Without parts' means where the superimposed entity is applied in separation from its parts. 'With parts' means where the superimposed entity operates together with its parts. 'Indirect' means where the imposition of one comes about through the glory of another in succession. 'The first' refers to the partless variety. A 'garland' of a single...

Sequentially, for example: 'The kick of a master is fitting for a servant who has committed offence, O beautiful one — so I do not grieve; but it is your foot that is hurt by the sharp tips of the bristling <s>pulaka</s> (goosebump) sprouts — indeed that pain is mine!' // 'A fresh stream of nectar for the gods of sacrifice, a gift for the destruction of darkness, the celestial <s>Gaṅgā</s> — the faces of the <s>cakravāka</s> birds dismayed, O creeper of <s>mṛṇāla</s> (lotus-stalk) — the doubling of <s>Smara</s> (Love)...'

children.text: ekākinī yadabalā taruṇī tathāhamasmadgṛhe gṛhapatiḥ sa gate videśam /
children.translated_text: Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 16/2: 'Sequentially' means according to the order of enumeration. In 'the doubling of <s>Smara</s>'s bow,' through the analysis of sentence-meaning, the perception of the moon being superimposed as <s>Smara</s>'s bow arises — and the basis of this similarity is the curvature and other multiple properties. Since many superimpositions pertain to the single moon, it is a garland-<s>rūpaka</s>. For multiple [objects], however: 'The arms are young lotus-stalk creepers, the bosom is <s>Rati</s>'s ruby palace, the pearls...'

children.text: kaṃ yācase tadiha vāsamiyaṃ varākī śvaśrūrmamāndhabadhirā nanu mūḍha pāntha' //
children.translated_text: Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 16/2a: Sometimes, to strengthen the identity, this is seen with the negation of opposition as a preliminary to superimposition, or by positing the diminishment of the property that causes difference, or by the intensity of the superimposition. Sequentially, for example: 'The beloved wife who shows contempt toward venerable elders, fond of strife, disregarding the neglected — she herself is the [ritual] act, the act is not the act, for the straightforward person's...'

This [<s>rūpaka</s>] is also seen through dissimilarity. For example: 'A desert of generosity-water, a wall-painting of good conduct-sky, a dark fourteenth night of virtue-moonlight, a dog's curved tail of straightforward yoga — this line of kings in the Kali age, who serve even this evil-minded [ruler], what skill is there in their service when <s>Śūlin</s> (<s>Śiva</s>) is accessible by devotion alone?' Here, although the superimposed entity has manifest gender markers, the number...

children.text:
yadvā dvidheti pūrvavadeva lakṣaṇādvayāśrayeṇa vyākhyeyam /
tenādye svasiddhaye parākṣepaḥ, paratra tu aparārthaṃ svasamarpaṇam /
yattvatrānyairbhāvairnirvedādibhirupalakṣito vācyapratīyamānatvena dvividhā bhāvālaṅkāro vyakhyātastudutsūtrameva /
rudraṭena tathātvena tasyāpratipādanāt /
tatrāpi ca vastumātrasya vācyopaskārakatvābhidhānasamaye vaktumucitatvāt /
tadevaṃ guṇībhūtāguṇībhūtatvena dviprakāraṃ vastu tāvadvācyopaskārakatvena pratipāditam /
children.translated_text: Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 16/3: 'Through dissimilarity also' means: not only through similarity. To show another peculiarity of charm, he says 'here' etc. 'Even though the gender is manifest' — by this it is conveyed that even though the property-bearer's own form alone is the conclusion, the property of number belonging to another property-bearer is also adopted. 'Since the number cannot obtain' — although...

Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 16/3a: 'Due to the absence of prior establishment' — because <s>rūpaka</s> is the cause of <s>śleṣa</s> (paronomasia). 'Based on that' means: based on <s>rūpaka</s>. The word 'iti' is used in the sense of causation. Therefore, the purport here is that <s>śleṣa</s> alone is the <s>alaṅkāra</s>, not indirect <s>rūpaka</s>. But this is debatable. For <s>śleṣa</s> occurs with two relevant [meanings], two irrelevant [meanings], or one relevant and one irrelevant. Here...

Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 17: 'Of the superimposed entity' etc. — Showing the distinction from <s>rūpaka</s> despite the similarity of the superimposition-object relation, he explains this with 'the superimposed entity' etc. 'Through embellishing the primary' — as stated: 'Through the imposition of form by the superimposed upon the object possessing form, it is <s>rūpaka</s>.' 'As the nature of the primary' means: as a part of the primary. 'Serves the purpose' — meaning that without it the primary meaning would be incomplete...

children.text: 'bhūmabhrukuṭipannagīphaṇamaṇiḥ kāyasya caṇḍaṃ citā- kuṇḍaṃ kuṇḍalitendunālavalayaprabhuṃśi raktotpalam /
children.translated_text: <s>Sūtra</s> 18: When the object is in doubt, it is <s>saṃdeha</s> (poetic doubt). // <s>RuAss</s>_18 // '[This falls under] the predominance of identity through superimposition' alone. The 'object' is the primary meaning, upon whose basis the non-primary is doubted. When the non-primary is doubted, the object too is inevitably doubted. Therefore, when doubt — arising from both the primary and the non-primary — is evoked by the poet's imagination, it constitutes the <s>saṃdeha-alaṅkāra</s> (ornament of doubt).

children.text: ghrāṇasphāṭikamallikāparicite bhālāgraśālājire- dīprā dīpaśikhā śivasya nayanaṃ kārśānavaṃ pātu naḥ' //
children.translated_text: Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 18: 'Of the object' etc. — Since 'object' and 'superimposed entity' are correlative terms, the mention of the object implies the inclusion of the superimposed entity as well. Therefore, the meaning of the <s>sūtra</s> is that both the object and the superimposed entity become the domain of doubt-cognition. Now, even though the correlative term 'superimposed entity' is implied by the word 'object' without explicit statement, how is the state of being doubted obtained for the superimposed entity from mere implication alone?...

<s>Sūtra</s> 17: When the superimposed entity serves the purpose of the primary subject, it is <s>pariṇāma</s> (transformation). // <s>RuAss</s>_17 // In <s>rūpaka</s>, the superimposed entity does not serve the purpose of the primary subject, but only relates through embellishing the primary; in <s>pariṇāma</s>, however, the superimposed entity serves as the very nature of the primary — thus the primary transforms into the form of the superimposed. Since there is no <s>āgama</s> (accretion), <s>anugama</s> (conformity), <s>vigama</s> (departure), <s>khyāti</s> (appearance), or <s>abhāva</s> (absence), this is not the <s>Sāṃkhya</s> [notion of] <s>pariṇāma</s>...

children.text:
atra nayanādīnāṃ maṇiprabhṛtīnāṃ copamā vācyopaskārāyāvagamyate /
tāṃ vinā sādṛśyāpratipatteḥ /
children.translated_text: And this [<s>saṃdeha</s>] is threefold: pure, containing certainty within it, and ending in certainty. 'Pure' is where doubt alone is the conclusion. For example: 'Is this a fresh creeper bursting forth from the tree of youth with the weight of <s>rasa</s>? Is it a wave of the ocean of beauty playfully arising? Is it perhaps a direct teaching-staff of the blossoming season, confident in presenting its own time? Or...'

Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 18/1: He illustrates this threefold distinction with examples — 'pure' etc. Here, since the primary subject, the slender woman, is not the domain of doubt-cognition, only the superimposed entities like the creeper etc. are doubted. For [doubt of] both object and superimposed entity: 'Is it a lotus, or is it the orb of the nectar-maker (moon), or is it the face, weariness-removing, of the doe-eyed one? Which is seen with bees, deer, and beautiful [reflections]...'

Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 18/1a: He states another alternative view — 'some say' etc. And by this, the author himself has stated that doubt is rooted in <s>adhyavasāya</s> (determinate cognition). Therefore, this [figure], being based on <s>adhyavasāya</s>, is also threefold according to whether the essence, cause, or result is doubted. Therein, doubt regarding the essence is as in 'coloured' etc. Or alternatively: 'Consider this — [is it] the teacher of the initiation into <s>śṛṅgāra</s> (erotic sentiment), who removes the fatigue of the <s>kairava</s> (night-lotus)...'

<s>Sūtra</s> 19: The cognition of another thing due to similarity is <s>bhrāntimān</s> (the figure of illusion). // <s>RuAss</s>_19 // Due to the common characteristic of being erroneous cognition, this is defined immediately after <s>saṃdeha</s> (doubt). <s>Bhrānti</s> (illusion) is a property of the mind. That poetic mode in which it is present is called <s>bhrāntimān</s>. And the illusion caused by similarity is its domain. For example: 'Mistaking the lips for <s>bimba</s>-fruits, the dark locks for ripe <s>jambū</s>-berries, the ear-ornaments...'

children.text: poḍhamahilaṃ a ramiuṃ viralaccia ke vi jāṇanti' //
children.translated_text: Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 19: 'Due to the common characteristic of being erroneous cognition' — not because of kinship with superimposition-based [figures] — this is the purport. For superimposition occurs when both the object and the superimposed entity are simultaneously apprehended by a single cognizer — therefore, illusion containing superimposition is never possible anywhere, since when shells etc. are cognized as shells, there is no mistaking them for silver etc. Now, '<s>bhrānti</s> is a property of the mind; that in which it is present...'

children.text:
atraka prākṛtabandhapāṭhāderupamā vācyopaskārāyāvagamyate /
prakṛtasya prauḍhamahilāramaṇādeḥ sādṛśyopādānāyaivobhayorupanibandhanāt /

children.translated_text: Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 20: 'Of a single thing also' — 'manifold apprehension' means: not manifold imagining. For apprehension is possible both in spontaneous and in produced cognition, not only in spontaneous cognition. As they say: 'Therefore, all cognition that grasps genus etc. — whether conjoined with or independent of verbal determination — is considered perception.' But imagining, on the other hand, is cognition of the previously stated...

Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 20a: This [<s>ullekha</s>], even in its two varieties, can occur as based on <s>rūpaka</s> etc. and also on other <s>alaṅkāras</s> — he states this with 'thus in other <s>alaṅkāras</s>' etc. Therein, the first variety based on <s>saṃdeha</s> (doubt), for example: 'Is this the sun or the fire? — so the enemies deliberate; is this the wish-fulfilling gem or the wish-granting tree? — so wonder those who have come with hopes; is this the spring or the flower-arrowed one (<s>Kāma</s>)?...'

<s>Sūtra</s> 21: The negation of the object [of superimposition] is <s>apahnutti</s> (concealment). // <s>RuAss</s>_21 // The continuation from 'cognition of another thing' is maintained, distinguished from it by the presence of negation. In the context of superimposition, when the object upon which superimposition rests is negated and the superimposed entity is cognized, the <s>alaṅkāra</s> called <s>apahnutti</s> arises. And it has three modes of composition: negation preceding superimposition, superimposition preceding negation, and through words like 'pretence' etc. conveying unreality...

<s>Sūtra</s> 20: The apprehension of a single thing in manifold ways due to [its various] causes is <s>ullekha</s> (delineation). // <s>RuAss</s>_20 // Where one entity is apprehended in many ways — that is <s>ullekha</s>, from the delineation of multiple forms. And this is not mere causeless delineation; rather, it is done due to causes such as possessing various kinds of properties. Therein, relish, desire, and etymology are the motivating factors as appropriate. As stated...

Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 21a: 'Of that' — of the <s>alaṅkāra</s> called <s>apahnutti</s>. 'Division of sentences' and 'single sentence' — by this the nature of the three varieties is indicated according to appropriateness. 'Not faultless' — because the stated order cannot be maintained. Therefore he presents another example — 'of the full moon' etc. Because of the use of the word 'manye' (I think), which conveys conjecture, it is not <s>utprekṣā</s> (poetic fancy) — [for] that requires determinate...

Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 21b: 'In this' — in what is conveyed by words like 'pretence' etc. 'But mere conjecture is shown by this example.' 'Denoting the nature of another thing' — because the word 'vapus' (body) denotes the meaning of 'body/form.' Here, however, when the <s>upamāna</s> (standard of comparison) is transformed into the form of the <s>upameya</s>, it would be <s>pariṇāma-alaṅkāra</s> (transformation). But here, since the falling of <s>Madana</s> (Love) burnt by <s>Śarva</s> (<s>Śiva</s>) serves as the inferential indicator through bristling of body-hair...

children.text: tayā gṛhītaṃ nu mṛgāṅganābhyastato gṛhītaṃ nu mṛgāṅganābhiḥ' //
children.translated_text: Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 21c: And from the word 'ādi' (etc.), unreality is sometimes conveyed through the instrumental case as well. For example: 'O creeper, abandon this dealing with my hands! O dearest, do not commit such an audacity — the servant is your life-breath! These trees, made to grow by you with flowers, now weeping, grasp as if taking scissors, under the pretext of the bee-swarm, to cut the noose.' Here, 'with flowers' in the instrumental case...

Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 21: 'Of the object' etc. — 'Of another thing' — this is a continuation from [the definition of] <s>bhrāntimān</s>. Therefore some, [arguing] that continuation by the 'leaping frog' method (<s>maṇḍūkapluti-nyāya</s>) is inappropriate, have rearranged the text so that <s>apahnutti</s> is defined right after <s>bhrāntimān</s> and <s>ullekha</s> after <s>atiśayokti</s> (hyperbole). But this is not correct. For <s>ullekha</s> being placed after <s>atiśayokti</s> in the text...

children.text:
atra vācyāyā nidarśanāyā upaskāratvenopameyopanā gamyate /
tāmantareṇāsaṃbhavadvastusaṃbandhatvena vācyasyāviśrānteḥ /
ataścātrālaṅkāro gamyamānaḥ sthito na vastumātram /
tena pūrvatra yadādigrahaṇaṃ saphalayitumanyairetadudāhṛtaṃ tadayuktameva /
tatra vastumātrasya vācyopaskārakatvena pratipipādayiṣitatvāt /
vācyopaskārakatvenotprekṣā kathitetisamanvayaḥ /

children.translated_text: <s>Sūtra</s> 22: Having thus defined the <s>alaṅkāras</s> that contain superimposition under the predominance of identity, he now defines those that contain <s>adhyavasāya</s> (determinate cognition) — Therein, when <s>adhyavasāya</s> predominates in the operation, it is <s>utprekṣā</s> (poetic fancy). // <s>RuAss</s>_22 // <s>Adhyavasāya</s> (determinate cognition) is the cognition of identity through the absorption of the object into the superimposed entity.

Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 22: 'Containing superimposition' — here, since the quality of containing <s>adhyavasāya</s> is also present, the designation [as 'superimposition-based'] is made because of the predominance of the superimposition aspect, just as in the case of a wrestler's village (<s>mallagrāma</s>). Therein, first he defines <s>utprekṣā</s> — with '<s>adhyavasāya</s>' etc.

children.text: diahaṃ aṇaṇṇaammā aṅgaṃ taṇuaṃ pi taṇuei' //
children.translated_text: Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 22a: '<s>Adhyavasāya</s>' — and not '<s>saṃdeha</s>' (doubt). For here, cognitions are of two kinds: those of the nature of certainty and those of uncertainty. And certainty is that which does not deviate from its object — the distinction between correct, incorrect, and otherwise does not concern us here, since only the mode of cognition is being examined. And this [analysis] is useful for the investigation of validity. Uncertainty, on the other hand, takes the form of doubt and <s>tarka</s> (hypothetical reasoning)...
Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 21d: Concluding this, he introduces another topic — 'thus' etc.

Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 22b: Even so, since <s>utprekṣā</s> is rooted in the <s>saṃbhāvanā</s> (conjecture) — a cognition of uncertainty — how can it be rooted in <s>adhyavasāya</s>? For <s>adhyavasāya</s>'s nature is the absorption of the object and the certainty regarding the superimposed. And neither of these is possible here — since the object is not abandoned and there is no certainty. To this we reply: here <s>adhyavasāya</s> is of two kinds — spontaneous and produced. In the spontaneous kind, without abandoning the object...

And this [<s>utprekṣā</s>] is twofold: that which is to be established (<s>sādhya</s>) and that which is already established (<s>siddha</s>). The 'to be established' is where there is a cognition of the non-reality of the superimposed entity. Non-reality means: when a property of the superimposed entity is perceived as grounded in the object — through the possibility of belonging to the superimposed or the impossibility of belonging to the object. The property has the form of quality, action, or substance; and in the cognition of its possibility or impossibility...

Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 22/1: He explains this very point with 'of the object' etc. 'Cognition of identity' means: through the absorption of the object. Even though the <s>sādhya-adhyavasāya</s> (to-be-established determinate cognition) is of the nature of a conjectural cognition, to show its distinction from the standpoint of reality, he says 'to be established' etc. Through the purification of the object, since the conjectural cognition supports the means of valid knowledge, 'one must be this person'...

Now this [<s>utprekṣā</s>] is illustrated in outline. Therein, <s>utprekṣā</s> of genus is as follows: 'May that moon protect you — curved like the tip of a fresh lotus stalk, placed upon the head of the enemy of <s>Smara</s> (<s>Śiva</s>), glowing tawny with fire, as if it were a sprout released from a skull white as crystal, watered daily by the flowing waters of the <s>Mandākinī</s> (Ganges).' Here, since the word 'sprout' (<s>aṅkura</s>) is a genus-term, the <s>utprekṣā</s> pertains to genus...

Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 22/2: 'Now' means: the occasion having arrived. 'In outline' — by this the non-exhaustiveness of the genus-divisions etc. is implied. 'By virtue of being associated with darkness' — meaning: through the absorption of properties such as the pervading nature of darkness etc. For here, the property-bearer darkness, having its identity as one property-bearer absorbed, is established as another property-bearer — as we shall explain further. '<s>Dravyotprekṣā</s>' (substance-fancy) — the substance's own...

children.text:
adhunā rasasyāpi vācyopaskārakatvaṃ darśayitumāha-rasavadityādi /
prabhṛtiśabdādūrjasvyādayaḥ /
ādiśabdācca tadābhāsādayaḥ /

children.translated_text: Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 22/3: 'To be inferred' means: this is an example of imagining absence. 'Of the mention of the cause' — because the curvature and the attainment of emaciation are directly stated. 'Without mention' — because the cause, being a concealer etc., is only implied. 'In the other varieties' — in those pertaining to essence, result, etc. 'Should be understood' — because it is implied. Therein, <s>utprekṣā</s> of essence, for example: 'At the meeting with the <s>Malaya</s> breeze...'

children.text: 'kṛcchreṇoruyugaṃ vyatītya suciraṃ bhrāntvā nitambasthale madhye 'syāstrivalītaraṅgaviṣame nispandatāmāgatā /
children.translated_text: Based on <s>śliṣṭa</s> (double-meaning) words as cause, for example: 'He who is celebrated on earth as a renunciant due to his unparalleled nature — truly he became an extraordinary ground for the arrows of <s>Smara</s> (Love), preceded by the ego.' Here the word '<s>mārgaṇa</s>' is a <s>śliṣṭa</s> word in relation to the property — [meaning both 'arrow' and 'seeking'].

children.text: maddṛśṭistṛṣiteva saṃprati śanairāruhya tuṅgau stanau sākāṅkṣaṃ muhurīkṣate jalalavaprasyandinī locane' //
children.translated_text: Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 22/4: '<s>Śliṣṭa</s>' — because it denotes both 'arrow' and 'seeker.'

In the imagining of absence, for example: 'Alas, her cheek-surfaces, having become thus, as if unable to see each other, have attained such emaciation!' Here 'as if unable to see' is the imagining of the absence of an action. The same should be applied to genus etc. as well. The quality being the cause, for example — the curvature in the previously cited 'curved like the tip of a fresh lotus stalk.' The action [being the cause], for example: 'such emaciation...'

children.text:
atra vatsarājasya parasparāsthābandharūpo ratyākhyaḥ sthāyibhāvo vibhāvānubhāvavyabhicārisaṃyogād rasībhūtaḥ san vācyopaskārakaḥ /
tatsaṃvalitatvena vācyasya sacamatkāra pratipatteḥ /
children.translated_text: <s>Utprekṣā</s> beginning with <s>upamā</s> (simile-initiated fancy), for example: 'On the forehead-surface of the goddess's lotus-face they act as musk-<s>tilaka</s>; on the <s>tamāla</s>-tree young buds they crown the head; at the ear they are blooming blue lotuses; and on the bosom they are dark <s>aguru</s> (aloe) — may those ornaments of <s>Śrīkaṇṭha</s>'s (<s>Śiva</s>'s) throat bestow auspiciousness upon you!' Here, although the <s>kvip</s> suffix is applied to every nominal stem by the rule '<s>sarvaprātipadikebhyaḥ kkip</s>'...

Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 22/5: 'At the outset' — not at the conclusion. 'The cognition of <s>upamā</s>' — because the <s>kvip</s> suffix is employed precisely for that purpose. Therefore one should not say that there is no <s>utprekṣā</s> here due to the absence of an explicit marker. For the mere possibility or impossibility of an explicit marker alone is not the determining factor for the presence or absence of <s>alaṅkāras</s>. For thus, in <s>vyājastuti</s> (ironic praise), even though censure etc. is expressed, the implied praise is the <s>alaṅkāra</s>...

<s>Utprekṣā</s> containing <s>apahnava</s> (concealment), for example: 'When the city-women hastily went to the bank due to the striking of the <s>timi</s> fish, the <s>Siprā</s> river shines as if giving a great peal of laughter, under the pretext of its foaming waves.' Here, by the force of the word 'iva' (as if), there is conjecture, and from the use of the word 'chala' (pretext), concealment is understood. The same should be understood with the use of words like '<s>chadma</s>' (disguise) etc. In expressions like 'another <s>Pākaśāsana</s> (<s>Indra</s>) as it were'...

children.text: 'tiṣṭhotkopavaśātprabhāvapihitā dīrghaṃ na sā kupyati svargāyotpatitā bhavenmayi punarbhāvārdramasyā manaḥ /
children.translated_text: Commentary on <s>RuAss</s> 22/6: With the use of the word '<s>chadma</s>' (disguise), for example: 'Your bosom shines, with the pretext of drops of perspiration, as if <s>Smara</s> (Love) has offered <s>arghya</s> (ritual offering) to the priceless [beauty].' And to show the distinction of this [figure] from other <s>alaṅkāras</s> through the difference in cognition arising from the use or non-use of such words, he says 'another' etc. 'With that use' means: with the use of the word 'apara' (another). Since the word 'iva' conveys conjecture...

children.text: tāṃ hartuṃ vivudhadviṣo 'pi na ca me śaktāḥ purovartinīṃ sā cātyantamagocaraṃ nayanayoryāteti ko 'yaṃ vidhiḥ' //
children.translated_text: 'But even the foes of the gods are not able to carry her off as she stands before me — and yet she has passed utterly beyond the range of my two eyes: what manner of ordinance is this?' //
Here, the <s>vyabhicāribhāva</s> (transitory emotion) called <s>vitarka</s> (deliberation) serves only to enhance the beauty of the <s>vācya</s> (literal meaning).
[Section marker: RuAssC_[Bhū.1g]]
An example of a vigorous <s>alaṅkāra</s> (ornament):

children.text: 'haglīlāsu sakautukaṃ yadi manastanme dṛśāṃ viṃśati- rniḥsaṃdhau parirambhaṇe ratiratho dormaṇḍalī dṛśyatām /
children.translated_text: 'If in amorous play your mind eagerly approaches the range of my glances, then in an uninterrupted embrace where <s>Rati</s>'s chariot is love, let the circle of arms be displayed; if there is delight in kissing, O <s>Vaidehī</s>! The ten-faced one stands ready before you — behold the great difference in conduct between the son of <s>Paulastya</s> and the son of <s>Raghu</s>!'

children.text: prītiścetparicumbane daśamukhī vaidehi!sajjā puraḥ paulastyasya ca rāghavasya ca mahatpaśyopacārāntaram' //
children.translated_text: Here, <s>Rāvaṇa</s>'s erotic sentiment (<s>rati</s>) directed toward <s>Sītā</s>, proceeding through impropriety, constitutes <s>rasābhāsa</s> (semblance of rasa) that serves to embellish the <s>vācya</s> (literal meaning). The rest should be inferred by the reader.

children.text:
atra sītāṃ prati rāvaṇasya ratiranocityena pravṛtteti rasābhāso vācyopaskārakaḥ /
anyattu svayamabhyūhyam /
children.translated_text: Here, <s>Rāvaṇa</s>'s erotic sentiment (<s>rati</s>) toward <s>Sītā</s>, proceeding through impropriety, constitutes <s>rasābhāsa</s> (semblance of <s>rasa</s>) that serves to embellish the <s>vācya</s> (literal meaning). The rest is to be inferred by the reader.
[Section marker: RuAssC_[Bhū.1h]]

children.text:
etadevopasaṃharati-taditthamityādinā /
trividhamiti /
paryāyoktādau vastu, rūpakādāvalaṅkāraḥ, rasavadādau rasaḥ /
tadevaṃ cirantanaiḥ pratīyamānasyālaṅkārāntarbhāva eva tāvaduktaḥ /
tadupaskāryaḥ punarātmā kaiścidapi nābhyupagataḥ /
children.translated_text: He concludes this very point with 'tad ittham' etc. 'Threefold' means: in <s>paryāyokti</s> (circumlocution) etc. it is subject matter (<s>vastu</s>), in <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor) etc. it is <s>alaṅkāra</s> (ornament), and in <s>rasavat</s> etc. it is <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic emotion). Thus, the ancient scholars have stated the subsumption of the <s>pratīyamāna</s> (suggested meaning) within <s>alaṅkāra</s>. However, the essential nature (<s>ātman</s>) that is to be embellished by it has not been acknowledged by anyone.

children.text:
vāmanena tu sādṛśyanibandhanāyā lakṣaṇāya vakroktyalaṅkāratvaṃ bruvatā kaściddhvanibhedo 'laṅkāratayaivoktaḥ /
kevalaṃ guṇaviśiṣṭapadaracanātmikā rītiḥ kāvyātmakatvenoktā /
udbhaṭādibhistu guṇālaṅkārāṇāṃ prāyaśaḥ sāmyameva sūcitam /
viṣayamātreṇa bhedapratipādanāt /
saṃghaṭanādharmatvena ceṣṭeḥ /
tadevamalaṅkārā eva kāvye pradhānamiti prācyānāṃ matam / [RuAss_Bhū.2]
children.translated_text: By <s>Vāmana</s>, however, in declaring that <s>vakrokti</s> (oblique expression) — which is <s>lakṣaṇā</s> (secondary signification) based on similarity — is a type of <s>alaṅkāra</s>, a certain variety of <s>dhvani</s> (suggestion) was effectively classified as <s>alaṅkāra</s>. Only <s>rīti</s> (style), whose nature is a composition of words distinguished by <s>guṇas</s> (literary qualities), was declared to be the soul of poetry. By <s>Udbhaṭa</s> and others, however, the essential equivalence of <s>guṇas</s> and <s>alaṅkāras</s> was for the most part indicated — since distinction was established merely on the basis of subject matter, and because both were held to be properties of composition (<s>saṃghaṭanā</s>). Thus, the view of the ancients is that <s>alaṅkāras</s> alone are the principal element in poetry.
[Section marker: RuAssC_[Bhū.2]]

children.text:
vāmanena pratīyamānasyālaṅkārāntarbhāvamabhidadhatāpi tadupaskāryaṃ ātmā kaścidukta ityāha-vāmanenetyādi /
tuśabdaḥ pūrvebhyo vyatirekadyotakaḥ /
ātmano 'pi pratipādakatvāt /
bruvateti /
yadāha-'sādṛśyāllakṣaṇā vakroktiḥ' iti /
etadevodājahāra ca 'unmīmīlakamalaṃ sarasīnāṃ kairavaṃ ca nimimīla mugurtam' iti /
kaściddhvanibheda iti /
'avivakṣitavācyādiḥ' /
kevalamiti /
yadi paramityarthaḥ /
gumeti /
yadāha-'viśiṣṭā padaracanā rītiḥ' iti /
kāvyātmakatveneti /
yadāha-'rītirātmā kāvyasye'ti kāvyatvebhyupagatāyā rīteḥ 'tadatiśayahetavastvalaṅkārāḥ' ityādyuktyāntarbhāvitadhvanayo 'laṃṅkārā upaskārakā ityetanmatam /
children.translated_text: Even though <s>Vāmana</s> stated the subsumption of the <s>pratīyamāna</s> (suggested meaning) within <s>alaṅkāra</s>, he also posited a certain essential nature (<s>ātman</s>) to be embellished by it — this is stated with 'Vāmanena' etc. The word 'tu' indicates contrast with the previous thinkers, because he also establishes an essential nature (<s>ātman</s>). 'Bruvatā' refers to his statement: '<s>lakṣaṇā</s> based on similarity is <s>vakrokti</s>.' And he cited this very example: 'The lotus of the lake has bloomed, and the night-lily has closed for a moment.' 'A certain variety of <s>dhvani</s>' means the type beginning with <s>avivakṣitavācya</s> (unintended literal meaning). 'Kevalam' means 'however.' 'Guṇa' refers to his statement: '<s>Rīti</s> is a distinguished composition of words.' 'As the soul of poetry' refers to his statement '<s>Rīti</s> is the soul of poetry' — the view being that <s>rīti</s>, accepted as the essence of poetry, subsumes <s>dhvani</s> within <s>alaṅkāras</s> through the reasoning 'those that cause its excellence are <s>alaṅkāras</s>,' making them subsidiary.
[Section marker: RuAssC_[Bhū.2a]]

children.text:
anyaiḥ punaretadapi pratyuktamityāha-udbhaṭādibhirityādinā /
prāyaśa iti /
bāhulyenetyarthaḥ /
viṣayamātreṇeti /
bhinnakakṣyāṇāṃ hyupaskāryopaskārakatvasyānupapatteḥ /
tathātve cālaṅkārāmapi guṇopaskāryatvaṃ prasajyate /
samānanyāyatvāt /
tadguṇālaṅkārāṇāṃ tulyatvavādina evaudbhaṭāḥ /
itthamanena vācyāśrayāṇāmalaṅkārāṇāṃ madhya eva dhvanerantarbhāvādibhidhāvyāpāragocara eva dhvaniḥ, na punastadvyatiriktaḥ kaściddhvanirnāmeticirantanānāṃ matamityuktam /
idānīṃ yadapyanyairasya bhaktyantarbhūtatvamuktaṃ tadapi darśayitumāha-vakroktītyādi /
children.translated_text: Others have refuted even this — he states with '<s>Udbhaṭa</s> etc.' 'Prāyaśaḥ' means 'for the most part.' 'Viṣayamātreṇa' — because the relation of embellisher and embellished is untenable for things of different ranks; and if such a relation were accepted, even <s>alaṅkāras</s> would be subject to embellishment by <s>guṇas</s>, since the same principle would apply. Therefore, the followers of <s>Udbhaṭa</s> maintain the equality of <s>guṇas</s> and <s>alaṅkāras</s>. Thus it has been stated that the view of the ancients is that <s>dhvani</s> is subsumed within the <s>alaṅkāras</s> that reside in the <s>vācya</s> (literal meaning), and that <s>dhvani</s> falls within the scope of the <s>abhidhā</s> (denotative) function alone — there is no separate entity called <s>dhvani</s> beyond it. Now, to show what others have said about its subsumption within <s>bhakti</s> (figurative usage), he states 'vakrokti' etc.

children.text:
vakroktijīvitakāraḥ punarvaidagdhyabhaṅgībhaṇitisvabhāvāṃ bahuvidhāṃ vakroktimevaprādhānyātkāvyajīvitamuktavān /
vyāpārasya prādhānyaṃ ca [kāvyasya] pratipede /
abhidhānaprakāraviśeṣā eva cālaṅkārāḥ /
satyapi tribhede pratīyamāne vyāpārarūpā bhaṇitireva kavisaṃrambhagocaraḥ /
upacāravakratādibhiḥ samasto dhvaniprapañcaḥ svīkṛtaḥ /
kevalamuktivaicitryajīvitaṃ kāvyaṃ, na vyaṅgyārthajīvitamiti tadīyaṃ darśanaṃ vyavasthitam / [RuAss_Bhū.3]
children.translated_text: The <s>Vakroktijīvitakāra</s> (<s>Kuntaka</s>), on the other hand, declared <s>vakrokti</s> (oblique expression) — which is multifarious and whose nature is the articulation of a mode of poetic ingenuity (<s>vaidagdhya</s>) — to be principally the life-force of poetry. And he maintained the primacy of the poetic activity (<s>vyāpāra</s>). <s>Alaṅkāras</s> are merely particular modes of expression (<s>abhidhānaprakāra</s>). Even though the <s>pratīyamāna</s> (suggested meaning) is of three kinds, it is the mode of expression (<s>bhaṇiti</s>) in the form of poetic activity that is the object of the poet's creative effort. Through figurative obliquity (<s>upacāravakratā</s>) and other such devices, the entire expanse of <s>dhvani</s> (suggestion) has been appropriated. The established view of <s>Kuntaka</s> is simply that poetry lives by the charm of expression (<s>uktivaicitrya</s>), not by the suggested meaning (<s>vyaṅgyārtha</s>).
[Section marker: RuAssC_[Bhū.3]]

children.text:
vaidagdhyetyanena vakrokteḥ svarūpamuktam /
yadāha-'vakroktireva vaidagdhyabhaṅgībhaṇitirucyat' iti /
evakāro 'nyasya kāvyajīvitatvavyavacchedakaḥ /
kāvyajīvitamiti kāvyasyānuprāṇakam /
tāṃ vinā kāvyameva na syādityarthaḥ /
yadāha-vicitro yatra vakroktivaicitryaṃ jīvitāyate'iti /
vyāpārasyeti kavipratibhollikhitasya karmaṇaḥ /
kavipratibhānirvartitatvamantareṇa hi vakroktireva na syāditi kasya jīvitatvaṃ ghaṭata iti tadanuṣaktamevānvāsyātra prādhānyaṃ vivakṣitam /
ataśca dvayoḥ prādhānyasya duryojatvamatra nāśaṅkanīyam /
children.translated_text: By the word '<s>vaidagdhya</s>' (ingenuity), the essential nature of <s>vakrokti</s> is stated.
