As he says: '<s>Vakrokti</s> alone is called the articulation of the mode of ingenuity.' The word 'eva' (alone) excludes anything else from being the life-force of poetry. 'The life of poetry' means that which animates poetry — without it, poetry itself would not exist. As he says: 'Where the charm of <s>vakrokti</s> constitutes its varied life-force.' '<s>Vyāpāra</s>' refers to the creative activity delineated by the poet's genius. For without being produced by poetic genius, <s>vakrokti</s> itself would not exist — so how could it be the life-force of anything? Thus the primacy of poetic activity is intended as inseparably connected to it. Therefore, no objection should be raised about the difficulty of establishing primacy for both simultaneously.
[Section marker: RuAssC_[Bhū.3a]]

children.text:
alaṅkārā iti /
tenokta iti śeṣaḥ /
evakāraścirantanoktadhvaniprakāraviśeṣanyavacchedakaḥ /
satyapīti /
sadapi pratīyamānamanādṛtyetyarthaḥ /
vyāpārarūpeti vakrasvabhāvetyarthaḥ /
bhaṇitirityuktiḥ kavīti /
tatraiva kaviḥ saṃrabdha ityarthaḥ /
tatsaṃrambhamantareṇa hi vakroktireva na cāretyādi /
upacāravakratādīnāmeva madhye dhvanirantarbhūta iti tātparyārthaḥ /

children.translated_text: As he says:
'Where similarity is figuratively applied to something far removed from it,
Even to a slight degree it can produce a somewhat elevated mode of expression.'

'<s>Alaṅkāras</s>' — the supplement is 'as stated by him.' The word 'eva' excludes the particular varieties of <s>dhvani</s> as stated by the ancients. 'Satyapi' means 'even though the <s>pratīyamāna</s> (suggested meaning) exists, disregarding it.' '<s>Vyāpārarūpa</s>' means 'having the nature of obliquity.' '<s>Bhaṇiti</s>' means 'expression.' '<s>Kavi</s>' means the poet alone is engaged in that. For without that engagement, <s>vakrokti</s> would not function, etc. The purport is that <s>dhvani</s> is subsumed within the devices of figurative obliquity (<s>upacāravakratā</s>) and the like.
'The ornamentation such as <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor) etc., which is rooted in spirited delineation,
Is regarded as a certain kind of obliquity (<s>vakratā</s>) in which figurative usage (<s>upacāra</s>) predominates.'
And he cited this very example:
'The sky with its intoxicated clouds, the forests with their <s>Arjuna</s> trees tossed by rain-showers,
The prideless moon — the dark blue nights captivate.'
Thus.
('The sky with its intoxicated clouds, the forests with their <s>Arjuna</s> trees tossed by rain-showers,
The prideless moon — the dark blue nights captivate.')

children.text:
atra madanirahaṅkāratve aupacārike ityupacāravakratā /
ādipadena kriyāvakratādīnāmapi grahaṇam /
evaṃ sarvo 'pi dhvaniprapañco vakroktibhireva svīkṛtaḥ sansthita eva /
yadi paraṃ tasya prādhānyameva nāstītyāha-kavelamityādi /
tadīyamiti /
vakroktijīvitakārasaṃbandhītyarthaḥ /
taditthaṃ lakṣaṇāmūlavakroktimadhyāntarbhāvāddhvanereva tattvaṃ pratipāditam /
children.translated_text: Here, the figurative attribution of intoxication and pridelessness constitutes <s>upacāravakratā</s> (figurative obliquity). By the word 'ādi' (etc.), <s>kriyāvakratā</s> (obliquity of action) and other types are also included. Thus the entire range of <s>dhvani</s> has been appropriated by the various forms of <s>vakrokti</s>. However, it simply does not have primacy — he states 'kevalam' etc. '<s>Tadīya</s>' means 'belonging to the <s>Vakroktijīvitakāra</s> (<s>Kuntaka</s>).' Thus, since <s>dhvani</s> is subsumed within <s>vakrokti</s>, which is rooted in <s>lakṣaṇā</s> (secondary signification), the true nature of <s>dhvani</s> has been demonstrated.
[Section marker: RuAssC_[Bhū.3b]]
By some, it has been said that <s>dhvani</s> is beyond the reach of language and therefore cannot be defined — he states this with '<s>Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka</s>' etc.

children.text:
bhaṭṭanāyakena tu vyaṅgyavyāpārasya prauḍhoktyābhyupagatasya kāvyaṃśatvaṃ bruvatā nyagbhāvitaśabdārthasvarūpasya vyāpārasyaiva prādhānyamuktam /
tatrāpyabhidhābhāvakatvalakṣaṇavyāpāradvayottīrṇo rasacarvaṇātmā bhogāparaparyāyovyāpāraḥ prādhānyena viśrāntisthānatayāṅgīkṛtaḥ / [RuAss_Bhū.4]
children.translated_text: <s>Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka</s>, however, while declaring the status of the <s>vyaṅgya</s> (suggestive) function — accepted through bold assertion (<s>prauḍhokti</s>) — as a component of poetry, affirmed the primacy of the poetic activity (<s>vyāpāra</s>) whose nature as word-and-meaning has been subordinated. Within that framework too, a function called <s>bhoga</s> (aesthetic enjoyment), synonymous with <s>rasacarvaṇā</s> (savoring of rasa), which transcends the two functions of <s>abhidhā</s> (denotation) and <s>bhāvanā</s> (actualization), was principally accepted as the ultimate resting place.
[Section marker: RuAssC_[Bhū.4]]

children.text:
prauḍhoktyeti /
na punarlakṣaṇakaraṇena /
ata evokteḥ prauḍhatvaṃ yallakṣayitumaśakyaistasyāpyabhyupagamaḥ /
kāvyāṃśatvamiti na punaḥ kāvyātmatvam /

children.translated_text: As he says:
'<s>Dhvani</s>, which is another function whose nature is <s>vyañjana</s> (suggestion),

children.text: tasya siddhe 'pi bhede syātkāvyāṃśatvaṃ na rūpitā' //
children.translated_text: Even though its distinctness is established, its status as a component of poetry is affirmed, not its being the essential form.'

'By bold assertion (<s>prauḍhokti</s>)' — not by means of <s>lakṣaṇā</s> (secondary signification). Hence the boldness of the assertion lies in the acceptance even of that which cannot be defined. 'As a component of poetry' — not as the soul of poetry.

children.text:
iti /
vyāpārasyeti /
kavikarmaṇaḥ /
anyathā śabdapradhānebhyo vedādibhyor'thapradhānebhyaścetihāsādibhyaḥ kāvyasya vailakṣaṇyaṃ na syāt /

children.translated_text: As it has been stated:
'Based on the predominance of words, they regard <s>Śāstra</s> (scripture) as separate;
That which is endowed with the truth of meaning, they call <s>Ākhyāna</s> (narrative) among these two.

Thus. '<s>Vyāpāra</s>' means the creative activity of the poet. Otherwise, there would be no distinction of poetry from the <s>Vedas</s> and other texts where words predominate, or from <s>Itihāsas</s> and other texts where meaning predominates.
When both are subordinate and the poetic activity (<s>vyāpāra</s>) predominates, the apprehension of poetry arises.'

children.text:
iti /
tatrāpīti /
kavikarmarūpasya vyāpārasya prādhānye satyapītyarthaḥ /
'abhidhā bhāvanā cānyā dadbhogīkṛtireva ca' iti kāvyaṃ tāvat tryaṃśaṃ tenoktam /

children.translated_text: And among these:
'<s>Abhidhā</s> (denotation) has the power of <s>tātparya</s> (intentional purport); <s>lakṣaṇā</s> (secondary signification) and <s>anumiti</s> (inference) are twofold;
<s>Arthāpatti</s> (presumption) is sometimes the governing principle; <s>samāsokti</s> (condensed expression) and other <s>alaṅkāras</s> belong here.'

Thus. 'Tatrāpi' — even when the primacy of the poetic activity, which is the creative work of the poet, is accepted. He stated that poetry has three components through the formulation: '<s>Abhidhā</s> (denotation), <s>Bhāvanā</s> (actualization), and also <s>Bhogīkṛti</s> (aesthetic enjoyment).'
'The effect-nature of <s>rasa</s>, the varieties, the refutation of other functions —
Thus twelve are the established points of controversy regarding this <s>dhvani</s>.'

children.text:
iti /
nītyā bahavo vipratipattiprakārāḥ saṃbhavanti, tathāpi
'kāvyasyātmā dhvaniriti budhairyaḥ samāmnātapūrva- stasyābhāvaṃ jagadurapare bhāktamāhustamanye /
kecidvācāṃ sthitamaviṣaye tattvamūcustadīyam'- ityuktanītyaiva dhvanervipratipattiprakārannayamiha prādhānyenoktam /
children.translated_text: Thus. By this method, many types of controversy are possible; nevertheless, as stated in the verse: 'That which the wise have traditionally proclaimed as <s>dhvani</s>, the soul of poetry — some have declared its non-existence, others have called it figurative (<s>bhākta</s>), and some have said its true nature lies beyond the reach of words' — it is in accordance with this very formulation that the types of controversy regarding <s>dhvani</s> are principally stated here.
[Section marker: RuAssC_[Bhū.4a]]

children.text: evamidānīmetadvipratipattiprakāratrayaṃ nirākurvan dhvanereva kāvyātmatvaṃ sādhayati- dhvanikāra ityādinā /
children.translated_text: Now, refuting this threefold controversy, he establishes that <s>dhvani</s> alone is the soul of poetry — with '<s>Dhvanikāra</s>' etc.

children.text:
dhvanikāraḥ punarabhidhātātparyalakṣaṇākhyavyāpāratrayottīrṇasya dhvananadyotanādiśabdābhidheyasya vyañjanavyāpārasyāvaśyābhyupagamyatvād vyāpārasya ca vākyārthatvābhāvād vākyārthasyaiva ca vyāṅgyarūpasya guṇālaṅkāropaskartavyatvena prādhānyād viśrāntidhāmatvādātmatvaṃ sidhdāntitavān /
vyāpārasya viṣayamukhena svaruṇpratilambhāt tatprādhānyena prādhānyāt svarūpeṇa vicāryatvābhāvād viṣayasyaiva samagrabharasahiṣṇutvam /
tasmād viṣaya eva vyaṅgyanāmā jīvitatvena vaktavyaḥ,yasya guṇālaṅkārakṛtacārutvaparigrahasābhrājyam /
rasādayastu jīvitabhūtā nālaṅkāratvenavācyāḥ /
alaṅkārāṇāmupaskārakatvād,rasādīnāṃ ca prādhānyenopaskāryatvāt /
tasmād vyaṅgya eva vākyārthībhūtaḥ kāvyajīvitamityeṣa eva pakṣo vākyārthavidāṃ sahṛdayānāmāvarjakaḥ /
vyañjanavyāpārasya sarvairanapahnutatvāt tadāśrayeṇa ca pakṣāntarasyāpratiṣṭānāt / [RuAss_Bhū.5]
children.translated_text: The <s>Dhvanikāra</s> (<s>Ānandavardhana</s>), for his part, established <s>dhvani</s> as the soul of poetry on the following grounds: the <s>vyañjana</s> (suggestive) function — which transcends the three functions called <s>abhidhā</s> (denotation), <s>tātparya</s> (intentional purport), and <s>lakṣaṇā</s> (secondary signification), and which is denoted by terms such as <s>dhvanana</s> (resonance) and <s>dyotana</s> (illumination) — must necessarily be accepted; and the poetic activity (<s>vyāpāra</s>) does not have the status of sentence-meaning (<s>vākyārtha</s>); and the <s>vyaṅgya</s> (suggested content) itself, which has the form of sentence-meaning, has primacy because it is that which is to be embellished by <s>guṇas</s> and <s>alaṅkāras</s>, and because it is the ultimate resting place. Since the poetic activity obtains its own form through its object, and since by virtue of the primacy of the object its own form need not be independently examined, it is the object alone that bears the entire weight. Therefore, the object alone, called <s>vyaṅgya</s> (the suggested), is to be declared the life-force of poetry — it shines resplendent through its embrace of the beauty created by <s>guṇas</s> and <s>alaṅkāras</s>. And <s>rasa</s> and the like, which constitute this life-force, should not be classified as <s>alaṅkāras</s> — because <s>alaṅkāras</s> are embellishers, while <s>rasa</s> and the like are principally that which is to be embellished. Therefore, the <s>vyaṅgya</s> alone, having become the sentence-meaning, is the life of poetry — this is the very position that wins over the connoisseurs (<s>sahṛdayas</s>) who understand sentence-meaning. For the <s>vyañjana</s> function is denied by no one, and any alternative position founded upon it lacks firm establishment.
[Section marker: RuAssC_[Bhū.5]]

children.text:
samayāpekṣārthāvagamaśaktirabhidhā /
sāmānyānāṃ parasparānvitatvena viśeṣārthāvabodhanaśaktistātparyam /
mukhyārthabādhādisahakāryapekṣārthaṃpratibhāsanaśaktirlakṣaṇā /
etadvyāpāratrayāduttūrṇasya tadatiriktasyetyarthaḥ /
tathā ca 'gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ' ityatra gaṅgāśabdo ghoṣaśabdaśca sāmānyātmake jalapravāhe gṛhanikurambe ca saṃketitau /
sāmānya evodyogāt /
viśeṣasya hi saṃketakaraṇe ānantyaṃ vyabhicāraśca syāt /
tataścābhidhayā jalapravāhamātraṃ gṛhanikurambamātraṃ ca pratītimityekā kakṣyā /
etatpratipādyānyapratipādanāyāpyabhidhā na samarthā /

'viśeṣyaṃ nābhidhā gacchet kṣīṇaśatkirviśeṣaṃ gamayanti hi' iti nyāyāttātpraryaśaktyā sāmānyānyādhārādheyabhāvenāvasthitaṃ viśiṣṭaṃ gaṅgāghoṣādyāgūrayantīti tātparyeṇa parasparānvitatvamātrameva pratīyata iti dvitīyā /
children.translated_text: By the principle that '<s>abhidhā</s> does not reach the qualified; it is the qualifiers that convey the particular with diminished force' — through the power of <s>tātparya</s>, the general terms, situated in the relation of substrate and superstratum, intimate the qualified entity such as '<s>Gaṅgā</s>-<s>ghoṣa</s>' (the settlement on the Gaṅgā). Thus through <s>tātparya</s>, only the mutual connection is cognized — this is the second level.

children.text: jalapravāhasya ca ghoṣādhikaraṇatvamayuktamiti pramāṇāntarabādhitaḥ san gaṅgāśabdastadadhikaraṇayogyaṃ taṭaṃ lakṣayatīti tṛtīyā /
children.translated_text: And since it is inappropriate for a flow of water to be the locus of a cowherd settlement — being contradicted by other means of knowledge — the word '<s>Gaṅgā</s>' secondarily denotes the bank (<s>taṭa</s>), which is a suitable locus for it. This is the third level.
In this regard, 'When the primary meaning is obstructed, through connection with it, either by conventional usage or by purpose,

children.text: anyor'tho lakṣyate yat sā lakṣaṇā'ropitā kriyā' //
children.translated_text: Another meaning is indicated — that is <s>lakṣaṇā</s> (secondary signification), an imposed operation.'

<s>Abhidhā</s> (denotation) is the capacity for apprehending meaning that depends on convention (<s>samaya</s>). <s>Tātparya</s> (intentional purport) is the capacity for conveying particular meaning through the mutual connection of general terms. <s>Lakṣaṇā</s> (secondary signification) is the capacity for making meaning flash forth, dependent on auxiliaries such as the obstruction of the primary meaning. 'Transcending this triad of functions' means 'beyond and different from these.' Thus, in the example '<s>Gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ</s>' ('The cowherd settlement is on the <s>Gaṅgā</s>'), the word '<s>Gaṅgā</s>' and the word '<s>ghoṣa</s>' are conventionally established in their general senses as a flow of water and a cluster of houses respectively — because convention operates only with respect to the general. For if convention were applied to particulars, there would be infinite regress and deviation. Therefore, through <s>abhidhā</s>, only a flow of water and only a cluster of houses are cognized — this is the first level. <s>Abhidhā</s> is not capable of conveying anything beyond what it directly denotes.
Thus.

children.text:
nītyā lakṣaṇā tritayasaṃnidhāveva bhavati /
tatra mukhyārthabādhā tāvatpratyakṣādipramāṇāntaramūlā /
yaśca sāmīpyādisaṃbandhaḥ sa ca pramāṇāntarāvagamya eva /
yatpunaridaṃ ghoṣasya śettayapāvanatvādilakṣaṇaṃ prayojanaṃ pratīyate tacchabdāntarānuktaṃ pramāṇāntarāpratipannaṃ ca kuta āgatam /
na tāvatpratyakṣādeva tatpratītiḥ, asmādeva śabdādavagamāsiddheḥ /
śabdārthe ca tasyāpravṛtteḥ /
nāpyanumānāt /
sāmīpye 'pi śaityapāvanatvāderasaṃbhavādanaikāntikatvāt /
na smṛtiḥ /
tadanubhavābhāvāt /
satyamapi vā tasyāṃ niyamasmaraṇaṃ na syāt /
asmādeva ca śabdādetadeva budhyata iti ko hetuḥ /
tasmādasyaiva śabdasyaiṣa vyāpāro 'bhyupagantavyaḥ /
nirvyāpārasyārthapratītikāritvābhāvāt /
sa tāvannābhitmā /
samayābhāvāt /
na tātparyātmā /
tasyānvayapratītāveva parikṣayāt /
na lakṣaṇātmā /
mukhyārthabādhādyabhāvāt /
tasmādabhidhātātparyalakṣaṇāvyaktiriktaścaturthakakṣyānikṣitpo vyaṅgyaniṣṭovyañjanāvyapāro 'bhihitānvayavādināvaśyābhyupagantavyaḥ /
anvitābhidhānavādināpi yatparaḥ śabdaḥ sa śabdārtha iti śaravadabhidhāvyāpārameva dīrghadīrghamicchatāpi naimittikārthānusāreṇa nimittāni kalpyanta iti nimittaparikalpane 'pi samagraiveyaṃ prakriyānusāraṇīyevetyubhayathāpi siddha eva vyañjanavyāpāraḥ /
evacca gahanagahanamiti manageva siddharasanyāyenehoktam /
children.translated_text: By rule, <s>lakṣaṇā</s> (secondary signification) occurs only in the presence of the triad [of conditions]. Among these, the obstruction of the primary meaning (<s>mukhyārtha-bādhā</s>) is indeed rooted in other means of valid cognition such as perception and the like. And the relation of proximity and so forth is also to be ascertained through other means of valid cognition. But as for the purpose characterized by the coolness, purifying power, and the like of the cowherd settlement (<s>ghoṣa</s>) that is cognized — from where has it come, since it is not stated by any other word and not established by any other means of valid cognition? It is not cognized directly from perception alone, since cognition from this very word itself is unestablished. And because it [the purpose] does not apply to the literal meaning of the word. Nor is it from inference, since even with proximity, coolness, purifying power, and the like are not invariably present, making it inconclusive. It is not from memory either, since there is no prior experience of it. Or even if such memory were granted, there would be no recollection of an invariable connection. And what reason is there that precisely this is understood from this very word? Therefore, this must be accepted as the function (<s>vyāpāra</s>) of this very word, since without any function it cannot be the cause of cognition of meaning. Now, this [function] is not of the nature of <s>abhidhā</s> (denotation), due to the absence of convention. It is not of the nature of <s>tātparya</s> (purport), since that is exhausted in the cognition of syntactic connection alone. It is not of the nature of <s>lakṣaṇā</s> (secondary signification), due to the absence of obstruction of the primary meaning and the like. Therefore, a fourth level of function — distinct from <s>abhidhā</s>, <s>tātparya</s>, and <s>lakṣaṇā</s> — directed toward the suggested meaning (<s>vyaṅgya</s>), namely the function of <s>vyañjanā</s> (suggestion), must necessarily be accepted by the proponent of the <s>abhihitānvayavāda</s> (the doctrine that words first denote and then combine). Even for the proponent of <s>anvitābhidhānavāda</s> (the doctrine that words directly denote connected meanings), who wishes to extend the function of <s>abhidhā</s> further and further like an arrow, following the occasioned meaning, and who posits occasions — even with such positing of occasions, this entire procedure is to be followed in the same way. Thus, the function of <s>vyañjanā</s> is established on both accounts. And thus it has been stated here in a manner barely established, following the principle of hidden profundity.
<s>Ruyyaka's</s> commentary on <s>Alaṃkārasarvasva</s> [<s>Bhūmikā</s> 5a]:

children.text:
ādiśabdātpratyāyanāvagamanādīnāmapi grahaṇam /
avaśyeti /
tena vinā vyaṅgyasyārthattyāsaṃgrahaṇāt /
vyāpārasyeti /
vyañjanātmikāyāḥ kriyāyā ityarthaḥ /
sā khalu sādhyamānatvena pūrvāparībhūtāvayavatvānna svarūpeṇopalabhyata iti vicārapadavimeva svayamupāroḍhuṃ notsahata iti kathaṃ nāma tasyā vākyārthatvaṃ syāditi bhāvaḥ /
yad vakṣyati-'vyāpārasya viṣayamukhena svarūpapratilambhāt tatprādhānyena prādhānyātsvarūpeṇa vicāryatvābhāvād viṣayasyaiva samagrabharasahiṣṇutvam' iti /
upaskartavyatveneti /
tatparatayāvasyānenetvathaḥ /

children.translated_text: As has been stated —
'Of the various causes of beauty in the expressed meaning and the expressive words,
where there is subordination to <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic sentiment) and the like — that is considered the domain of <s>dhvani</s> (suggestion).'

By the word 'and so forth' (<s>ādi-śabda</s>), comprehension (<s>pratyāyana</s>), understanding (<s>avagamana</s>), and similar terms are also included. 'Necessarily' (<s>avaśya</s>) — because without it [the function of suggestion], the suggested meaning (<s>vyaṅgya</s>) would not be included within meaning at all. 'Of the function' (<s>vyāpārasya</s>) — meaning: of the activity that is of the nature of <s>vyañjanā</s> (suggestion). That [function] indeed, being something to be accomplished and having parts that are sequential, is not apprehended in its own form, and thus does not itself venture to mount the stage of inquiry — so how could it be the sentence-meaning? This is the purport. As will be stated: 'Since the function attains its own form only through the medium of its object, and since owing to the primacy of that [object], there is no possibility of examining [the function] in its own form, the object alone bears the entire weight.' 'As something to be supplemented' (<s>upaskartavyatvena</s>) — the meaning is that it necessarily has its purpose directed toward that [object].
Thus.

ata eva viśrāntidhāmatvādityuktum /
ātmatvamiti /
sārabhūtatvamityarthaḥ /

nahi nirjīvaṃ śarīraṃ kvāpyupayuktam /
nanu yadyevaṃ darhi 'gaṅgāyāṃ ghoṣaḥ' ityatrāpi vyaṅgyasya sadbhāvāt kāvyatvaṃ prasajyate /
naitat /
iha yadvadātmano vyāpakatvāccharīre ghaṭādau vartamānatve 'pi karaṇādiviśiṣṭe śarīre eva jīvavyavahāro na ghaṭādau, tadvadasyāpi vivadhaguṇālaṅkāraucityacāruśabdārthaśarīragatatvenaivātmatvavyavahāro nānyatreti na kaściddoṣaḥ /
nanu ca sarvatra kriyāyā eva prādhānyaṃ prasiddham,iha punarviṣayasyoktamiti kimetadityāśaṅkakyāha-vyāpārasyetyādi /
viṣayamukheneti /
yathā dyodanāderviklittyāmiti kimevadityāśaṅkāyāha-vyapārasyetyādi /
viṣayamukheneti /
yathā hyodanāderviklittyayayādimukhena pākādeḥ kriyāyāḥ svarūpopallambhaḥ /
tatprādhānyeneti /
viṣayapradhānatvenetyarthaḥ /
tena vyāpārasya prādhānyamupacaritamiti bhāvaḥ /
svarūpeṇoti /
svarūpaṃ hi tasya sādhyamānatvādi vicāravitumaśakyam /
sidhdasya hi vicārā bhavatīti bhāvaḥ /
evakāro vyañjanavyāpāravyavacchedakaḥ /

etadevopasaṃharati-tatsādityādinā /
yasyeti /
vyaṅgyanāmno rasāccāmano viṣayasya /
guṇālaṅkāra kṛta-rutveti /

children.translated_text: Of the <s>guṇas</s> (poetic qualities) —
'Of the various causes of beauty in the expressed meaning and the expressive words,
where there is subordination to <s>rasa</s> and the like — that is considered the domain of <s>dhvani</s>.'

For this very reason it has been said that it is 'the resting place' (<s>viśrāntidhāma</s>). 'Its being the soul' (<s>ātmatva</s>) — the meaning is: its being the essence. And therefore the purport is that without it, poetry would not be poetry at all. For a lifeless body is of no use anywhere. Now, if this is so, then even in 'the cowherd settlement is on the <s>Gaṅgā</s>,' the existence of a suggested meaning would entail poeticness — it is not so. Just as, although the <s>ātman</s> (soul) pervades everything and is present in the body, in a pot, and elsewhere, the designation 'living being' applies only to the body endowed with sense organs and the like, and not to a pot — similarly, the designation 'soul' applies to this [<s>dhvani</s>] only as residing in a body consisting of beautiful words and meanings adorned with various <s>guṇas</s> (qualities) and <s>alaṃkāras</s> (ornaments) and <s>aucitya</s> (propriety), and not elsewhere. So there is no defect. Now, it is well known everywhere that the activity itself has primacy, yet here the primacy of the object has been stated — what is this? Anticipating this objection, he says 'of the function' and so forth. 'Through the medium of the object' — just as the activity of cooking and the like is apprehended in its own form through the medium of the softening of rice and so forth. 'By the primacy of that' — meaning: by the primacy of the object. The implication is that the primacy of the function is figuratively attributed. 'In its own form' — for its own form, being something to be accomplished, cannot be examined. For inquiry pertains only to what is already established — this is the purport. The particle 'eva' serves to distinguish the function of <s>vyañjanā</s> [from others]. 'Entire' (<s>samagra</s>) — the meaning is the capacity to bear the entire weight, including the designation [as soul] and the like. He concludes this very point with 'therefore' and so forth. 'Of which' (<s>yasya</s>) — of the object, namely <s>rasa</s> and other [sentiments] designated as the suggested. 'Made by <s>guṇas</s> and <s>alaṃkāras</s>' —
Thus.

children.translated_text: Of the <s>guṇas</s> —
'Those qualities of <s>rasa</s> which are its limbs, like valor and the like of the self,
which are causes of its excellence and are of stable nature — those are called <s>guṇas</s> (poetic qualities).'

For this very reason it has been said 'because it is the resting place.' 'Its being the soul' — the meaning is: its being the essence. And therefore the purport is that without it, poetry would not be poetry at all. For a lifeless body is of no use anywhere. Now, if this is so, then even in 'the cowherd settlement is on the <s>Gaṅgā</s>,' the existence of the suggested meaning would entail poeticness — it is not so. Just as, although the soul pervades everything and is present in the body, in a pot, and elsewhere, the designation 'living being' applies only to the body endowed with sense organs and the like, not to a pot — similarly, the designation 'soul' applies to this [<s>dhvani</s>] only as residing in a body consisting of beautiful words and meanings adorned with various <s>guṇas</s>, <s>alaṃkāras</s>, and <s>aucitya</s>, and not elsewhere. So there is no defect. Now, it is well known everywhere that the activity itself has primacy, yet here the primacy of the object has been stated — what is this? Anticipating this objection, he says 'of the function' and so forth. 'Through the medium of the object' — just as the activity of cooking and the like is apprehended in its own form through the medium of the softening of rice and so forth. 'By the primacy of that' — meaning: by the primacy of the object. The implication is that the primacy of the function is figuratively attributed. 'In its own form' — for its own form, being something to be accomplished, cannot be examined. For inquiry pertains only to what is already established — this is the purport. The particle 'eva' serves to distinguish the function of <s>vyañjanā</s>. 'Entire' — the meaning is the capacity to bear the entire weight, including the designation and the like. He concludes this very point with 'therefore' and so forth. 'Of which' — of the object, namely <s>rasa</s> and other [sentiments] designated as the suggested. 'Made by <s>guṇas</s> and <s>alaṃkāras</s>' —
<s>Kāvyaprakāśa</s> 8
— by this rule, because they are directly properties of that [<s>rasa</s>].
And of the <s>alaṃkāras</s> (poetic ornaments) also —
'Let those that sometimes embellish the existing [<s>rasa</s>] through the medium of its limbs,
like necklaces and the like — those ornaments are <s>anuprāsa</s> (alliteration), <s>upamā</s> (simile), and the rest.'
<s>Kāvyaprakāśa</s> 8

children.text:
ityādinītyā śabdārthalakṣaṇāṅgātiśayadvāreṇa tadupaskārakatvāt /
alaṅkārāṇāṃ ca rasādirūpaṃ dhvañjyamarthamalaṅkurvatāṃ mukhyayā vṛttyālaṅkākaratvam,alaṅkāryasadbhāvanibandhanatvāt tasya, rasādyātmana eva ca vyaṅgyasyālaṅkāryatvena pratiṣṭhānāt /
ata eva ca yatrasphuṭavyaṅgyārtharahitatvaṃ tatra 'guṇavṛttyā punasteṣāṃ vṛttiḥ śabdārthayormatā'[kā.pra.8] ityādinītyā śabdārthamātranibandhanatvenoktivaicitryamātraparyavasitatvādeṣāṃ gauṇamalaṅkāratvam /
yadabhiprāyeṇaiva ca citrākhyakāvyabhedaprakāratvamalaṅkārāṇāṃ nirūpayiṣyate /
ata evānuprāsādayo 'laṅkārāścitrabhityādyanyairuktam /
sa ca pratīyamānor'tho yadyapi vastvalaṅkārarasatvena trividhaḥ, tathāpi [tena vinā kāvyātmatvābhāvāt] mukhyatvena rasatyaivātmatvaṃ yuktam /
ataśca vastvalaṅkārayokyadalaṅkārapakṣanikṣitpatvamanyairuktaṃ tattāvadāstām, kāvyātmano rasasya punaralaṅkāratvamatyantamevāvācyamityāha-rasādaya ityādi /
ādigrahaṇād bhāvatadābhāsādīnāṃ grahaṇam /
na vācyā iti /
vastumayuktā evetyarthaḥ /
alaṅkāryaṃsyālaṅkāratvānupapatteḥ /
tasya cālaṅkāratvakathane 'laṅkāryāntaraṃ prasajyate /
tena vinālaṅkārāṇāmanupapatteḥ /
etadevopasaṃharati-tasmādityādinā /
vyaṅgya iti rasādirūpaḥ /
tasyaivopakrāntatvāt /
vākyārthībhūta iti /
avākyārthībhūtastu rasādiralaṅkāro 'pi syāt /
children.translated_text: — by this rule, because they serve to embellish it through the excellence of limbs characterized as word and meaning. And for <s>alaṃkāras</s> that adorn the suggested meaning (<s>dhvañjya</s>) whose form is <s>rasa</s> and the like, their being ornaments in the primary sense obtains, since that [ornamentation] depends on the existence of something to be ornamented, and since it is the suggested meaning in the form of <s>rasa</s> and the like that is established as the thing to be ornamented (<s>alaṃkārya</s>). And for this very reason, where there is an absence of clearly manifest suggested meaning, there, by the rule 'their function with respect to word and meaning alone is through a secondary mode' [<s>Kāvyaprakāśa</s> 8], since they are dependent merely on word and meaning and culminate merely in novelty of expression — their status as ornaments is figurative (<s>gauṇa</s>). And it is with this very understanding that the status of <s>alaṃkāras</s> as a variety of the type of poetry called <s>citra</s> (pictorial) will be established. For this very reason, others have said that <s>anuprāsa</s> and other ornaments are of the <s>citra</s> type. And although the suggested meaning is threefold — as <s>vastu</s> (content), <s>alaṃkāra</s> (ornament), and <s>rasa</s> (sentiment) — nevertheless, since without it there is no status as the soul of poetry, the status of soul belongs primarily to <s>rasa</s> alone. Therefore, let the placement of <s>vastu</s> and <s>alaṃkāra</s> within the category of ornament, as stated by others, stand aside — the claim that <s>rasa</s>, the soul of poetry, is itself an ornament is utterly untenable — thus he says '<s>rasa</s> and the like' and so forth. By the word 'and the like' (<s>ādi</s>), <s>bhāva</s> (transient emotions), <s>bhāvābhāsa</s> (semblances of emotion), and the like are included. 'Not to be called' (<s>na vācyāḥ</s>) — meaning: they are simply not appropriate as things (<s>vastu</s>). Because it is impossible for that which is to be ornamented (<s>alaṃkārya</s>) to be itself an ornament. And if its being an ornament were asserted, another thing-to-be-ornamented would be entailed. And without that, the ornaments themselves would be impossible. He concludes this very point with 'therefore' and so forth. 'Suggested' (<s>vyaṅgya</s>) — meaning: having the form of <s>rasa</s> and the like, since that very topic has been taken up. 'Having become the sentence-meaning' — but <s>rasa</s> and the like that have not become the sentence-meaning can indeed be ornaments.
As has been stated —
'Where <s>rasa</s> and the like are subordinate elements while the principal sentence-meaning is something else,
in such poetry, <s>rasa</s> and the like are ornaments — this is my view.'
Thus.

children.text:
etacca rasavadādyalaṅkāraprastāva eva nirṇeṣyāmaḥ /
itiśabdaḥ prameyaparisamātpau /
etadeva yuktamityāha-eṣa evetyādi /
sarvairiti /
avākyārthavidbhirasahṛdayaprāyairityarthaḥ /
pakṣyāntarasyeti /
tatra tāvadvācyavācakamātrāśrayiṇāmalaṅkārāṇāṃ madhye vyaṅgyavyañjakabhāvasamāśrayeṇa vyavasthitatvādasyāntarbhāvo na yuktaḥ /

children.translated_text: As has been stated —
'How could <s>dhvani</s>, which is grounded in the relationship of the suggested and the suggestive,
fall within the causes of beauty of the expressed meaning and expressive words?'

And this we shall determine in the context of discussing the ornaments <s>rasavat</s> and the like. The word 'thus' (<s>iti</s>) indicates the conclusion of the topic under consideration. He affirms that precisely this is correct — saying 'this alone' and so forth. 'By all' — meaning: by those who do not know sentence-meaning, that is, by the majority who are not connoisseurs (<s>sahṛdaya</s>). 'Of the alternative position' — now, among the ornaments that depend merely on the expressed meaning and expressive words, since this [<s>dhvani</s>] is established through dependence on the relationship of suggested and suggestive, its inclusion within those is not appropriate.
Thus.

children.text:
lakṣaṇāyāmapyasyāntarbhāvo na yuktaḥ /
tadasadbhāve 'sya sadbhāvāt tatsadbhāve cāsyāmadbhāvāt /
yaduktam-'ativyātperathāvyātperna cāsau lakṣyate tayā' iti /

children.translated_text: Nor is it appropriate to classify this as something not to be categorized at all —
'Where a meaning or a word, having subordinated its own meaning,

children.text: vyaṅktaḥ kāvyaviśeṣaḥ sa dhvaniriti sūribhiḥ kathitaḥ' //
children.translated_text: is suggested — that special type of poetry is called <s>dhvani</s> by the learned.'

Its inclusion within <s>lakṣaṇā</s> (secondary signification) is also not appropriate — because this [<s>dhvani</s>] exists even in the absence of that [<s>lakṣaṇā</s>], and in the presence of that, this may not exist. As has been stated: 'It [<s>dhvani</s>] is neither excessively pervaded nor insufficiently pervaded by it [<s>lakṣaṇā</s>], nor is it indicated by that.'
Thus.
In this way, the groundlessness of the three-fold disagreement has been demonstrated.
<s>Ruyyaka's</s> commentary on <s>Alaṃkārasarvasva</s> [<s>Bhūmikā</s> 5b]:

children.text: idānīmanye 'pi yaḥ kaścidvipratipattiprakāraḥ kaiściduktaḥ so 'pi nopapadyate ityāhuyattvityādi /
children.translated_text: Now, whatever other type of disagreement has been stated by some — that too is untenable, he says with 'but that' (<s>yat tu</s>) and so forth.

children.text:
yattu vyaktivivekakāro vācyasya pratīyamānaṃ prati liṅgatayā vyañjanasyānumānāntarbhāvamākhyat tad vācyasya pratīyamānena saha tādāpmyatadutpattyabhāvādavicāritābhidhānam /
tadetatkuśāgradhiṣaṇaiḥ kṣodanīyamatigahanamiti neha pratanyate / [RuAss_Bhū.6]
children.translated_text: But the author of the <s>Vyaktiviveka</s> declared that <s>vyañjanā</s> (suggestion) is to be subsumed under inference (<s>anumāna</s>), since the expressed meaning serves as a logical mark (<s>liṅga</s>) for the suggested meaning — that is a statement made without proper examination, since there is neither identity (<s>tādātmya</s>) nor causal relation (<s>tadutpatti</s>) between the expressed and the suggested. This matter, being extremely profound, is to be examined by those of razor-sharp intellect, and is therefore not elaborated upon here. [<s>Ruyyaka's Alaṃkārasarvasva</s>, <s>Bhūmikā</s> 6]
<s>Ruyyaka's</s> commentary on <s>Alaṃkārasarvasva</s> [<s>Bhūmikā</s> 6]:

children.text:
dhvanikārānantarabhāvī vyaktivivekakāra iti tanmatamiha paścānnirdiṣṭam yadyapi vakroktijīvitahṛdayadarpaṇakārāvapi dhvanikārāntarabhānāveva, tathāpi tau cirantaramatānuyāyināveti tanmataṃ pūrvamevoddiṣṭam /
anena punaretatsvopajñamevoktam /
anumānantarbhāvamiti /
anumānarūpatvamevetyarthaḥ /
ākhyaditi /

children.translated_text: As he stated —
'Where a meaning, being expressed or inferred from that [expressed meaning], reveals another meaning
through some relation — that is called poetic inference (<s>kāvyānumiti</s>).'

The author of the <s>Vyaktiviveka</s> came immediately after the author of <s>Dhvani</s> [<s>Ānandavardhana</s>], and therefore his view has been mentioned here later. Although the authors of the <s>Vakroktijīvita</s> and the <s>Hṛdayadarpaṇa</s> also came after the author of <s>Dhvani</s>, nevertheless, since they followed doctrines of long standing, their views have been mentioned earlier. This [author of <s>Vyaktiviveka</s>], however, stated what was his own original doctrine. 'Subsumption under inference' — meaning: being of the very nature of inference. 'Declared' —
Thus.

children.text:
avicāritābhidhānamiti /
iha liṅgaliṅginostādātmyatadutpattibhyāmeva tāvatpratibandho niścīyate /
tanniścayenaiva ca sādhyasiddhiḥ /
anyathā hi sādhyasiddhirnasyādvyabhicārāt /
tatra tādātmyaṃ yathā kṛtakatvānityatvayoḥ /
tadutpattiryathā vahnidhūmayoḥ /
vācyapratīyamānayoḥpunastādātmyatadutpattī na staḥ /

children.translated_text: That is to say —

children.text: 'niḥśeṣacyutacandanaṃ stanataṭaṃ nirmṛṣṭarāgo 'dharo netre dūramanañjane pulakitā tanvī taveyaṃ tanuḥ /
children.translated_text: 'The breast-slope emptied of all sandal paste, the lip with its color wiped away, the eyes with their collyrium far removed, and this slender body of yours is bristling with goosebumps —

children.text: mithyāvādini dūti bāndhavajanasyājñātapūḍāgame vāpūṃ snātumito gatāsi na punastasyādhamasyāntikam' //
children.translated_text: O lying messenger! You went from here to bathe in the lake when the kinsmen did not know of your arrival, not again to that vile man's presence.'

'A statement made without proper examination' — here, the invariable connection (<s>pratibandha</s>) between the logical mark (<s>liṅga</s>) and what is marked (<s>liṅgin</s>) is determined only through identity (<s>tādātmya</s>) or causal relation (<s>tadutpatti</s>). And it is only through the ascertainment of that [invariable connection] that the establishment of what is to be proved is achieved. Otherwise, the establishment of what is to be proved would fail, due to deviation (<s>vyabhicāra</s>). In this regard, identity is illustrated by that between being produced (<s>kṛtakatva</s>) and being impermanent (<s>anityatva</s>). Causal relation is illustrated by that between fire and smoke. But between the expressed meaning and the suggested meaning, there is neither identity nor causal relation.

children.text:
ityatra vidhinā niṣedho niṣedhena vā vidhiḥ pratīyate /
na tasya vācyena saha tādātmyam /
viruddhatvāt /
nahyabhāvo bhāvātmā bhāvo 'pyabhāvātmā /
nāpi tadutpattiḥ /
abhāvasya janyajanakatvānupapatteḥ /
nāpi niḥśeṣacyutacandanādīnāṃ viśeṣaṇānāṃ tadantikagamanānumāpakatvaṃ yuktam, teṣāṃ snānādāvapi sadbhāvādanaikāntikatvāt /
etacca dhvanikāreṇādūṣitatvādgranthakṛtā svakaṇṭhena dūṣitam /
ata evānenānyā vipratipattaye na dūṣitāḥ /
etaditi /
vācyasya pratīyamānena tādātmyatadutpattyabhāvādi neha pratanyata iti vyaktivivekavicāre hi mayaivaitadvitatya nirṇītamiti bhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: Here, an injunction is understood through a prohibition, or a prohibition through an injunction. It does not have identity with the expressed meaning, because they are contradictory — for non-existence is not identical with existence, nor is existence identical with non-existence. Nor is there origination from it, since the relation of cause and effect in the case of non-existence is untenable. Nor is it proper that the qualifying attributes such as 'emptied of all sandal paste' etc. serve as inferential marks for going to his presence, since those attributes can also exist in bathing etc., making them inconclusive. And since this was not refuted by the author of the <s>Dhvani</s> (theory of suggestion), the author of the present work refuted it in his own voice. Therefore, the other disagreements were not refuted by him. 'This' — the absence of identity and origination between the expressed and the suggested meaning is not elaborated here, the sense being: 'For in the examination of the <s>Vyaktiviveka</s>, I myself have determined this at length.'
[Section heading: <s>Ruyyaka</s>'s commentary on <s>Bhūmikā</s> 6a]
Thus, having established <s>Dhvani</s> (suggestion) through the refutation of the false attributions and the removal of objections imposed by others, he states 'asti' (there exists) etc.

children.text:
astiṃ tāvad vyaṅgyaniṣṭo vyañjanavyāpāraḥ /
tatra vyaṅgyasya prādhānyāprādhānyābhyāṃ dhvaniguṇībhūtavyaṅgyākhyau dvau kāvyabhedau /
vyaṅgyasyāsphuṭatve 'laṅkārattvena citrākhyaḥ kāvyabhedastṛtīyaḥ /
tatrottamo dhvaniḥ /
tasya lakṣaṇābhidhāmūlatvenāvivakṣitavācyavivakṣitānyaparavācyavivakṣitānyaparavācyākhyau dvau bhedau /
ādyo 'pyarthāntarasaṃkramasaṃsalakṣyakramitavācyātyāntatiraskṛtavācyatvena dvividhaḥ /
dvitīyo 'pyasaṃlakṣyakramasaṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgyatayā dvividhaḥ /
lakṣaṇāmūlaḥ śabdaśaktimūlo vastudhvaniḥ,asaṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgyaḥ arthaśaktimūlo rasādidhvaniḥ /
saṃlakṣyakramavyaṅgyaḥ śabdārthobhayaśaktimūlo vastudhvaniralaṅkāradhvaniśceti /
tatra rasādidhvaniralaṅkāramañjaryāṃ darśitaḥ, kāvyasya śṛṅgārapradhānatvāt /
śiṣṭastu yathāvasaraṃ tatraiva vibhaktaḥ /
guṇībhūtavyaṅgyo vācyāṅgatvādibhedairyathāsaṃbhavaṃ samāsoktyādau darśitaḥ / [RuAss_Bhū.7]
children.translated_text: There exists indeed a <s>vyañjana-vyāpāra</s> (suggestive function) that culminates in the suggested meaning. In that, by the predominance or non-predominance of the suggested meaning, there are two types of poetry called <s>Dhvani</s> (suggestion) and <s>Guṇībhūtavyaṅgya</s> (subordinated suggestion). When the suggested meaning is indistinct, there is a third type of poetry called <s>Citra</s> (the Figurative), being of the nature of <s>alaṃkāra</s> (figure of speech). Among these, <s>Dhvani</s> is the highest. Its division is twofold based on <s>lakṣaṇā</s> (secondary signification) and <s>abhidhā</s> (primary denotation): <s>Avivakṣitavācya</s> (where the literal meaning is not intended) and <s>Vivakṣitānyaparavācya</s> (where another meaning is intended beyond the literal). The first is also twofold: by transference of the literal meaning to another sense (<s>Arthāntarasaṃkramita</s>) and by complete concealment of the literal meaning (<s>Atyantatiraskṛtavācya</s>). The second is also twofold: by suggestion whose process is imperceptible (<s>Asaṃlakṣyakrama</s>) and by suggestion whose process is perceptible (<s>Saṃlakṣyakrama</s>). That which is based on <s>lakṣaṇā</s>, rooted in the power of the word, is <s>Vastudhvani</s> (suggestion of a fact); the <s>Asaṃlakṣyakrama</s> type, rooted in the power of meaning, is <s>Rasādidhvani</s> (suggestion of <s>rasa</s> etc.). The <s>Saṃlakṣyakrama</s> type, rooted in the power of both word and meaning, comprises <s>Vastudhvani</s> and <s>Alaṃkāradhvani</s> (suggestion of a figure). Among these, <s>Rasādidhvani</s> has been shown in the <s>Alaṃkāramañjarī</s>, since poetry has <s>Śṛṅgāra</s> (the erotic sentiment) as its predominant <s>rasa</s>. The rest have been distributed there as occasion requires. <s>Guṇībhūtavyaṅgya</s> has been shown in <s>Samāsokti</s> etc. through the distinctions of being ancillary to the expressed meaning, as appropriate. [Section: <s>Bhūmikā</s> 7]

children.text:
RuAssC_[Bhū.7]:
tāvacchabdo vipratipattyabhāvadyotakaḥ /
asyaiva bhedanirdeśaṃ kartumāha-tatretyādi /
vyaṅgyaniṣṭhe vyañjanavyāpāre satyapītyarthaḥ /
prādhānyāprādhānyeti /

children.translated_text: As it has been said:
'Word and meaning that are entirely devoted to the suggested meaning,

children.text: dhvaneḥ sa eva viṣayo mantavyaḥ saṃkarojjhitaḥ' //
children.translated_text: that is to be regarded as the domain of <s>Dhvani</s>, free from confusion.'

[<s>Ruyyaka</s>'s commentary on <s>Bhūmikā</s> 7]: The word 'tāvat' (to begin with) serves to indicate the absence of dispute. To state the division of this, he says 'tatra' etc. The meaning is: even when the suggestive function culminating in the suggested meaning exists. 'By predominance or non-predominance' —
Thus.
For example:
'Another type, <s>Guṇībhūtavyaṅgya</s> (subordinated suggestion), is seen in poetry;
there, when the suggested follows, the charm of the expressed meaning would be pre-eminent.'
Thus.
As it has been said:
'When there is absence of the intention regarding the domain of <s>rasa</s>, <s>bhāva</s>, etc.,
that which is based on <s>alaṃkāra</s> (figures) is regarded as having <s>Citra</s> (the Figurative) as its domain.'
'Indistinctness' — the meaning is: when the suggested meaning is not intended.

children.text:
iti /
tatreti /
trayanirdhāraṇe /
tasyeti,uttamasya dhvaneḥ /
ādya iti avivakṣitavācyaḥ /
na kevalaṃ dhvanirdvividhaḥ yāvattatprabhodo 'pyayaṃ dvividha ityapiśabdārthaḥ /

children.translated_text: As it has been said:
'Transferred to another meaning, or completely concealed —
the expressed meaning of <s>Dhvani</s> whose literal meaning is not intended is regarded as twofold.'

Thus. 'Tatra' — in the determination of the three. 'Tasya' — of the highest, <s>Dhvani</s>. 'Ādya' — <s>Avivakṣitavācya</s>. Not only is <s>Dhvani</s> twofold, but even its subdivisions are twofold — this is the meaning of the word 'api'.
Thus.
[Section heading: <s>Ruyyaka</s>'s commentary on <s>Bhūmikā</s> 7a]
As it has been said:
'One whose manifestation is by imperceptible process, and the other illuminated by a perceptible process —
the nature of <s>Dhvani</s> whose expressed sense is intended is regarded as twofold.'
'The second' — <s>Vivakṣitānyaparavācya</s> (where another meaning beyond the literal is intended).

children.text:
iti /
atraiva vasturasālaṅkārāṇāṃ dhvanyamānatvaṃ darśayitumāha-lakṣaṇetyādi /
lakṣaṇāmūla ityavivakṣitavācyaḥ /
śabdaśaktimūla iti na punararthaśaktimūlaḥ /
yadyapi śabdaśaktimūler'thaśaktirapyasti tathāpi tatra tasyāḥ sahakāritayā vyavasthānamiti prādhānyācchabdaśaktimūlatvamuktam /
evamarthaśaktimūlatve 'pi jñeyam /
vastudhvaniriti /
rasālaṅkāravyatiriktasya vastumātrasya dhvanyamānatvāt /

children.translated_text: There, <s>Vastudhvani</s> of the type where the literal meaning is transferred to another sense, for example:

children.text: 'snigdhaśyāmalakāntilitpaviyato velladbalākā ghanā vātāḥ śīkariṇaḥ payodasuhṛdāmānandakekāḥ kalāḥ /
children.translated_text: 'The sky is anointed with dense, smooth, dark-blue beauty; clouds heavy with rows of swaying cranes; winds bearing sprays of rain; the cries of joy from the peacocks, friends of the rain-clouds —

children.text: kāmaṃ santu dṛḍhaṃ kaṭhorahṛdayo rāmo 'smi sarvaṃ sahe vaidehī tu kathaṃ bhaviṣyati hahā hā devī dhīrā bhava' //
children.translated_text: Let them be as they will — firm, of hard heart, I am <s>Rāma</s>, I endure all. But how will <s>Vaidehī</s> fare? Alas, alas, O queen, be brave!'

Thus. To show that facts, <s>rasa</s>, and figures are all capable of being suggested, he says 'lakṣaṇā' etc. 'Based on <s>lakṣaṇā</s>' means <s>Avivakṣitavācya</s>. 'Rooted in the power of the word' — and not in the power of meaning. Although in those rooted in the power of the word, the power of meaning also exists, nevertheless since it functions there as an auxiliary, 'rooted in the power of the word' is stated by reason of predominance. The same should be understood regarding being rooted in the power of meaning. '<s>Vastudhvani</s>' — because what is suggested is mere fact, distinct from <s>rasa</s> and <s>alaṃkāra</s>.
[Section heading: <s>Ruyyaka</s>'s commentary on <s>Bhūmikā</s> 7b]
An example of the type where the literal meaning is completely concealed:
'With its beauty transferred to the sun, its disk veiled by frost,
the moon does not shine, like a mirror dimmed by breath.'
Here the word '<s>Rāma</s>' suggests the factual substance of his being the recipient of innumerable sufferings such as exile from the kingdom etc.
There, an example of <s>Rasadhvani</s> (suggestion of <s>rasa</s>):

children.text: 'tvāmālikhya praṇayakupitāṃ dhāturāgaiḥ śilāyā- mātmānaṃ te caraṇapatitaṃ yāvadicchāmi kartum /
children.translated_text: 'Having drawn you on the rock with mineral pigments, angry in love, while I wish to depict myself fallen at your feet —

children.text: astraistāvanmuhurupacitairddaṣṭirālipyate me krūrasta- sminnapi na sahate saṃgamaṃ nau kṛtāntaḥ' //
children.translated_text: meanwhile my vision is obscured by tears welling up again and again. Cruel <s>Kṛtānta</s> (Death) does not permit even that union of ours!'

Here the word 'dimmed' (andha), using its own meaning as the basis, suggests the factual substance — the class of properties such as the loss of reflected image, which is common to both [mirror and moon]. '<s>Rasādi</s>' — by the word 'ādi' (etc.), <s>bhāva</s>, <s>bhāvābhāsa</s>, and others are included.
Here <s>rasa</s> is manifested through <s>vibhāvas</s> (determinants), <s>anubhāvas</s> (consequents), and <s>vyabhicāribhāvas</s> (transitory emotions).
[Section heading: <s>Ruyyaka</s>'s commentary on <s>Bhūmikā</s> 7c]
An example of <s>Bhāvadhvani</s> (suggestion of a transitory emotion):

children.text: 'jāne kopaparāṅmukhī priyatamā svapne 'dya dṛṣṭā mayā mā māṃ saṃspṛśa pāṇineti rudatī gantuṃ pravṛttā tataḥ /
children.translated_text: 'I know — my beloved, turned away in anger, was seen by me today in a dream. Weeping, saying "Do not touch me with your hand," she began to leave.

children.text: no yāvat parirabhya cāṭukaśataurāśrāsayāmi priyāṃ bhrātastāvadahaṃ śaṭhena vidhinā nidrādaridrīkṛtaḥ' //
children.translated_text: Before I could embrace her and console my beloved with a hundred flatteries, brother, I was by that cruel fate impoverished of sleep!'
An example of <s>Rasābhāsadhvani</s> (suggestion of a semblance of <s>rasa</s>):

children.text: 'stumaḥ kaṃ vāmākṣi kṣaṇamapi vinā ya na ramase vilebhe kaḥ prāṇān paṇamakhamukhe yaṃ mṛgayase /
children.translated_text: 'O lovely-eyed one, whom shall we praise — you who cannot bear to be without someone even for a moment? Who obtained his life when you hunt for him at the stake of the gambling board?

children.text: sulagne ko jātaḥ śaśimukhi yamāliṅgasi balāt tapaḥśrīḥ pasyaiṣā madananagari dhyāyasi tu yam' //
children.translated_text: O moon-faced one, who was born at an auspicious moment, whom you embrace by force? Behold this glory of austerity, O city of <s>Madana</s> (the Love-god) — upon whom you meditate!'
Here the transitory emotion called <s>asūyā</s> (indignation) is directed toward fate.
Here the desire directed toward many lovers constitutes a <s>rasābhāsa</s> (semblance of <s>rasa</s>).
[Section heading: <s>Ruyyaka</s>'s commentary on <s>Bhūmikā</s> 7d]
An example of <s>Bhāvābhāsadhvani</s> (suggestion of a semblance of <s>bhāva</s>):
'With a face like the full autumn moon, with trembling wide eyes, her limbs undulating with the waves of smiling youthfulness —

children.text: tatkiṃ karomi vidadhe kathamatra maittrīṃ tatsvīkṛtivyatikare ka ivābhyupāyaḥ //
children.translated_text: What shall I do about her? How shall I establish friendship here? What stratagem is there for the exchange of acceptance?'
An example of <s>Bhāvapraśama</s> (subsidence of emotion):

children.text: 'ekasmicchayane parāṅmukhatayā vītottaraṃ tāmya- toranyonyaṃ hṛdayasthite 'pyanunaye saṃpakṣatorgauravam /
children.translated_text: 'On the single bed, facing away from each other, the couple suffering intensely without remedy, though reconciliation dwells in both hearts, each maintaining pride —
The quarrel of love-jealousy is broken by the side-glances of the couple's eyes, mixed with each other, along with the sudden, impetuous turning and grasping of the neck!'
Here the reflection proceeding from impropriety constitutes a <s>bhāvābhāsa</s> (semblance of emotion).
There, an example of <s>Vastudhvani</s> rooted in the power of the word:
'May the sons of <s>Pāṇḍu</s>, in whom the fire of enmity is extinguished and who are caves of tranquility, rejoice together with <s>Mādhava</s> (<s>Kṛṣṇa</s>).

children.text: raktaprasādhitabhuvaḥ kṣatavigrahāśca svasthā bhavantu kururājasutāḥ sabhṛtyāḥ' //
children.translated_text: And may the sons of the <s>Kuru</s> king, whose land is adorned with blood, whose bodies are wounded, be well together with their servants!'
Here the subsidence of <s>asūyā</s> (jealous indignation) constitutes <s>Bhāvapraśamadhvani</s> (suggestion of the subsidence of emotion). '<s>Vastudhvani</s> and <s>Alaṃkāradhvani</s>' —

children.text: atra kauravāṇāṃ kṣataśarīrādikatvaṃ vasturūpaṃ śabdaśaktyaiva pratīyate /

children.translated_text: The same rooted in the power of meaning, for example:
'The crest-jewel of the lazy, the foremost of rogues, made of the fullness of wealth —' (Prakrit)
'Upon hearing this, the young woman became bent-bodied and wide-eyed with delight.' (Prakrit)
Here the fact that the <s>Kauravas</s> have wounded bodies etc. is understood through the power of the word alone as a suggested factual substance.
('The crest-jewel of the lazy, the foremost of rogues, made of the fullness of wealth —' (Sanskrit rendering))
('Upon hearing this, the young woman became bent-bodied and wide-eyed with delight.' (Sanskrit rendering))
The same rooted in the power of both, for example:

children.text: 'panthia ṇa ettha sattharamatthi maṇaṃ pattharatthale ggāme /
children.translated_text: 'O traveler, there is not the slightest bedding here in this rocky-terrain village.' (Prakrit)

children.text: uggaapaoharaṃ pekkhiūṇa jai vasasi tā vasasu' //
children.translated_text: 'Having seen the full-breasted one, if you wish to stay, then stay.' (Prakrit)
Then through the power of meaning, the factual substance is suggested that 'he too is one for my enjoyment alone.'
('O traveler, there is not the slightest bedding here in this rocky-terrain village.' (Sanskrit rendering))

children.text: udgatipayodharaṃ prekṣya yadi vasasi tad vasa') //
children.translated_text: ('Having seen the full-breasted one, if you wish to stay, then stay.' (Sanskrit rendering))

children.text: atra yadyupabhogakṣamo 'si tadā āssveti vastu vakraucityamāśritya śabdārthaśaktyābhivyajyata ityubhayaśaktimūlatvam /
children.translated_text: Here the factual substance — 'if you are capable of enjoyment, then be at ease' — is suggested through the power of both word and meaning, relying on oblique propriety; hence it is rooted in the power of both.
[Section heading: <s>Ruyyaka</s>'s commentary on <s>Bhūmikā</s> 7e]
An example of <s>Alaṃkāradhvani</s> (suggestion of a figure) rooted in the power of the word:
'Elevated, with gleaming pearl necklaces, fragrant with dark aloe,
heavy with the burden of breasts — whom did they not make desirous?'

children.text:
atra śabdaśaktyā meghalakṣaṇamarthāntaraṃ pratīyate /
prakṛtāprakṛtayoścārthayorasaṃbaddhābhidhāyitvaṃ mā prasāṅkṣīditi tayoraupamyaṃ kalpyata ityalaṅkāradhvaniḥ /

children.translated_text: The same rooted in the power of meaning, for example:
'At the time of stealing the jewel, the companion of <s>Śrī</s>, their hearts were of one essence —' (Prakrit)
'Placed by the Flower-Arrowed one on the <s>bimba</s>-fruit lips of the beloveds.' (Prakrit)

Here, through the power of the word, an alternative meaning pertaining to a cloud is understood. Lest the disconnected denotation of two unrelated meanings — the literal and the figurative — seem absurd, a similarity between them is imagined; thus it is <s>Alaṃkāradhvani</s>.
('At the time of stealing the jewel, the companion of <s>Śrī</s>, their hearts were of one essence —' (Sanskrit rendering))
('Placed by the Flower-Arrowed (<s>Kāmadeva</s>) one on the <s>bimba</s>-fruit lips of the beloveds.' (Sanskrit rendering))
An example rooted in the power of both:
'In the village on the rocky plateau, which tears apart people's hearts, drenched with streams of water, there is no delight —' (Prakrit)

children.text: tava diṭvī ciurabhare viāṇa jaha vairikhaggāmmi' //
children.translated_text: 'But your glance, heavy with curly hair, O beloved, is like an enemy's sword.' (Prakrit)

Here, through the power of meaning alone, a similarity between the <s>Kaustubha</s> (jewel) and the <s>bimba</s>-fruit lip is understood; thus it is <s>Alaṃkāradhvani</s> rooted in the power of meaning.
('In the village on the rocky plateau, which tears apart people's hearts, drenched with streams of water, there is no delight —' (Sanskrit rendering))
('But your glance, heavy with curly hair, O beloved, is like an enemy's sword.' (Sanskrit rendering))

children.text:
atrobhayaśaktyā cikurabharakhaṅgayoraupabhyaṃ gamyate /
iti śabdaḥ prameyaparimasātpau /
evaṃ dhvaneḥ prabhedajātaṃ pradarśya kramaprātpaṃ guṇībhūtavyaṅyasyāpyanyato yojayati-guṇībhūtetyādinā /
darśita iti dhvanikāreṇa /

children.translated_text: As he has said:
'Where the suggested, which merely follows the expressed meaning, is non-predominant,
there <s>Samāsokti</s> (condensed expression) etc. are clearly figures of the expressed meaning.'

Here, through the power of both word and meaning, a similarity between the mass of curly hair and a sword is understood. The word 'iti' marks the conclusion of the extent of the subject matter. Having thus demonstrated the varieties of <s>Dhvani</s>, he also connects the varieties of <s>Guṇībhūtavyaṅgya</s> elsewhere in due order — with 'guṇībhūta' etc. 'Shown' — by the author of the <s>Dhvani</s> (theory).
Thus.

children.text: evaṃ guṇībhūtavyaṅgyasyāpyanyato bhedajātaṃ yojayitvā citrasyāpi prabhedajātaṃ darśayitumāha-citramityādi /
children.translated_text: Having thus also connected the varieties of <s>Guṇībhūtavyaṅgya</s> elsewhere, he states the varieties of <s>Citra</s> (the Figurative) with 'citram' etc.
[START <s>Sūtra</s> 1]

children.text:
citraṃ tu śabdārthāṃlakārasvabhāvatayā bahutaraprabhedam /
tathā hi-
children.translated_text: <s>Citra</s> (the Figurative), being of the nature of verbal and semantic figures, has many more subdivisions. For here —

children.text: ihārthapaunaruktyaṃ śabdapaunaruktyaṃ śabdārthapaunaruktyaṃ ceti trayaḥ paunaruktyaprakārāḥ || 1 ||
children.translated_text: There are three types of <s>paunarukya</s> (repetition): repetition of meaning, repetition of words, and repetition of both words and meaning. [<s>Ruyyaka</s>, <s>Alaṃkārasarvasva</s>, <s>Sūtra</s> 1]

children.text:
ādau paunaruktyaprakāraravacanaṃ vakṣyamāṇālaṅkārāṇāṃ kakṣāvibhāgaghaṭanārtham /
arthāpekṣayā śabdasya pratītāvantaraṅgatve 'pi prathamamarthatadharmanirdeśaścirantanaprasiddhyā punaruktakavadābhāsasya pūrvaṃ lakṣaṇārthaḥ /
ihaśabdaḥ pratthāne /
itiśabdaḥ prakāre, triśabdādeva saṃkhyāparisamātpisiddheḥ /
children.translated_text: The statement of the types of <s>paunarukya</s> (repetition) at the outset is for the purpose of establishing a hierarchy among the figures to be discussed. Although in the cognition of meaning, the word is more proximate, the description of meaning and its properties first is for the purpose of defining the semblance of the repetition-like appearance (<s>punaruktavadābhāsa</s>), following the ancient established tradition. The word 'iha' means 'in the subject at hand.' The word 'iti' refers to the types; since the exact number is already established from the word 'three' alone.
[<s>Ruyyaka</s>'s commentary on <s>Sūtra</s> 1:]

children.text:
tuśabdaḥ kāvyaprakāradvayādasya vailakṣaṇyadyotakaḥ /
ata eva bahutaraprabhedamityuktam /
śabdārthetyeka śeṣaḥ /
tenobhayālaṅkārāṇāmapi grahaṇam /
tadeva darśayitumāha-tathāhītyādi /
citrākhyakāvyabhedanirūpaṇāvasare kiṃ paunaruktyaprakāravacanenetyāśaṅkyāha-ādāvityādi /
vakṣyamāṇālaṅkārāḥ punaruktavadābhāsādayaḥ pañca /
śabdapratītipuraḥsarīkāreṇārthapratītiriti prathamaṃ śabdagata eva dharmanirdeśo nyāyyo nārthagata ityāśaṅkyāha-arthetyādi /
cigtaṃna prasiddheti /
na punaryujyamānatayeti bhāvaḥ /
'punaruktavadābhāsaṃ chekānuprāsa eva ca' iti cirantanaprasiddhiḥ /
arthālaṅkāratvādarthālaṅkāraprakaraṇe punarasya yujyamānatvam /
nanvādau śabdagato, dharmanirdeśaḥ kāryaḥ paścādarthagata iti kramasya na kiñcitprayojanamutpaśyāma iti kiṃ teneti yadanyairuktaṃ tadayuktam /
śabdārthayoḥ krameṇaiva pratītāvavabhāsanāttathātvenaiva dharmanirdeśasyopapatteḥ kiṃ ca 'vardhamānotkarṣāṇi śāstrāṇi prathante' iti nītyā parimitacamatkārāṇāmarthālaṅkārāṇāṃ paścānnirdeśaḥ kārya iti saprayojana eva kramaḥ /
cirantanamatānullaṅghanena ca vayaṃ pravṛttā ityayuktamapi granthakṛtā tanmatamāśritam /
agre 'pyanenāśayena tanmatāśrayaṇaṃ karipyatyeva /
tena vayaṃyaccirantanamatāśrayaṇaṃ vyākhyāsyāmastadyuktameva /
children.translated_text: The word 'tu' (but) indicates the distinctness of this [type] from the two kinds of poetry. Hence the expression 'of more numerous divisions' is used. '<s>Śabdārtha</s>' etc. is an <s>ekaśeṣa</s> (elliptical compound), by which figures of both [word and meaning] are also included. To demonstrate precisely that, he says 'tathāhi' etc. If one objects 'why mention the varieties [again] when describing the division of poetry called <s>citra</s> (ornate)?', he responds with 'ādau' (at the beginning) etc. The figures to be discussed later are five, beginning with <s>punaruktavadābhāsa</s> (semblance of repetition). Anticipating the objection that since the cognition of meaning follows upon the cognition of word, it is proper to first state the properties pertaining to word alone and not those pertaining to meaning, he responds with 'arthe' etc. '<s>Citra</s> is not well-known' means: not established [in that way]. The sense is: not as being appropriate. The ancient tradition states: '<s>punaruktavadābhāsa</s> and <s>chekānuprāsa</s> indeed' — this is the long-established view. Since it is a figure of meaning, its being placed in the section on figures of meaning is appropriate. Now, the statement by others that 'first the property pertaining to word should be stated, then that pertaining to meaning — we see no purpose in this sequence, so what is the point?' — that is unjustified. Because properties are stated precisely in the order in which word and meaning are sequentially cognized; moreover, by the principle that 'treatises progress with increasing excellence,' the figures of meaning with limited aesthetic charm should be stated later — thus the sequence has a purpose. And since the author has proceeded without transgressing the ancient doctrine, even what appears unjustified has been adopted by him following that tradition. Hereafter too, with this very intent, he will follow that tradition. Therefore, our explanation following the ancient tradition is indeed justified.
[Commentary on <s>Ruyyaka</s>'s <s>Alaṃkārasarvasva</s> 1a:]
To determine this very matter in the order of enumeration, he says 'tatra' (among these) etc.
START <s>Sūtra</s> 2:
Among these, repetition of meaning that is established [as such] is a defect. [<s>Ruyyaka</s>'s <s>Alaṃkārasarvasva</s> 2]

children.text:
praruḍhāpraruḍhatvena dvaividhyam /
prathamaṃ heyavacanamupādeye viśrāntyartham /
tatreti trayanirdhāraṇe /
yathāvabhāsanaviśrāntiḥ prarohaḥ /
children.translated_text: There is a twofold division into established and non-established. The first statement regarding what is to be rejected is for the purpose of resting [the mind] upon what is to be accepted. 'Tatra' (among these) is for the determination among the three. Establishment means resting in [the state of] appearance as such.
[Commentary on <s>Ruyyaka</s>'s <s>Alaṃkārasarvasva</s> 2:]

children.text:
kimalaṅkāraprastāve doṣakathanenetyāśaṅkyāha-prathamamityādi /
upādeya ityalaṅkārasvarūpe /
yatheti /
yathaiva dṛṣṭastathaiva paryavasita ityarthaḥ /

children.translated_text: For example:
"Look upon the woman with deer-eyes, with <s>sāraṅga</s>-eyes (gazelle-eyed), with antelope-glances, with lotus-face, with <s>rājīva</s>-face (lotus-faced), resembling a water-lily,

children.text: vilulitakacāṃ cañcatkeśīṃ calaccikurotkarāṃ surataviratau saṃbhogānte vilokaya kāminīm' //
children.translated_text: With disheveled hair, with trembling tresses, with swaying locks of hair — behold the beloved woman at the cessation of lovemaking, at the end of union!"

Anticipating the objection 'why speak of defects in the context of discussing figures?', he responds with 'prathamam' (first) etc. 'What is to be accepted' means the essential nature of the figure. 'Yathā' means: just as it appears, so it is finally determined — that is the meaning.

children.text:
atra sāraṅāgākṣīmityādiṣu punarvacanaṃ praruḍham /
apraruḍhaṃ punaralaṅkāraḥ /
na caitāvataiva doṣābhāvamātreṇālaṅkāratvamasyāśaṅkyam, vakṣyamāṇanītyālaṅkāratvocitasya vicchittiviśeṣasyāpi bhāvāt /
tadevāha-āmugvetyādi /
children.translated_text: Here, in '<s>sāraṅgākṣī</s>' etc., the repetition is established [as actual redundancy]. Non-established repetition, on the other hand, is a figure. Nor should one suspect that merely by the absence of defect it becomes a figure, for there also exists a specific charm appropriate to a figure, as will be stated by rule. He states precisely that with 'āmukhe' etc.
START <s>Sūtra</s> 3:
<s>Punaruktavadābhāsa</s> (semblance of repetition) is the appearance of identity of meaning at the outset, again [resolved differently at the end]. [<s>Ruyyaka</s>'s <s>Alaṃkārasarvasva</s> 3]

children.text:
āmukhagrahaṇaṃ paryavasāne 'nyathātvapratipattyartham /
lakṣyanirdeśe nāpuṃsakaḥ saṃskāro laukikālaṅkāravaidharyeṇa kāvyālaṅkāraṇāmalaṅkāryaṃpāratantryadhvananārthaḥ /
arthapaunaruktyādevārthīśritatvādarthālaṅkāratvaṃ jñeyam /
prabhedāstu vistarabhayānnocyante /
udāharaṇaṃ madīye śrīkaṇṭhastave yathā-
children.translated_text: The word '<s>āmukha</s>' (outset) is used so that at the conclusion one understands the difference. In the statement of the defined [figure], the neuter gender is used to convey, by contrast with worldly ornaments, the dependence of poetic figures on what is ornamented. Since it is based on repetition of meaning alone, its being a figure of meaning should be understood. The varieties are not stated for fear of prolixity. An example [is found] in my <s>Śrīkaṇṭhastava</s>, as follows:
"Having the body of the lord of serpents as a coiled bracelet,
Whose deeds beginning from the mountain are celebrated through <s>Nandin</s>, who crushed the pride of <s>Kandharpa</s> (Kāma),
Bearing the mark of the bull, the foremost one, having the peacock-fire as his eye,
Accompanied by all auspiciousness, I praise <s>Īśvara</s> (the Lord), the companion of <s>Pārvatī</s>."
"Terrible, born from wood, the supreme one who produces prosperity from ashes,
Red, with blazing flames, exceedingly fierce — may <s>Pāvaka</s> (Fire), the crested one, protect you!"
"The serpent-ringed one, clearly having the moon's bright cool rays, may <s>Śiva</s>, the captivator of minds, always protect the worlds from calamity!"
[Commentary on <s>Ruyyaka</s>'s <s>Alaṃkārasarvasva</s> 3:]

children.text:
anyathātveti /
yathāvabhātasyārthasya paryavasāne tathātvenaivāviśrāntirityarthaḥ /
anyathā hyaktanītyā doṣaḥ syāt /
nanu punaruktavadābhāsaśabdasyālaṅkāraśabdasāmānādhikaraṇyādupamādivadajahalliṅgatvayogācca puṃlliṅgatve kimitīha nāpuṃsakaḥ saṃskāraḥ kṛta ityāśaṅkyāha-lakṣyetyādi /
lakṣyasya lakṣaṇīyasya punaruktavadābhāsasya punaḥśabdāpekṣayā nirdeśo vacanamityarthaḥ /
alaṅkāryapāratantreti /
kāvyasāmānādhikaraṇyena nirdeśāt /
laukikā hārādayaḥ /
eṣāṃ hyalaṅkāryeṇa saha saṃyogaḥ saṃbandhaḥ /
ata evaiṣāṃ tatparatantratāpi na syāt /
kāvyālaṅkārāṇāṃ punaralaṅkāryeṇa saha samavāyaḥ saṃbandhaḥ /
ata evaiṣāmayutasiddhatvādalaṅkāryapāratantryameveti laikikālaṅkāravaidharmyameva nyāyyam /
āśrayāśrayibhāvenālaṅkāryālaṅkaraṇabhāvopapatteḥ kimāśrayamasyālaṅkāratvamityāśaṅkāyāha-arthetyādi /
evakāraḥ śabdapaunaruktyāvacchedadyotakaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'Anyathātva' (difference) means: the meaning that appeared at the outset does not rest at the conclusion in exactly that same form — that is the sense. Otherwise, if there were no such [resolution], it would be a defect. Now, if one objects: since the word '<s>punaruktavadābhāsa</s>' stands in co-reference with the word '<s>alaṃkāra</s>' (figure), and since like <s>upamā</s> (simile) etc. it does not abandon its gender [i.e., should be masculine], why is the neuter gender used here? — anticipating this, he says 'lakṣya' etc. The statement of the defined — meaning the description of <s>punaruktavadābhāsa</s>, which is to be defined — with reference to the word 'punaḥ' is in the neuter — that is the meaning. 'Dependence on what is ornamented' — because it is stated in co-reference with 'kāvya' (poetry) [which is neuter]. Worldly [ornaments] are necklaces etc. For these have conjunction as their relation with what is ornamented. Therefore, their dependence on that [ornamented thing] would not follow. But poetic figures have inherence as their relation with what is ornamented. Therefore, since they are inseparable [from their substrate], their dependence on what is ornamented is precisely [the case] — thus the contrast with worldly ornaments is justified. Anticipating the objection 'given the relation of substrate-and-superstratum between the ornamented and the ornament, what is the basis for calling this a figure?', he says 'arthe' etc. The particle 'eva' (alone) indicates the exclusion of repetition of word.
[Commentary on <s>Ruyyaka</s>'s <s>Alaṃkārasarvasva</s> 3a:]

children.text:
tena śabdasyāpaunaruktyānna śabdālaṅkāro nāpyubhayālaṅkāro 'yamityarthaḥ /
paryavasāne vastutor'thasyāsattvāt dharmyaṃbhāve ca dharmaṃsya nirviṣayatvātpaunaruktyaṃ kasya dharmaḥ syāditi na vācyam /
āmukher'thasyāvabhāsamānatvena sattvāddharmidharmabhāvasya naivāniṣṭerarthagatayoḥ sattvāsattvayoranupayogāt /
āmukhāvagataiva ca pratītiralaṅkārabījaṃ na pāryavasānikī /
tathātve hyupamārūpakādīnāmapyaviśeṣaḥ syāt /
paryavasāne 'pyarthasya 'dāruṇaḥ kāṣṭato jātaḥ'ityādāvindhanārthasya sattvādanaikāntikatvābhāvācchraśaśṛvadabhāvo na vācyaḥ /
paryavasāne 'pyatrandhanārthaḥ sannapi nālaṅkāratvaprayojaka iti 'arivadhadehaśarīraḥ' [kāvya prakāśa 91389]ityādāpyasatā kāyārthenāviśeṣātsamānaḥ /
kiṃ va ito na paryavasāner'thasyāsattvam /
iha hi pratītimātrasāratvātkavyasya yadyathaiva pratīyate tattathaiva bhavatītyāvivādaḥ /
tadvādhotpattāvapi taimirikadvicandrapratītivat punaruktatayāvabhātasyārthasyāvabhāsamānatvātsattvameva /
nahi śataśīpi krūrādyarthopalambhe kāṣṭhāderarthasyāpunaruktatayā bhānamasti /
bādhotpatteḥ punardvicandrapratītivatpaunaruktyapratīteranupapadyamānatvaṃ bhavati, natu śuktikāyāmiva rajatapratyayasya svarūpata evābhāvaḥ /
ata evābhātapaunaruktyāpi pratītirapaunaruktyaparyavasāyinyasya svarūpam /
evamapi vastutaḥ kāyādyarthābhāvastadavastha iti cet,satyam /
kiṃ tu tathā vastuto bahirasaṃbhavannapi dvitīyaścandraḥ pratītau kañcana viśeṣamādhātuṃ notsahate tathehāpi vastuvṛttena kāyāderthasyāsaṃbhave 'pi pratītau na kaścidviśeṣa iti diṇḍikārāga eva vāstavatvānveṣaṇam /
tasmādatrāvabhāsamānatvamevārthasya sattvapratīṣṭhāpakaṃ pramāṇam /
children.translated_text: Therefore, since there is no repetition of word, this is neither a figure of word nor a figure of both — that is the meaning. One should not object that at the conclusion, since the meaning does not actually exist, and in the absence of the property-bearer the property would be without object — whose property would the repetition be? For since the meaning is appearing at the outset, and thus the property-bearer exists, there is no such undesirable consequence; [moreover,] the existence or non-existence of meaning-level [features] is irrelevant. And the cognition obtained at the outset alone is the seed of the figure, not the final [resolution]. For if it were otherwise, there would be no distinction even for <s>upamā</s> (simile), <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor) and the like. Nor should one say that because at the conclusion too the meaning exists — as in 'terrible, born from wood' where the meaning of firewood exists — there is lack of invariable concomitance, like the hare's horn [fallacy]. For even at the conclusion here, the firewood-meaning, though existing, is not what produces the figure-status — thus, just as in 'enemy-slaying-body-embodied' [<s>Kāvyaprakāśa</s> 91389], where the non-existent body-meaning makes no difference, this is analogous. Or alternatively, there is no non-existence of meaning at the conclusion. For here, since poetry has its essence in cognition alone, whatever is cognized in whatever way exists in that very way — this is undisputed. Moreover, even if there were sublation, just as in the perception of a double moon by one with an eye-disease, the meaning that appeared as repeated has existence precisely because it appears. For even though in '<s>śataśas</s>' (hundredfold) etc. there is perception of cruel and other meanings, there is no appearance of the firewood-meaning as non-repeated. From the sublation, furthermore, just as the perception of a double moon, the perception of repetition becomes [recognized as] not ultimately valid — but it is not the case that, like the silver-cognition in a shell, the cognition itself is entirely non-existent. Therefore, the cognition, even though the repetition that appeared is [ultimately] of non-repetition, this is the essential nature of the [figure] whose resolution is in non-repetition. Even so, if it be said that the actual non-existence of body-meaning etc. remains the same — true. But just as a second moon, not actually existing outside, does not manage to produce any special effect in cognition, similarly here too, when by actual fact the body-meaning etc. does not exist, there is no special [defect] in cognition — thus the search for actuality is mere obstinacy. Therefore, the appearance itself is the authoritative proof that establishes the existence of meaning.
[Commentary on <s>Ruyyaka</s>'s <s>Alaṃkārasarvasva</s> 3b:]

children.text:
nanu avabhāsamānatvaṃ pramātṛdharma iti kathaṃ tadāśrayo dharmaḥ kāvyālaṅkāra iti cet, asadetat /
avabhāsamānatvasyāvabhāsyaniṣṭatayā pratīterarthadharmatvāt /

children.translated_text: Thus, according to certain advocates of the cognition-theory:
"Indeed, cognizability is the very nature of a thing's own form;

children.text: caitreṇa vedyaṃ vedmīti kiṃ hyatra pratibhāsate' //
children.translated_text: By <s>Caitra</s>, 'I know the knowable' — what indeed appears here?"

Now, if one objects that 'appearance' is a property of the cognizer, so how can a property dependent on that be a poetic figure? — this is wrong. Because appearance belongs to what appears, and cognition is a property of meaning, [established] by reason.

children.text:
ityādyuktayuktyā kaumārilavannīlatayā iva vedyatāyā apyarthadharmatvabheveṣṭam /
iha ca tadupakrama eveti na vastuvādasaṃsparśo nyāyyaḥ /
āmukhatulyārthatvasya ca śabdadharmatvena śabdāśrayatvāt śabdālaṅkāratvaṃ yadyasyocyate tathāpi paryavasāne vastutastulyārthatvasyāsaṃbhavāt śaśaśṛṅgavaddharmadharmibhāvo duṣṭaḥ syāt /
sattve 'pi doṣa evetyasmatpakṣoktasamagracodyavakāśaḥ /
atrāpi yadyāmukha evaikārthatvenāvabhāsanaṃ samādhistadāsmatpakṣeṇa kimaparāddham /
evaṃ ca virodhe 'pi vastuto viruddhasyāsaṃbhavādviruddhārthatvasya ca śabdadharmatvāt śabdālaṅkāratvaṃ prasajyate /
atra viruddhasyārthasyāsaṃbhavepi kartrādibhirvācyatayādhyavasāyaḥ,iha tu paunaruktyāśrayasyānanvitatvena na vācyateti cet,naitat,yataḥ 'dāruṇaḥ kāṣṭato jātaḥ' ityādau tāvatpaunaruktyāśrayasya kāṣṭāderarthasya jātatvādinā sahānavitatvāvagamādastyeva mukhyayā vṛttyā vācyatvam /
'arivadhadehaśarīraḥ' ityādau tu vastutaḥ kāyāderavācye 'pyavabhātapaunaruktyāśrayatvādakṛtrimārthaśobhāparyāvasāyi tvena vācyatayāstyeva vivakṣitatvam /
atra jhakṛtrimor'tho 'laṅkṛtakṛtrimārthopaskṛto yathā camatkārakṛt na tathā tadupaskṛtayocyamānaḥ syāt /

'strīṇāṃ hi kaṇṭhābharaṇāni hārāḥ payodharānapyabhibhūṣayanti' ityādidṛśā ca hārasya kaṇṭhālaṅkāratve 'pi sāmīpyāttāvatiśobhātiśayādhāyakatvādyathā payodharādāvapyalaṅkāratvaṃ tathaiva kṛtrimārthāśrayatve 'pyavabhāsamānasya paunaruktasyākṛtrimārthopaskārakatvamapi pratīyata eveti nānubhaghavāpahnavaḥ kāryaḥ /
children.translated_text: "For women's necklaces, though ornaments of the neck, also adorn the breasts due to proximity" — by such an illustration, just as even though the necklace is an ornament of the neck, it also brings beauty to the breasts etc. due to proximity, similarly, even when [the figure] resides in artificial meaning, the apparent repetition's capacity to enhance the unartificial meaning is also perceived — hence one should not deny the experience.

children.text: evaṃ ca paunaruktyāśrayasyārthasya yatraiva vāttyatvena vivakṣitatvaṃ tatraivāsyālaṅkāratvaṃ nānyatra /
children.translated_text: And thus, wherever the meaning that is the substrate of repetition is intentionally expressed as expressible, there alone is its status as a figure, and not elsewhere.
"She whose face is not [dark like] the moon in the dark fortnight, whose lip-radiance is [bright like] the <s>bandhujīva</s> flower,
This enchanting woman — for whom is she not a festival for the eyes?"

By such reasoning, as stated above, just as <s>Kumārila</s> [holds] that cognizability, like blue-ness, is a property of the object — this is the preferred view. And here this is adopted from the very outset, so contact with realist doctrine is not appropriate. And if one argues that since the synonymy at the outset is a property of word and thus word-dependent, it should be called a figure of word — even so, since at the conclusion actual synonymy is impossible, the property-property-bearer relation would be vitiated like a hare's horn. Even if it exists, it would simply be a defect — there is scope for the entire objection stated in our position. Here too, if the appearance at the outset alone as having one meaning is accepted, then what fault has our position committed? And similarly, even in the case of contradiction, since what is actually contradictory is impossible, and since the contradictory nature of meaning is a property of word, it would follow that it is a figure of word. [If one objects:] in the case of contradiction, although the contradictory meaning is impossible, there is expressibility through agency etc. by conventional agreement; but here, the substrate of repetition, being unconnected [syntactically], is not expressible — this is not so, because in 'terrible, born from wood' etc., since the meaning of firewood etc. that is the substrate of repetition is understood as unconnected with 'born' etc., there is indeed expressibility through primary denotation. In 'enemy-slaying-body-embodied' etc., although the body-meaning actually does not exist, since it is the substrate of apparent repetition and thus [functions as] a natural ornament of meaning culminating in unartificial beauty, there is indeed intentional expression through expressibility.

children.text:
'atrākṛṣṇatyarthapaunaruktyasya saṃbhave 'pi vācyatvenāvivakṣitatvānnāyamalaṅkāraḥ /
evaṃ vakṣyamāṇānāmapyalaṅkārāṇāṃ kavivivakṣaiva svarūpapratiṣṭhāpakaṃ pramāṇaṃ jñeyam /
kiṃ bahunā, sarveṣāmapyalaṅkārāṇāmupamitārthatvādeḥ śabdadharmatvācchabdālaṅkāratvaṃ syāt /
tadarthālaṅkāratvamasya jyāyaḥ, yāvatā hyarthasyāmukha eva punaruktatayāvabhāso 'sya jīvitam /
ata eva punaruktavadābhāsamityanvarthasaṃghajñā /
arthasya ca paunaruktyapratītau na kasyacidvivādaḥ , tāmevāśrittaya śabdālaṅkārasya bhavadbhiruktatvāt /
evaṃ ca pratyāsattestadāśrayatvamevāsyālaṅkāratvaṃyuktam /
anyathā tulyārthaśabdatāpi vākyadharmaṃ iti tadāśrayo 'pi syādityanavasthāprasaṅgaḥ /
children.translated_text: Here, even though the repetition of meaning in 'akṛṣṇa' (not-dark) etc. is possible, since it is not intentionally expressed as expressible, this is not a figure. Similarly, for the figures to be discussed later as well, the poet's intention alone should be understood as the authoritative proof that establishes their essential nature. In short, since the simile-status etc. of all figures involves word-level properties, all would become figures of word. [Yet] its being a figure of meaning is preferable, inasmuch as the very life of this [figure] is the appearance of meaning as repeated at the outset alone. Hence the compound name '<s>punaruktavadābhāsa</s>' (semblance of repetition) is etymologically significant. And regarding the cognition of repetition of meaning, no one disputes it — and it is precisely relying on that [cognition] that you [opponents] have stated it to be a figure of word. And thus, its dependence on that [meaning-level cognition] by virtue of proximity is what constitutes its figure-status. Otherwise, the synonymous-word-nature too would be a property of the sentence, and [the figure] would depend on that as well — leading to an infinite regress.
[Commentary on <s>Ruyyaka</s>'s <s>Alaṃkārasarvasva</s> 3c:]

children.text:
athātra śabdasvarūpavaiśiṣṭyanibandhanaṃ camatkārakāritvamiti tadalaṅkāratvamiti cet, kiṃ nāma śabdasya svarūpe vaiśiṣṭam /
kiṃ paunaruktyam, uta punaruktārthaṃvācitvam,utasabhaṅgābhaṅgapadena śliṣṭatvam /
tatra na tāvadādyaḥ pakṣaḥ /
śabdasya dviruccāraṇābhāvāttathātvāpratibhāsanāt /
nāpi dvitīyaḥ /
vācyavācakabhāvenālaṅkaraṇabhāvāttasyāśrayāśrayibhāve, nopapatteḥ /
ata eva sarveṣāmevārthālaṅkārāṇāmupamitārthādivācitvācchabdasya tadalaṅkāratvaṃ syādityuktam /
nāpi tṛtīyaḥ /
punaruktavadābhāsamityanvarthasaṃjñāśrayaṇāt /
paunaruktyākhyadharmaprayojakīkāreṇālaṅkārasyopakrāntatvāt śliṣṭatvasyehānaupayitakatvāt /
tat punaratrārthepaunaruktyāvagame nimittamātrām /
nimittanimittabhāvaśca nālaṅkāratvaprayojaka ityavivādaḥ /
tasmādarthāśrayatvātpaunaruktyasya tadalaṅkāratvameti yuktam /
evaṃ vaktralaṅkāratāpi nirastā /
sarveṣāmapi naktratiśayarūpatvāt tathātvopapatteḥ /
