tacca dharmiṇāmastu dharmāṇāṃ veti ko viśeṣo yenāvyātpiḥ syāt /
pratyutadharmayorabhedādhyavasāyābhyupagame upamādīnāmapyatiśayoktiprasaṅgaḥ syāt /
tatrāpi dharmāṇāmeva bhede 'bhedavivakṣaṇāt /
evaṃ cavijātīyatvena bhede dharmayorapyabhyātpiḥ prasajyata ityalamasaṅgatagranthārthodīraṇena /
prapañcārthamiti /
na tu nirṇayārtham /
ihaiva tasya viścitatvāt /
prapañcaśca tatraiva darśiyiṣyate /
children.translated_text: 'In these' and so forth. 'In these' is a locative of domain. And this is a reference to the parts. 'Transcending ordinary [experience]'—the meaning is that the domain of these is only exaggerated reality produced by the poet's creative imagination. 'Here' refers to the five varieties of difference. The word 'and' serves to include another thing to be established. 'The result'—because that alone is what is to be demonstrated. 'Therein'—in the statement of identity despite the actual beauty and the beauty attributed by the poet. Now, since the superimposition of the face and others upon the lotus and others is perceived here, how can this be said?—anticipating this objection, he says 'but not' and so forth. And why is there no applicability to those?—anticipating this doubt, he says 'for there' and so forth. For in 'the lotus is upon the water,' if the construal of identity-superimposition of the face and other substantives is made, then since that would be desired only as belonging to the substantive, here there would be no applicability to the qualities. Therefore, in the former case, the superimposition of identity of qualities should be construed, so that there would be a single position everywhere—this is the purport. And this is illustrative. For insofar as the predominance of the superimposed is the defining characteristic of this [<s>atiśayokti</s>], whether it pertains to substantives or to qualities—what difference would there be that would cause non-applicability? On the contrary, if the identity-superimposition of qualities were accepted, then even <s>upamā</s> (simile) and other [ornaments] would become instances of <s>atiśayokti</s>. For there too, identity of qualities despite difference is intended. And thus, the non-applicability to qualities of different class through difference would also follow—enough with expounding the meaning of an incoherent text. 'For the purpose of elaboration'—but not for the purpose of determination, since that has been settled here itself. And the elaboration will be shown there [in that later section].
Commentary on <s>Ruyyaka</s>, <s>Alaṃkārasarvasva</s>, Sūtra 23/4a:
Concluding this, he introduces another [topic].
START Sūtra 24:

children.text:
evamadhyavasāyāśrayamalaṅkāradvayamuktvā gamyamānaupamyāśrayā alaṅkārā idānīmucyante /
tatrāpi padārthavākyārtagatatvena teṣāṃ dvaividhye padārthagatamalaṅkāradvayaṃ krameṇocyate-
children.translated_text: Having thus described the two figures of speech that depend on <s>adhyavasāya</s> (determination/identification), the figures that depend on implied similarity (<s>gamyamāna-aupamya</s>) are now described. Among these, since they are of two kinds — pertaining to word-meaning (<s>padārtha</s>) and sentence-meaning (<s>vākyārtha</s>) — the two figures pertaining to word-meaning are described in order:

children.text: aupamyasya gamyatve padārthagatatvena prastutānāmaprastutānāṃ vā samānadharmābhisaṃbandhe tulyayogitā || 24 ||
children.translated_text: When similarity is implied, if there is a connection of common properties among things that are contextually relevant (<s>prastuta</s>) or contextually irrelevant (<s>aprastuta</s>) at the level of word-meaning, that is <s>tulyayogitā</s> (equal conjunction). || 24 ||

children.text:
ivādyaprayoge hyaupanyasya gamyatvam /
tatra prākaraṇikānāmapraraṇikānāṃ vārthānāṃ samānaguṇakriyāsaṃbandhe anvitārthā tulyayogitā /

children.translated_text: For example:
'The days, whose canopies are adorned with rows of parasol-like [clouds], bear forth a bright reddish hue,
and the lotuses, blossoming by the power of the sun's rays, also attained growth.'

For when words like 'iva' (like) are not employed, the similarity is understood implicitly. Here, when contextually relevant or irrelevant things are connected by common qualities or actions with their meanings construed together, it is <s>tulyayogitā</s>.

children.text:
atra ṛtuvarṇanasya prakāntatvāddinānāṃ padmānāṃ ca prakṛtatvād vṛddhigamanaṃ kriyā /
evaṃ guṇe 'pi /

children.translated_text: For example:
'The yoga-band, the mass of matted locks, the bark garment, the deerskin —
if these are fitting for your limbs, then let it be declared so.'
Here, since the description of the season is the main topic, the days and lotuses are contextually relevant, and the attainment of growth is the action. Similarly with respect to quality:
With respect to contextually irrelevant things, for example:
'Let your horse-army charge forth! Upon the face of this [enemy], fallen [in defeat], by some slender woman with limbs delicate as blue lotus petals,

children.text: bhagnasya gūrjaranṛpasya rajaḥ kayāpi tanvyā tavāsilatayā ca yaśaḥ prabhṛṣṭam' //
children.translated_text: the dust of the broken <s>Gurjara</s> king, and your fame through the sword, have been wiped away.'
Fittingness is the quality.

children.text: atra gūrjaraṃ prati nāyikāsilatayoraprākaraṇikatve mārjanaṃ kriyā /

children.translated_text: With quality, for example:
'In whose mind does not shine the softness of your limbs, beholding
the hardness of the jasmine, the crescent moon, and the plantain?'
Here, with respect to the <s>Gurjara</s> [king], the heroine and the sword are contextually irrelevant, and the wiping away is the action.
Hardness is the quality. Thus this [figure] has been explained as fourfold.
Commentary on RuAss_24:
Sūtra

children.text: 'sādṛśya yadi gamya [śabdataḥ akathita] ho ora [kevala] prasturto athavā [kevala] aprastutoṃ kā padārthastara para samānadharma-sambandha ho to tulyayogitā [hotī hai]' //24//
children.translated_text: : 'When similarity is implied [unstated in words], if there is a connection of common properties at the level of word-meaning among either only contextually relevant or only contextually irrelevant things, that is <s>tulyayogitā</s>.' //24//
Commentary on RuAss_24a:

children.text:
evamityādinā /
gamyamānaupabhyāśrayā iti ivādyaprayogāt /
padārthamiti /
vākyārthāpikṣayā padārthapratīterantaraṅgatvāt /
tatra prathamaṃ tulyayogitāmāha - aupamyetyādi /
etadeva vyācaṣṭe - ivetyādinā /
tatretyaupamyasya gamyatve sati /
prākaraṇikānāmiti dvayoḥ samānadharmasaṃbandhasya saṃbhavādeva grahaṇasiddherbahuvacananirdeśo bahūnāṃ grahaṇārtham /
ata eva ca bahūnāmaupamyagrahaṇāyeti na vācyam /
vakṣyamāṇodāharaṇeṣu dvayoraupamyasyodbhāsamānatvāt /
evaṃ dīpake 'pi jñeyam /
anvitārtheti /
samānadharmasaṃbandhināmatra bhāvāt /
anenaiva cāsyāḥ prakṛtānāmaprakṛtānāṃ ca guṇakriyātmamakadharmayogād dvaividhyena catuṣprakāratvamatyuktam /
na cāsyātiśayoktiranuprāṇakatayā vācyā /
tāṃ vināpi vakṣyamāṇodāharaṇeṣvasyāḥ saṃbhavāt /
aupamyābhāve 'pi guṇasāmyodāharaṇadvayaṃ prācyodāhṛtatvādgranthakṛtodāhṛtam /

children.translated_text: Where, however, similarity is perceived, that is illustrated as follows:
'At the occasion of the display of jealousy, O beloved, this is fitting for you:
the faltering of your speech and the playful swaying of your gait.'

By 'evam' (thus) and so forth. 'Depending on implied similarity' means because words like 'iva' are not employed. 'Word-meaning' — because the cognition of word-meaning is more intrinsic than that of sentence-meaning. There, first <s>tulyayogitā</s> is stated by 'aupamya' etc. This itself is explained by 'iva' etc. 'There' means when similarity is implied. 'Of contextually relevant things' — since the connection of common properties is possible between two things, the plural usage indicates the inclusion of many. And therefore it need not be said 'for grasping the similarity of many things.' Because in the examples to be given, the similarity of [at least] two is manifested. The same should be understood in <s>dīpaka</s> as well. 'With construed meaning' — because the things connected by common properties exist here. And by this very fact, through the connection of contextually relevant and irrelevant things with a common property that is either a quality or an action, the fourfold classification has been stated. Nor should <s>atiśayokti</s> (hyperbole) be said to be its animating principle, because even without it, this [figure] occurs in the examples to be given. Even in the absence of similarity, the two examples of quality-based similarity are cited by the author because they were cited by earlier [scholars].
With contextually irrelevant things, for example:
'While you stand unwearied for a long time, bearing the burden of the earth,
O god, <s>Phaṇin</s> (the serpent <s>Śeṣa</s>) and <s>Kūrma</s> (the tortoise) are supremely happy.'
Here fittingness is the quality.

children.text: kecicca nāyikāmilitagroḥ prākaraṇikatvaṃ manyanta ityudāharaṇāntareṇodāhriyate yathā -
children.translated_text: Since some consider that the heroine who has met [her beloved] is also contextually relevant, it is illustrated with another example, as follows:

children.text: 'śaṃbhoryannakharaśmibhiḥ praṇamataścūḍāmaṇitve sthitā gaṅgā candrakalā ca sarvajagatāṃ vandyatvamāpāditā /
children.translated_text: 'The <s>Gaṅgā</s> and the crescent moon, established as crest-jewels by the rays of the nails of the prostrating <s>Śambhu</s>, have been brought to the state of being worshipped by all the worlds.

children.text: yuktāyāḥ paratāpadāvavipadaḥ kanyāpitṝṇāmasau dūrīkāryahimālayā kathamumāpādadvayī prāpyate' //
children.translated_text: For a woman united [with her lord], the calamities of causing pain to others [cease] — how can the pair of feet of <s>Umā</s>, from which the <s>Himālaya</s> should be kept at a distance, be attained?'
Here happiness is the quality.

children.text:
atra bhagavatīpādadvayasyaiva varṇanīyatvād gaṅgācandrakalayoraprakṛtatvam /
āpādanaṃ ca kriyā /
'bimbapratibimbabhāvenāpīyaṃ bhavati /

children.translated_text: For example:
'Casting incredible steps playfully, and mounted upon the royal swans,

children.text: kavīndravaktreṣu ca yatra śāradā sahastrapatreṣu ramā ca rajyati' //
children.translated_text: there <s>Śāradā</s> (Sarasvatī) delights in the mouths of great poets, and <s>Ramā</s> (Lakṣmī) in the thousand-petaled lotuses.'

Here, since only the pair of feet of the Goddess is the subject of description, the <s>Gaṅgā</s> and crescent moon are contextually irrelevant. And the bringing about (<s>āpādana</s>) is the action. 'This also occurs in the mode of object and reflection (<s>bimba-pratibimba</s>).

children.text:
atra vaktrapadmayorbimbapratibimbabhāvaḥ /
anenaiva cāśayenātrālaṅkāravārtike granthakṛtā vaiśiṣṭyamasyāḥ darśitam /

children.translated_text: In the form of pure generality, for example:

children.text: 'āstāṃ tālasya saṃniddhe dve dhātryī tasya vṛddhaye /
children.translated_text: 'Let two nurses stand near the palm tree for its growth:
one who causes the flow of milk, and the other who produces all prosperity.'

Here there is the object-reflection relationship between mouths and lotuses. And it is with this very intention that the author has shown the distinctive feature of this [figure] in the <s>Alaṅkāravārttika</s>.
Here the flowing has the form of pure generality. Thus by 'evam' etc.
Commentary on RuAss_24b:
Concluding this [topic], he introduces another.
Beginning of Sūtra 25:
Having established <s>tulyayogitā</s> when the contextually relevant and irrelevant are separate, <s>dīpaka</s> (illuminator) is now described when they are combined:
When [they are] of the contextually relevant and irrelevant together, it is <s>dīpaka</s> (illumination). || 25 ||

children.text:
aupamyasya gamyatva ityādyanuvartate /
prākaraṇikāprākaraṇikayormadhyādekatra nirdiṣṭaḥ samāno dharmaḥ prasaṅganānyatropakārāddīpanāddīpasādṛśyena dīpakākhyālaṅkārotthāpakaḥ /
tatrevādyaprayogādupamānopameyabhāvo gamyamānaḥ /
sa ca vāstava eva /
pūrvatra śuddhaprākaraṇikatve śuddhāprākaṇikatvai vā vaivakṣikaḥ, prākaraṇikatvanirvartitatvādupamānopameyabhāvasya /
anekasyaikakriyābhisaṃbandhādaucityātpadārthatvoktiḥ /
vastutastu vākyārthatve ādimadhyāntavākyagatatvena dharmasya vṛttāvādibhamadhyāntadīpakākhyāstrayo 'sya bhedāḥ /
children.translated_text: The phrase 'when similarity is implied' etc. continues from before. When a common property stated with respect to one of the contextually relevant and irrelevant items illuminates the other by association — like a lamp, hence it is called <s>dīpaka</s> (illuminator), giving rise to the figure of that name. And here too, because words like 'iva' are not used, the relation of <s>upamāna</s> (standard of comparison) and <s>upameya</s> (thing compared) is implied. And that is indeed real. In the previous case [of <s>tulyayogitā</s>], when there is pure contextual relevance or pure contextual irrelevance, it is discretionary, because the <s>upamāna-upameya</s> relationship is established by contextual relevance. The statement that it pertains to word-meaning is because of the propriety of multiple things being connected to a single action. But in reality, when it pertains to sentence-meaning, through the property being located in the beginning, middle, or end of the sentence, there are three varieties of this [figure] known in practice as <s>ādi-dīpaka</s>, <s>madhya-dīpaka</s>, and <s>anta-dīpaka</s>.
Commentary on RuAss_25:

children.text:
prastutāprastutānāmiti /
ekatreti prākaraṇike 'prākaraṇike vā /
anyatreti prākaraṇikādau dīpaketi 'saṃjñāyām' ityanena kan /
sādṛśyena samudāyagamyāyāḥ saṃjñāyā abhāvāt /
tatreti dīpake /
vāstava iti /
prakṛtāprakṛtayorupamānopameyarūpatvāt /
pūrvatreti tulyayogitāyām /
iyāneva ca dīpakatulyayogitayorviśeṣo 'stītyapyanena darśitam /
na caitāvataivānayoḥ pṛthaglakṣaṇaṃ yuktam /
aupamyagarbhatvākhyasya sāmānyasya dvayorapyanugamāt /
evaṃ ca samucitopamāderapi pṛthaglakṣaṇaṃ syāt /
granthakṛtā punaścirantanānurodhātkṛtam /
vaivakṣika iti /
yatraiva vakturupamānatvamupameyatvaṃ vā vaktumiṣṭaṃ tatraiva prakaraṇādibalādāśrayaṇīyamityarthaḥ /
ataśca 'prastutasya tu nānyena vyabhicārasya darśanāt' iti nītyāprastutāprastutatvamātranibandhana evopamānopameyabhāvo na bhavatīti bhāvaḥ /
evaṃ 'prasiddhenāprasiddhasya sādṛśyamupamā matā'ityādidṛśā prasiddhāprasiddhatvamātranibandhano 'pyupamānopameyabhāvo na vācyaḥ /
'khamiva jalaṃ jalamiva kham' ityādau dvayorapi tulyatvāt prasiddhaguṇatvādyabhāve 'pyupamānopameyabhāvasyeṣṭervyabhicārasya darśasanāt /
nanu cātra sādharmya vākyārthagatatvenaiva pratīyata iti kathaṃ tasya padārthagatatvamuktamityāśaṅkyāha-anekasyetyādi /
evaṃ pūrvatrāpi jñeyam /
children.translated_text: 'Of the contextually relevant and irrelevant' — 'in one' means in the contextually relevant or irrelevant. 'In the other' means beginning from the contextually relevant. '<s>Dīpaka</s>' — with the suffix 'kan' according to [the rule] 'in the sense of a name.' Because there is no name conveyed by the aggregate [of meanings]. 'There' means in <s>dīpaka</s>. 'Real' — because the contextually relevant and irrelevant have the nature of <s>upamāna</s> and <s>upameya</s>. 'In the previous' means in <s>tulyayogitā</s>. And by this, the specific difference between <s>dīpaka</s> and <s>tulyayogitā</s> has been shown. Nor is a separate definition of these two justified merely on this basis, since the general property called 'containing similarity' applies to both. And thus <s>samucita-upamā</s> etc. would also require separate definitions. But the author has done so following earlier authorities. 'Discretionary' means — wherever the speaker wishes to express the nature of <s>upamāna</s> or <s>upameya</s>, there it should be adopted on the strength of context etc. And therefore, the <s>upamāna-upameya</s> relationship is not based merely on the contextual relevance or irrelevance, according to the rule 'because deviation of the relevant [from being compared] with another is observed.' Similarly, the <s>upamāna-upameya</s> relationship based merely on being well-known or not well-known, as in 'similarity of the unknown with the known is considered <s>upamā</s>,' should also not be stated, because in cases like 'the sky is like water, water is like the sky,' both being equal, even in the absence of a well-known quality etc., the <s>upamāna-upameya</s> relationship is desired, and deviation is observed. Now, if the common property here is perceived only as pertaining to sentence-meaning, how can it be said to pertain to word-meaning? Anticipating this doubt, he says 'of many' etc. The same should be understood in the previous case as well.
Examples of RuAss_25/1:

children.text: krameṇodāharaṇam - 'rehai mihireṇa ṇahaṃ raseṇa kavvaṃ sareṇa jovvaṇaaṃ /
children.translated_text: Examples in order: 'The sky shines by the sun, poetry by <s>rasa</s> (aesthetic sentiment), youth by love,
the course of the river by nectar, O lord of men, and this world [by you].'

children.text: ('reyate mihireṇa nabho rasena kāvyaṃ sareṇa [smareṇa] yauvanam amṛtena dhunīdhavaḥsvayā naramātha! bhuvanamidam' //)//
children.translated_text: (Sanskrit rendering: 'The sky shines by the sun, poetry by <s>rasa</s>, youth by love (<s>smara</s>), the river's course by nectar, O lord of men, this world [by you].')
'Having purified the regions of the sky through their movement, to return to their resting place at the day's end,

children.text: pracakrame pallavarāgatāmrā prabhā pataṅgasya munaśca dhenuḥ' //
children.translated_text: the glow of the sun, red as fresh sprouts, and the sage's cow set forth.'
'The wealth of the miserly, the crest-jewel of serpents, the manes of lions,
the breasts of well-born maidens — how can the dead touch [these]?'
(Sanskrit rendering: 'The wealth of the miserly, the crest-jewel of serpents (<s>nāgas</s>), the manes of lions,
the breasts of well-born maidens — how can the dead touch [these]?')

children.text:
evamekakriyaṃ dīpakatrayaṃ nirṇītam /
atra ca yathānekakārakagatatvennaikakriyā dīpakaṃ tathānekakriyāgatatvenaikakārakamapi dīpakam /

children.translated_text: For example:
'To assist the virtuous, to sustain <s>Lakṣmī</s>, to traverse the sky,

children.text: na kutūhali kasya manaścaritaṃ ca mahātmanāṃ śrotum' //
children.translated_text: whose mind is not eager to hear the deeds of great souls?'

Thus the three [types of] single-action <s>dīpaka</s> have been determined. And here, just as a single action constitutes <s>dīpaka</s> through being related to multiple case-relations (<s>kārakas</s>), so too does a single case-relation constitute <s>dīpaka</s> through being related to multiple actions.

children.text:
atropakaraṇādyanekakriyākartṛtvena kutūhalaviśiṣṭaṃ mano nirdiṣṭam /
chāyānrareṇa tu mālādīpakaṃ prastāvāntare lakṣyayiṣyate /
children.translated_text: Here the mind, qualified by eagerness, is stated as the agent of multiple actions such as assisting etc. The <s>mālā-dīpaka</s> (garland-illumination) will be illustrated elsewhere in another context by <s>Chāyānara</s>.
Commentary on RuAss_25/1:
Since the cow and the twilight are both contextually relevant, others consider this to be <s>tulyayogitā</s>; therefore it is illustrated with another example:
'By the pursuit of <s>dharma</s> for some, and for some by the pursuit of <s>artha</s> (wealth), it passes away;

children.text: kāmajjaṇeṇa kāṇa vi kāṇa vi emea saṃsāro' //
children.translated_text: by the pursuit of <s>kāma</s> (desire) for some, and for some — thus indeed is <s>saṃsāra</s> (worldly existence).'
(Sanskrit rendering: 'By the pursuit of <s>dharma</s> for some, and for some by the pursuit of <s>artha</s>, it passes;
by the pursuit of <s>kāma</s> for some, and for some — thus indeed is <s>saṃsāra</s>.')
That is as follows:
'Below, the thousand-hooded one [<s>Śeṣa</s>]; in heaven, the thousand-eyed one [<s>Indra</s>];
and on earth, you, O unrivalled one, the bearer of a thousand names.'
By the phrase 'single-action,' it is indicated that single-quality <s>dīpaka</s> should also be illustrated by the reader himself.

children.text:
advitīyatvaṅguṇaḥ /
evamekāṃ kriyāṃ guṇaṃ vānekakārakagatatvenābhidhāya tadeva ca dṛṣṭāntīkṛtyaikakārakamapyanekakriyāgatatvena dīpakaṃ bhavatītyāha-atretyādi /
atra cocchravāsavarṇanīyaṃ bhairavācāryādisaktamupakārakāraṇādiviśeṣarūpaṃ prastutaṃ śrotṝnavabodhayituṃ kavikartṛkamidaṃ sādhūpakārakaraṇādīnāṃ sāmānyānāmaprastutānāṃ praśaṃsanam /
teṣāṃ ca sāmānyānāṃ parasparamaupamyapratīterekakārakagatatveneyaṃ kārakatulyayogitā /
ataśca nedaṃ kārakadīpakasyodāharaṇam /

children.translated_text: That is as follows:

children.text: 'āliṅgituṃ śaśimukhīṃ ca sudhāṃ ca pātuṃ kīrti ca sādhayitumarjayituṃ ca lakṣmīm /
children.translated_text: 'To embrace a moon-faced woman, to drink nectar, to accomplish fame, to acquire wealth,

children.text: tvadbhaktimadbhatarasāṃ hṛdaye ca kartuṃ mandādaraṃ janamahaṃ paśumeva jāne' //
children.translated_text: and to create devotion in your devotees' hearts — I consider a person who is indifferent to these as a mere animal.'

Unrivalledness is the quality. Thus, having stated a single action or quality as related to multiple case-relations, and then making that very thing an illustration, a single case-relation related to multiple actions also constitutes <s>dīpaka</s> — this is stated by 'here' etc. And here, what is to be described is the exaltation, connected with <s>Bhairavācārya</s> and others, in the specific form of helpful agents etc. — this is the contextually relevant topic, and the poet's praise of the general [qualities] of helping the virtuous etc., which are contextually irrelevant, serves to make the audience understand. And the mutual perception of similarity among those general qualities, being related to a single case-relation, constitutes <s>kāraka-tulyayogitā</s> (case-relation equal conjunction). Therefore this is not an example of <s>kāraka-dīpaka</s>.

children.text:
atrāliṅganādyanekakriyākartṛtvenaika eva jano nirdiṣṭaḥ /
prastutāprastutaṃ sphuṭameva /
children.translated_text: Here a single person is stated as the agent of multiple actions such as embracing etc. The contextually relevant and irrelevant are quite clear.
Commentary on RuAss_25/1a:

children.text: svidyati kūṇati vellati vivalati nimiṣati vilokayati tiryak /
children.translated_text: She sweats, she squints, she trembles, she becomes agitated, she blinks, she glances sideways,
she rejoices inwardly, she desires to be kissed — [such is] the newly married bride on the bed.

children.text:
ityatra tu svaidanādikriyāṇāṃ prastutānāmekādhāragatatvena samuccīyamānatvācca samuccayālaṅkāro na tu kārakadīpakam /
taddhi prastutāprastutānāṃ kriyāṇāmaupamyasadbhāve bhavati /
evaṃ sardhakriyāṇāṃ prastutatve 'pi samucyayasyopamyābhāvādeva tulyayogitāto 'pi bhedaḥ /
aupamyasadbhāve 'pi tulyayogitaiva /

children.translated_text: For example:
'He who showed forbearance toward the weak and even toward transgressors,
and he who endured even the innocent among the powerful.'

Here, however, since the contextually relevant actions of sweating etc. pertain to a single subject and are being enumerated together, this is the figure of <s>samuccaya</s> (accumulation), not <s>kāraka-dīpaka</s>. For that [<s>kāraka-dīpaka</s>] occurs when there is similarity between contextually relevant and irrelevant actions. Similarly, even when all the actions are contextually relevant, because of the absence of similarity in mere accumulation, it differs from <s>tulyayogitā</s> as well. When similarity is present, it is <s>tulyayogitā</s> itself.

children.text:
atra karaṇaharaṇayoḥ prakṛtatvam /
dvayorapi rājagatatvena varṇanīyatvāt /
children.translated_text: Here, the taking (<s>karaṇa</s>) and the removing (<s>haraṇa</s>) are what is under discussion, since both pertain to the king and are thus fit subjects for poetic description.
[Reference marker: <s>Ruyyaka</s>'s commentary on <s>Alaṃkārasarvasva</s>, verse 25/1b]
For example:

children.text: 'maṇiḥ śāṇellīḍhaḥ samaravijayī hetinihataḥ kalaśeṣaścandraḥ suratamṛditā bālallanā /
children.translated_text: 'A gem polished on the whetstone, a warrior victorious in battle yet struck by weapons, the moon at the end of its waning, a young woman exhausted by lovemaking,

children.text: madakṣīṇo nāgaḥ śaradi saridāśyānapulinā tanimnā śobhante galitavibhavāścārthiṣu janāḥ' //
children.translated_text: an elephant weakened by rut, a river in autumn with its sandy banks exposed — all these are beautiful in their diminished state, just as people who have lost their wealth are beautiful in the eyes of supplicants.'
This also occurs in the form of <s>bimbapratibimbabhāva</s> (object-and-reflection relationship).
An example of the pure common-property form (<s>śuddhasāmānyarūpatva</s>) is as follows:
'Adorned with the royal markings of its hood, the lord of serpents (<s>bhujaṅganātha</s>) supports the earth;
Likewise, O lord, your arm-staff (<s>bhujadaṇḍa</s>), marked with scars of battle and resplendent with glory, also upholds it.'
Here, the qualities such as 'being polished on a whetstone' and so on stand in an object-reflection (<s>bimbapratibimba</s>) relationship.

children.text:
atra rājitatvaśobhitatvayoḥ śuddhasāmānyarūpatvam /
nanvetadanantarameva mālādīpakamanyairlakṣaghitaṃ tadihāpi kiṃ na lakṣyata ityāśaṅkyāha-chāyetyādi /
chāyāntareṇeti śṛṅkalārūpeṇa /
prastāvāntara iti /
śṛṅkalābandhopacitarūpatvāt /
children.translated_text:
Here, the properties of 'being marked' and 'being resplendent' represent the pure common-property form.
Now, anticipating the objection that what follows immediately — namely the <s>mālādīpaka</s> (garland-lamp figure) as defined by others — should also be recognized here, the author says 'chāyā' and so on.
'By means of another shadow' means 'in the form of a chain (<s>śṛṅkalā</s>).'
'On another occasion' — because it takes on the form of an accumulated chain-binding.
[Beginning of <s>Sūtra</s> 26]

When the common property, by virtue of being situated at the level of sentence-meaning, is expressed separately in two sentences, it is <s>prativastūpamā</s> (counter-example simile). [<s>Alaṃkārasarvasva</s>, sūtra 26]

children.text:
padārthārabdho vākyārtha iti padārthagatālaṅkārānantaraṃ vākyārthagatālaṅkāraprastāvaḥ /
tatra sāmānyadharmasyevādyupādāne sakṛnnirdeśe upamā /
vastuprativastubhāvenāsakṛnnirdeśe 'pi saiva /
ivādyanupādāne sakṛnnirdeśe upamā /
vastuprativastubhāvenāsakṛnnirdeśe tu śuddhasāmānyarūpatvaṃ bimbapratibimbabhāvo vā /
ādyaḥ prakāraḥ prativastūpamā /
vastu-śabdasya vākyārthavācitve prativāvākyārthamupamā sāmyamityanvarthāśrayaṇāt /
kevalaṃ kāvyasamayātparyāyāntareṇa pṛthaṅnirdeśaḥ /
dvitīyaprakārāśrayeṇa dṛṣṭānto vakṣyate /
tadevamaupamyāśrayeṇaiva prativastūpamā /

children.translated_text: For example:
'Only the <s>cakora</s> birds are clever at the task of sipping moonlight;
only the women of <s>Avantī</s> are skilled in the sport of love.'

Since sentence-meaning is constituted by word-meanings, after discussing figures pertaining to word-meanings, the occasion arises for discussing figures pertaining to sentence-meaning.
In that context: when the common property is presented once with 'iva' (like) and similar particles, it is <s>upamā</s> (simile).
Even when presented more than once, in the manner of an object and its counterpart, it is still the same simile.
When 'iva' and similar particles are not employed, and the property is stated once, it is <s>upamā</s>.
But when stated more than once in object-counterpart fashion without 'iva,' it is either pure common-property form (<s>śuddhasāmānyarūpatva</s>) or object-reflection relationship (<s>bimbapratibimbabhāva</s>).
The first variety is <s>prativastūpamā</s>.
Since the word <s>vastu</s> means 'sentence-meaning,' <s>prativastūpamā</s> etymologically means 'simile corresponding to each sentence-meaning,' relying on the transparent meaning of the compound.
However, by poetic convention, the separate statement is made using a different synonym.
The second variety, based on the reflection mode, will be discussed as <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> (illustration).
Thus, <s>prativastūpamā</s> is based solely on the relation of likeness (<s>aupamya</s>).

children.text:
atra caturatvaṃ sādhāraṇe dharmaṃ upamānavākye, upameyavākye tu nipuṇapadena nirdiṣṭaḥ /
na kevasamiyaṃ sādharmyeṇa yāvad vaidharmyeṇāpi /
yathātraivottarasthāne 'vināvantīrna nipuṇāḥ sudṛśo ratanarmaṇi' iti pāṭhe /
children.translated_text:
Here, 'cleverness' is the common property stated in the illustrating sentence (<s>upamānavākya</s>), while in the illustrated sentence (<s>upameyavākya</s>) it is expressed by the word 'skilled' (<s>nipuṇa</s>).
This figure operates not only through similarity (<s>sādharmya</s>) but also through dissimilarity (<s>vaidharmya</s>).
As in the alternative reading in the latter position of this very example: 'Without the women of <s>Avantī</s>, none are skilled in the sport of love.'
[Reference marker: <s>Ruyyaka</s>'s commentary on <s>Alaṃkārasarvasva</s>, sūtra 26]

children.text:
vākyārthetyādi /
etadeva vyākhyātumalaṅkārāntaraiḥ sahāsyā vibhāgaṃ darśayati-tatretyādinā /
'tayā sa pūtaśca vibhūṣitaśca' ityatropamāyāṃ sakṛnnirdeśaḥ /
'pāṇḍyo 'yamaṃsārpitalambahāraḥ' ityādāvapi cāsakṛnnirdeśaḥ /
tadevabhivādyupādāne sādhāraṇadharmasya yathāsaṃbhavaṃ svarūpaṃ nirūpyevādyanupādāne 'pi nirūpayati-ivādītyādinā /
yadyapi dīpakatulyayogitayoḥ sāmānyasyāsakṛnnirdeśo 'pi saṃbhavati, tathāpi sakṛnnirdeśaṃ vinā tayoranutthānāttadeveha prādhānyenoktam /
asakṛnnirdeśaśca dvidhā bhavatītyāha-asakṛdityādi /
ādyaḥ prakāra iti śuddhasāmānyarūpatvam /
yadi cātra sāmānyasyaikarūpatvamevāsti tartki paryāyāntareṇa pṛthaṅnirdeśaḥ kriyata ityāśaṅkyāha-kevalamityādi /
yaduktam-'naikaṃ padaṃ dviḥ prayojyaṃ prāyeṇa' iti /
bimbapratibimbabhāvo dvitīyaḥ prakāraḥ /
evametadupasaṃharan prakṛtameva siddhāntayati-tadevamityādinā /
aupamyāśrayeṇeti /
etadabhidadhatā granthakṛtā prativastūpamāyā dṛṣṭāntābhedo darśitaḥ /
yato 'syāḥ prakṛtārthasya viśeṣābhidhitsayā sādṛśyārthamaprakṛtamarthāntaramupādīyate,ata eva cātra prakṛtāprakṛtayorupamānopameyabhāvaḥ /
dṛṣṭante puraretādṛśo vṛttānto 'nyatrāpi sthita iti prakṛtasyārthasyāvispaṣṭā pratītirbhā bhūditi pratītiviśadīkaraṇārthamarthāntaramupādīyate /
ata evātrārthāntaropādānaṃ prakṛtasya na kvāpyupayuktamapi tu pratipattaḥ prakṛtārthapratīteravispaṣṭatānirāsāt /
kecicca dṛṣṭānte dvayoḥ samarthyasamarthakabhāvenānayorbhāvenānarbhedamāhuḥ /
tadasat /
yataḥ svarūpayorvaśeṣayoḥ samarthyasamarthakabhāvo na bhavati /
vastvantareṇa vastvantarasiddhyanupapatteḥ /
sa hi sāmānyaviśeṣayoreva bhavati /
sāmānyasya niyamena viśeṣaniṣṭatvādviśeṣasya ca niyamena sāmānyāśrayatvāt /
yadi cātra samarthyasamarthakabhāvaḥ syādarthāntaranyāsādasya pṛthagalaṅkāratā na syāt /
samarthyasamarthakabhāvātmanaḥ sāmānyasyobhayatrāpyanugamāt /
anye punarubhayatrāpyārthamaupamyamāśritya sāmānyasya śuddhasāmānyarūpatvabimbapratibimbabhāvābhyāṃ vyavasthiteranayorbhedamāhuḥ /
tadapyasat /
etāvataivaupamyākhyasya sāmānyalakṣaṇasyānugatatvādupamābhedavadanayoḥ pṛthagalaṅkāratvānupapatteḥ /
tadevaṃ vākyanairapūkṣye 'pi vaktṛpratipattroreva viśeṣādayorbhedaḥ siddhaḥ /
vaidharmyeṇāpīti /
bhavatīti śeṣaḥ /
children.translated_text:
The words 'vākyārtha' and so on.
To explain this very point, the author shows the distinction of this figure from other figures by means of the passage beginning 'tatra' and so on.
In the verse 'By her he was both purified and adorned,' there is a single statement of the simile.
In the verse beginning 'This <s>Pāṇḍya</s> with his long garland resting on his shoulder' and so on, there is also a repeated statement.
Thus, having determined the nature of the common property as far as possible when 'iva' and similar particles are employed, the author also determines it when they are not employed, with the words 'ivādi' and so on.
Although in <s>dīpaka</s> (illumination) and <s>tulyayogitā</s> (equal conjunction) the common property may also be stated more than once, nevertheless since these two cannot arise without a single statement, that alone is stated here as primary.
And the repeated statement is of two kinds, as the author says with 'asakṛt' and so on.
The first variety is the pure common-property form.
Anticipating the objection that if there is only a single form of the common property here, then the separate statement should use different synonyms, the author says 'kevalam' and so on.
As has been stated elsewhere: 'Generally, the same word should not be used twice.'
The object-reflection relationship is the second variety.
Summarizing this and establishing the main thesis, the author says 'tadevm' and so on.
'Based on likeness' — by saying this, the author of the treatise has shown that <s>prativastūpamā</s> is not different from <s>dṛṣṭānta</s>.
For in this figure, in order to express the specific meaning of the primary subject, a secondary, non-primary matter is introduced for the sake of resemblance; and hence the primary and non-primary stand in the relationship of <s>upameya</s> (compared) and <s>upamāna</s> (standard of comparison).
In <s>dṛṣṭānta</s>, however, since a precedent of similar nature is cited to clarify the understanding of the primary subject — which might otherwise remain unclear — a secondary matter is introduced for the purpose of making the cognition vivid.
Therefore, the introduction of the other matter in <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> does not serve the primary subject in any way; rather, it serves the listener by removing the lack of clarity in understanding the primary meaning.
Some say that in <s>dṛṣṭānta</s>, since both stand in the relationship of proving and that which is to be proved, there is no difference between these two.
That is incorrect.
For between two particular things as such, there cannot be a proving-proved relationship,
since one particular thing cannot establish another particular thing.
That relationship exists only between the universal and the particular.
Because the universal necessarily resides in the particular, and the particular necessarily depends on the universal.
If there were a proving-proved relationship here, then this figure would not be a separate <s>alaṃkāra</s> (figure of speech) distinct from <s>arthāntaranyāsa</s> (corroboration),
since the universal, which consists of the proving-proved relationship, would pervade both cases.
Others, relying on the relation of likeness in both cases, say the difference between these two lies in the common property being distinguished as either pure common-property form or object-reflection relationship.
That too is incorrect,
since the common characteristic called 'likeness' pervades both equally, and therefore — just as with varieties of <s>upamā</s> — there would be no justification for treating them as separate figures.
Thus, even though the sentences may be identical in form, the difference between these figures is established based on the intention of the speaker and the understanding of the listener.
'Through dissimilarity also' — 'it occurs' is to be supplied.
[Beginning of <s>Sūtra</s> 27]
When that very [common property] is also expressed in the manner of object-and-reflection, it is <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> (illustration). [<s>Alaṃkārasarvasva</s>, sūtra 27]

children.text:
taṣṇāpīti na kevalamupamānopameyayoḥ /
tacchabdena sāmānyadharmaḥ pratyavamṛṣṭaḥ /
ayamapi sādharmyavaidharmyābhyāṃ dvividhaḥ /

children.translated_text: The first is illustrated as follows:

children.text: 'abdhirlaṅghita eva vānarabhaṭaiḥ kiṃ tvasya gambhīratā- , māpātālanimagnapīvaratanurjānāti manthācalaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'The ocean was indeed crossed by the monkey-warriors, but does the mountain <s>Manthācala</s>, whose massive body sank to the netherworld, truly know its depth?

children.text: devīṃ vācamupāsate hi bahyavaḥ sāraṃ tu sārastvataṃ jānīte nitarāmasau gurukulakliṣṭo murāriḥ kaviḥ' //
children.translated_text: Many worship the goddess of speech (<s>Devī Vāc</s>), but only that poet <s>Murāri</s>, who toiled long at the feet of his master, truly knows her essence.'

'That also' — not merely of the <s>upamāna</s> (standard of comparison) and <s>upameya</s> (compared subject).
The word 'tat' refers to the common property just discussed.
This too is of two kinds: through similarity (<s>sādharmya</s>) and through dissimilarity (<s>vaidharmya</s>).

children.text:
atra yadyapi ñcānākhya eko dharmo nirdiṣṭastathāpi na tannibandhanamaupabhyaṃ vivakṣitam /
yannibandhanaṃ ca vivakṣitaṃ tatrābdhilaṅghanādāvastyeva divyavāgupāsanādinā pratibimbanam /

children.translated_text: The second is illustrated as follows:

children.text: 'kṛtaṃ ca garvābhimukhaṃ manastvayā kimanyadevaṃ nihatāśca no 'rayaḥ /
children.translated_text: 'You have indeed made your mind incline toward pride — what more is there to say? — and our enemies have been slain.
For darkness persists only so long as the sun has not yet reached the crest of the eastern mountain.'

Here, although one property — namely depth — is stated, the likeness intended is not based on that alone.
Rather, the reflection-relationship occurs through the ocean-crossing and so on finding their counterpart in the worship of divine speech and similar acts.
Here, the reflection-relationship of the property of 'being slain' occurs through dissimilarity with 'remaining' and so on.
[Reference marker: <s>Ruyyaka</s>'s commentary on <s>Alaṃkārasarvasva</s>, sūtra 27]

children.text:
tasyāpīti [sāmānyadharmasyāpītyarthaḥ] upamānopameyayoriti /
prakṛtāprakṛtayordharmiṇorityarthaḥ /
ataśca dharmāṇāṃ dharmiṇāṃ ca bimbapratibimbabhāvena nirdeśo 'yamalaṅkāraḥ /
yaduktamanyatrāpi-'dṛṣṭāntaḥ punareteṣāṃ sarveṣāṃ pratibimbanam' iti /
upamānopameyayoriti tu svārthaeva na vyākhyeyam,arthāntarasya prakṛtadārḍhyāyopādānātsādṛśyāvivakṣaṇāt /
ādya iti sādharmyeṇa /

children.translated_text: Or, for example:

children.text: 'sthāneṣu śiṣyanivahaiḥ pratipādyamānā vidyā guruṃ hi guṇavattaramātanoti /
children.translated_text: 'Knowledge (<s>vidyā</s>), being imparted by groups of students in [various] institutions, indeed makes the teacher all the more distinguished;

children.text: ādāya śuktiṣu balāhakaviprakīrṇai ratnākaro bhavati vāribhiramburāśiḥ' //
children.translated_text: The ocean becomes a mine of gems through the waters scattered by the rain-clouds and received in the oyster-shells.'

'That also' means 'of the common property also.' 'Of the <s>upamāna</s> and <s>upameya</s>' means 'of the two substrates — the primary and the non-primary subject.'
Thus, this figure involves the expression of both the properties and the substrates in an object-reflection manner.
As stated elsewhere too: '<s>Dṛṣṭānta</s> is the reflection of all of these.'
The phrase 'of <s>upamāna</s> and <s>upameya</s>' should not be interpreted in its literal sense, because since the secondary matter is introduced for strengthening the primary subject, resemblance is not the intended import.
'The first' means through similarity.

children.text:
atra sthānādīnāṃ śuktyādibhiḥ pratibimbanam /
yannibandhanaṃ ceti /
arthālaṅkāratvaṃ na punaraupamyam /
tasya ca samanantaroktayurktyāsaṃbhavāt /
children.translated_text:
Here, the institutions and similar elements find their reflection in the oyster-shells and similar elements.
'On the basis of which' — it is a figure of meaning (<s>arthālaṅkāra</s>), not a figure of likeness.
And the impossibility of that [likeness] follows from the reasoning just stated.
[Beginning of <s>Sūtra</s> 28]

children.text: saṃbhāvatāsaṃbhavatā vā vastusaṃbandhena gamyamānaṃ pratibimbakaraṇaṃ nidarśanā || 28 ||
children.translated_text: When the reflection-making is apprehended through a relation of things that is either possible or impossible, it is <s>nidarśanā</s> (exemplification). [<s>Alaṃkārasarvasva</s>, sūtra 28]

children.text:
pratibimbakaraṇaprastāvenāsyā lakṣaṇam /
tatra kkacitsaṃbhavanneva vastusaṃbandhaḥ svasāmarthyāddhimbapratibimbabhāvaṃ kalpayati /
kvacitpunaranvayabādhādasaṃbhāvatā vastusaṃbandhena pratibimbanamākṣipyate /

children.translated_text: An example with a possible relation between things is as follows:
'He who bears the sun-god upon his head in the position of a crest-jewel,
thereby instructing householders (<s>gṛhamedhin</s>) that hospitality to the virtuous is a duty.'

In the context of discussing reflection-making, the definition of this figure is given.
In some cases, a relation between things that is indeed possible, by its own power, constructs the object-reflection relationship.
In other cases, however, due to the impossibility of logical connection, the reflection is suggested through a relation of things that cannot actually obtain.
An example with an impossible relation between things is as follows:
'May that moon protect you — naturally curved, touching the playful sport of <s>Smara</s>'s (Cupid's) bow when strung,
its two tips licked by the rays of the jewel on the great serpent's head, which is bound in <s>Jaṭā</s>'s (Śiva's) matted locks.'

Here, the word 'instructing' (<s>bodhayan</s>) with the causal suffix (<s>ṇic</s>) is used in the sense of an action that is competent to produce the result; hence the relation between the things is possible.

Here, the touching of the playful sport — which pertains to <s>Smara</s>'s bow — by the moon, which is an entirely different entity, is impossible; and since this suggests a playful quality resembling that sport, the construction of reflection is said to arise from the great distance [between the two terms].
[Reference marker: <s>Ruyyaka</s>'s commentary on <s>Alaṃkārasarvasva</s>, sūtra 28]

children.text:
saṃbhavatetyādi /
bimbapratibimbabhāvamiti upamānopameyatvamityarthaḥ /
dharmadharmiṇorabhedopakṣārāt /
evaṃ cātra nidarśatāyāṃ sādṛśyāvinābhāvaḥ /

children.translated_text: Therefore:
'In the morning, the companions ask the newly-wed bride about the secret events of the night; she, with face closed like a bud in modesty, does not speak of them.

children.text: likhantīnāṃ pattrāṅkuramaniśamasyāstu kucayoścamatkāro gūḍhaṃ karajapadamāsāṃ prathayati' //
children.translated_text: But the nail-marks on her breasts, constantly being sketched as leaf-patterns, reveal the wonder — those marks of her companions' fingers disclose the secret.'

'Is possible' and so on.
'The object-reflection relationship' means the relationship of <s>upamāna</s> and <s>upameya</s>, because of the implicit identification of property and substrate.
Thus in this figure of <s>nidarśanā</s>, the inseparability from resemblance is established.

children.text:
ityādau saṃbhavatyapi vastusaṃbandhe prathanasyaupamyābhāvānna nidarśanālaṅkāratvamṣa /
anenaiva vastusaṃbandhasya saṃbhavāsaṃbhavābhyāmasyā bhedadvayamapyuktam /
tadevodāharati-cūḍāmaṇītvādinā /
tatsamarthācaraṇe prayogāditi 'kārīṣo 'dhyāpayati' ityādivat /
abhyāgatasya ravergiriṇā śirasā dhāraṇaṃ tatsamarthācaraṇam /
ata evātra bodhayanniti ṇicastatsamarthā caraṇe prayogānmayeva bhavadvibharapyatithisaparyā kāryeti saṃbhavatsaṃbandhamūlamatrārthamaupamyam /
evaṃ ca parvatasya bodhanakriyākartṛtvāsaṃbhavādevādevābhimantṛvyāpāropārohābhāvānnātra pratīyamānotprekṣā /
nāpi smṛtyalaṅkāraḥ /
gṛhamedhināṃ parvatakartṛkasya sadviṣayātithyabodhakatvasyavākṣyārthatvāt /
tatra hi sadṛśadarśanādvastvantarasya smṛtirbhavati /
nacātra gṛhamedhināṃ ravidarśanādatithismṛtau kartṛtvam /
teṣāṃ sadātithyakartavyatāyā bodhyatvāt /
nāpyatra raviṇātitheratithinā vā raveḥ sāmyaṃvivakṣitam /
api tu mayeva gṛhamedhibhirapi satāmātithyaṅkāryamiti /
ata eva nātra vastvantarakaraṇātmāpi viśeṣālaṅkāraḥ /
tapānāvagame 'tithyāderasaṃbhāvyasyāvagamo jāta ityevamātmikāyāḥ pratipatterabhāvāt /
ataśca satyasati vā saṃbandhe nidṛśaṃneti vācyam /
tena yathoktameva bhedadvayaṃ syāt /
asaṃbhavaditi /
dharmyantarasaṃbandhino dharmasya dhamyantare 'nyadāyogāt /
adraviprakarṣāditi /
dharmamukhenasādṛśyasya kiñcitpratyāsaccatvāt /

children.translated_text: Or, for example:
'Horripilation on the body, trembling of the limbs, speaking with sighs —

children.text: savvaṃ sisireṇa kaaṃ jaṃ kāavvaṃ piaameṇa' //
children.translated_text: all this was done by the cold, which was to be done by the beloved.'

In this and similar cases, even though a relation between things is possible, since the act of revealing lacks the character of likeness (<s>aupamya</s>), there is no figure of <s>nidarśanā</s>.
By this very reasoning, the two varieties of this figure — based on whether the relation between things is possible or impossible — have been stated.
The author illustrates this very point with the verse about the crest-jewel and so on.
'Because of its use in an action competent to produce the result' — just as in the expression 'the dried dung teaches' and similar usages.
The bearing of the approaching sun upon the head by the mountain is an action competent to produce the result.
Therefore, since here the causal form 'instructing' is used in the sense of an action competent to produce the result, the likeness — whose basis is a possible relation, namely 'just as by me, so too by you householders, hospitality to the virtuous should be performed' — is operative.
Thus, since the mountain cannot actually be an agent of the act of instructing, and since there is no figurative attribution of a divine will or purpose, this is not <s>pratīyamānā utprekṣā</s> (implied poetic fancy).
Nor is it the figure of <s>smṛti</s> (recollection),
since the mountain's act of instructing householders about hospitality to the virtuous is the intended sentence-meaning.
For in that figure, the seeing of a similar thing triggers the memory of another thing.
But here, the seeing of the sun does not make the householders agents of remembering hospitality;
rather, they are the objects of instruction, since the duty of hospitality is what needs to be taught to them.
Nor is the resemblance of the sun to a guest, or of a guest to the sun, what is intended here;
rather, the point is: 'Just as by me (the mountain), so too by you householders, hospitality to the virtuous should be performed.'
For this very reason, this is not the figure of <s>vastvantarakaraṇa</s> (substitution) either,
since the cognition of the form 'an inconceivable thing like hospitality has been apprehended through the comprehension of heat' does not arise here.
Therefore, whether the relation is real or unreal, what exemplifies is <s>nidarśanā</s> — this must be stated.
Hence the two varieties are exactly as described.
'Impossible' — because a property belonging to one substrate cannot logically pertain to another substrate.
'Due to the great distance' — because the resemblance, expressed through the property, has only a slight proximity.

children.text:
atra vallabhakāryasya pulakāderdharmasya vastvantarabhūtena śiśireṇa kāraṇamasaṃbhavattasya sāmyamavagamayatīti śiśirasya ballabhatulyatāpratīteraupamyam /
ataścātra dharmāṇāmasaṃbandhāt nidarśanetyuktvā pratimālaṅkāratvaṃ na vācyam /
pratibhāyāścānyodāharaṇeṣvalaṅkārāntarāviyogaḥ sphuṭa eveti na pṛthagalaṅkāratvaṃ vācyam /
evamanyeṣāmapi samagrāṇāmabhinavālaṅkārāṇāṃ cānyairanyālaṅkārayogo yojayituṃ śakya eveti granthavistarabhayādasmadarśane taddūkṣaṇoddhārasyaiva ca pratijñātatvādasmābhiḥ prātipadyena na dūṣitam /
na punaretāvataiva paramatamapratiṣiddhamanumatameveti dṛśā eṣāmapi pṛthagalaṅkāratvaṃ yuktaṃ mantavyam /
children.translated_text: Here, the property belonging to the beloved's effect -- goosebumps and the like -- being caused by cold, which is a different entity, since that is impossible, conveys its similarity -- thus from the perception of cold's equality with the beloved, there is <s>aupamya</s> (simile-relation). And therefore, here, since there is no connection of properties, one should not say it is <s>nidarśanā</s> (illustration) and then assert it is the figure <s>pratimā</s> (image). And since <s>pratibhā</s> (poetic intuition) is clearly inseparable from other figures in the other examples, it should not be asserted as a separate figure. Thus, the combination of other complete and novel figures with yet other figures can also be conjoined -- but out of fear of extending the text, and since in our view only the extraction of definitions was promised, we have not refuted [each] individually. But one should not consider that thereby the opposing view, not having been refuted, is accepted -- with this perspective, their status as separate figures too is to be considered appropriate.
[<s>Ruyyaka</s>'s <s>Alaṃkārasarvasva</s> 28/1:]
The sentence-meaning function is illustrated as follows --
"That removal of the lac-dye from the jewels of your toenails --
This is the whitening of the moon through the application of sandalwood paste."
This [<s>nidarśanā</s>] too, due to the distinction between word-meaning and sentence-meaning functions, is twofold. The word-meaning function has been illustrated just previously.

children.text:
kecittu dṛṣṭāntālaṅkāro 'yamityāhustadasat /
nirapekṣayorvākyārthayorhi bimbapratibimbabhāvo dṛṣṭāntaḥ /
yatra ca prakṛte vākyārthe vākyārthāntaramāropyate sāmānādhikaraṇyena tatra saṃbandhānupapattimūlā nidarśanaiva yuktā, na dṛṣṭāntaḥ /

children.translated_text: And thus --
"If this body, rare even in the inner apartments, belongs to a person dwelling in a hermitage,
Then surely the garden creepers have been surpassed in qualities by the forest creepers!"

Some, however, say this is the figure <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> (example) -- that is incorrect. For <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> is the relation of original and reflection between two independent sentence-meanings. But where upon the primary sentence-meaning another sentence-meaning is superimposed through co-referentiality, there, due to the impossibility of connection being the root, <s>nidarśanā</s> (illustration) alone is appropriate, not <s>dṛṣṭānta</s>.
Here, the cognition of <s>dṛṣṭānta</s> (example) should not be applied, because of the applicability of <s>nidarśanā</s> (illustration) according to the stated principle.
[Commentary on <s>Ruyyaka</s>'s <s>Alaṃkārasarvasva</s> 28/1:]

children.text:
eṣetyasaṃbhavadvastusaṃbandhanibandhanā /
na kevalaṃ nidarśanā yāvattadbhedo 'pyayaṃ dvividha ityapiśabdārthaḥ /
udāhṛteti 'avyātsa vaḥ' ityādinā /
keciditi śrīmammaṭādayaḥ / 18 a. sa. taditi dṛṣṭāntālaṅkāravacanam /
children.translated_text: 'Some' refers to the venerable <s>Mammaṭa</s> and others. 'That' refers to the statement that it is the figure <s>dṛṣṭānta</s>.

children.text:
etadanyatrāpi yojayati-evamityādinā /
uktanyāyeneti,prakṛtavākyārthe vākyārthāntarasya sāmānādhikaraṇyenādhyāropyamāṇatvāt /
ataścānyairvākyārthayoḥ sāmānādhikaraṇyanidaśācchrautāropasadbhāvena vākyārtharūpakaṃ yaduktaṃ tattāvadāstām,yatputraḥ prativastūpamodāharaṇatvamuktaṃ tadayuktameva /
nirapekṣayorvākyārthayordharmasya śuddhasāmānyarūpatve prativastūpamā /
children.translated_text: He applies this to other [examples] as well, beginning with 'evam' etc. 'According to the stated principle' means: because another sentence-meaning is being superimposed upon the primary sentence-meaning through co-referentiality. And therefore, what others have stated -- that through the co-referentiality of two sentence-meanings, due to the presence of literal superimposition, it is <s>vākyārtharūpaka</s> (sentence-level metaphor) -- let that stand aside; but what was stated by some as being an example of <s>prativastūpamā</s> (correlative simile) is entirely inappropriate. <s>Prativastūpamā</s> occurs when there is pure generic similarity of a property between two independent sentence-meanings.
And not even one of these [conditions] is possible here.
Because of the mutual dependence of the sentence-meanings and the absence of pure generic similarity, its being an example of <s>arthāpatti</s> (presumption) is also inappropriate here.
"That he seized <s>Lakṣmī</s> from the lotus while it was awake -- that is wonderful!
The pair of feet has the gait of a rutting elephant -- but what praise is there in thievery?"

'This' -- that which is grounded in the connection of an impossible entity. Not only <s>nidarśanā</s>, but its subdivision too is twofold -- this is the meaning of the word 'api' (also). 'Has been illustrated' refers to 'may he protect you' and so forth.

children.text:
ityatra tu prativastūpamodāharaṇatvaṃ pāpātpāpīyaḥ /
atra hi vākyārthayoḥ parasparaṃ sādṛśyamātramapi nāstīti kā kathā prativastūpamāyāḥ /
evaṃvidhameva cānyatra sarvālaṅkārodāharaṇeṣvāsamañjasyaṃ saṃbhavadapi samanantaroktahetudvayāśca darśitam /

children.translated_text: And thus --
"The five-arrowed one (<s>Kāma</s>) is a servant before [her]; the nectar, again, is a craftswoman of [her] face;
And even he, the moon, is a prisoner of [her] special beauty -- where the doe-eyed women [dwell]."

Asserting this as an example of <s>prativastūpamā</s> (correlative simile) is worse than bad. For here there is not even mere similarity between the two sentence-meanings, so what talk of <s>prativastūpamā</s>? Such inconsistency in all [their] figure-examples, though possible elsewhere too, has been shown by the two reasons just stated.

children.text:
ityatra viṣayaviṣayiṇordvayorapyupādānātsphuṭe 'pi rūpakatve 'tiśayoktyudāharaṇatvamuktaṃ tatra cātiśayoktitvameva nāstīti kiṃ kāryakāraṇabhāvapūrvakatvanidarśanenanetyalaṃ bahunā /
asaṃbhavadvastusaṃbandhanibandhanāyāśca yadyapi vastusaṃbandhasyāviśeṣeṇa saṃbhava uktastathāpi samanantaroktodāharaṇeṣu yathopamānasaṃbandhī dharma upameyagatatvenaiva saṃbhavati tathaivopameyasaṃbandhī dharmaḥ kvacidupamāne 'pītyāha-iyamityādi /
children.translated_text: Here, since both the object and the subject are employed, even though <s>rūpaka</s> (metaphor) is evident, it was stated as an example of <s>atiśayokti</s> (hyperbole), and there, <s>atiśayokti</s> itself does not exist -- so what is the use of demonstrating through illustration with prior cause-effect relation? Enough of this elaboration. And although it was stated that the connection of entities is possible without distinction for [<s>nidarśanā</s>] grounded in the connection of an impossible entity, nevertheless, just as in the examples just cited, the property belonging to the standard of comparison is possible as belonging to the object of comparison, so too the property belonging to the object of comparison is sometimes [possible] in the standard -- thus he says beginning with 'iyam' etc.
[<s>Ruyyaka</s>'s <s>Alaṃkārasarvasva</s> 28/2:]

children.text: iyaṃ copemeya upamānavṛttasyāsaṃbhavātpratipāditā pūrvaiḥ vastutastūpameyavṛttasyopamāne 'saṃbhavādapi bhavati /
children.translated_text: This [<s>nidarśanā</s>] was taught by the earlier [authorities] as arising from the impossibility of what pertains to the standard of comparison [occurring] in the object of comparison; but in reality, it also arises from the impossibility of what pertains to the object of comparison [occurring] in the standard.
Because the disruption of connection exists in both cases.
For example -- "In the separation of <s>Gauḍa</s> women, the pallor of their cheeks
Was perceived in the pollen within the clusters of date-palm flowers."

children.text:
atra gaṇḍatalaṃ prakṛtam /
taddharmasya pāṇḍimnaḥ kharjūrīreṇuṣvasaṃbhavādaupamyapratītiḥ /
eṣa ca prakāraḥ śṛṅkhalānyāyenāpi bhavati /
yathā-
'muṇḍasire boraphalaṃ borovari boraaṃ thiraṃ dharasi /
viggucchāai appā ṇāliacheā chalijjanti' /
children.translated_text: Here, the cheek is the primary [subject]. Since the pallor, which is its property, is impossible in the date-palm pollen, there arises the perception of simile-relation. And this mode also occurs through the chain-principle. For example -- '[Prakrit:] On your shaved head you bear a <s>bora</s> fruit, a <s>bora</s> necklace, a firm <s>bora</s> [garment]; the self, disgusted, [and] the <s>nāḍī</s>-chedas (severed channels) slip away.'
[Commentary on <s>Ruyyaka</s>'s <s>Alaṃkārasarvasva</s> 28/2:]

children.text:
ubhayatretyupameye upamāne vā /
vasantavarṇanasya prakrāntatvād dvayoḥ prakṛtatve 'pi gaṇḍatalasyopameyatvam /
tadbhatatvenaiva pāṇḍimnaḥ sisādhayiṣitatvāt /
sidhdasādhyadharmatvameva kṣopamānopameyatvamṣa /

children.translated_text: Or for example --
"This charm of your face, O doe-eyed one, is perceived even in the lord of the night (the moon).
How has he stolen this today? Or rather, what is impossible for one skilled in arts?"

'In both cases' means: whether in the object of comparison or the standard of comparison. Even though both [cheek and pollen] are primary due to the spring-description being the ongoing topic, the cheek has the status of object of comparison because pallor is intended to be established specifically as belonging to it. The status of having a property to be established versus an already-established property is precisely what constitutes the relationship of standard and object of comparison.

children.text:
atra cāṭuṣu nāyikāyāḥ prastutatvādvaktramupameyam /
taddharmasya ca lāvaṇyasyopamāne śaśinyasaṃbhavaḥ /
eṣa iti asaṃbhavadvastusaṃbandhanibandhano vā vācyaḥ /
children.translated_text: Here, since in [the context of] flattering speeches the heroine is the primary topic, her face is the object of comparison. And the impossibility of its property, charm, in the standard of comparison, the moon, [establishes the figure]. 'This' -- should be called [<s>nidarśanā</s>] grounded in the connection of an impossible entity.
[<s>Ruyyaka</s>'s <s>Alaṃkārasarvasva</s> 28/3:]
For example --
"Crying in the wilderness was done; a corpse's body was massaged; a lotus was planted on dry land; it rained long upon barren soil;

children.text: śvapucchamavanāmitaṃ badhirakarṇajāpaḥ kṛtaḥ dhṛto 'ndhamukhadarpaṇo yadabudho janaḥ sevitaḥ' //
children.translated_text: A dog's tail was straightened; whispering into a deaf ear was done; a mirror was held before a blind face -- [all this happens] when a foolish person is served."
This [<s>nidarśanā</s>] is also sometimes seen occurring in a garland [series].
For example --

children.text: 'utkope tvayi kiñcideva calati drāggūrjarakṣmābhṛtā muktā bhūrna paraṃ bhayānmarujuṣāṃ yāvattadeṇīdṛśām /
children.translated_text: "When you are even slightly angry, the king of <s>Gūrjara</s> at once releases the land; not more than that do the doe-eyed ones [show] fear from the march of warriors.

children.text: padbhyāṃ haṃsagatirmukhena śaśinaḥ kāntiḥ kucābhyāmapi kṣāmābhyāṃ sahasaiva vanyakariṇāṃ gaṇḍasthalīvibhramaḥ' //
children.translated_text: From their feet, the gait of swans; from their face, the beauty of the moon; and even from their slender breasts, at once the grandeur of the temples of wild elephants."
Sometimes, however, due to the force of negation, even through the impossibility of connection arising from implication, it occurs.

children.text:
atra muktena niṣedhapadaṃ tadanyathānupapattyā pādayorhasagatiprātpirākṣipyate /
sā ca tayoranupapannā sādṛśyaṃ gamayatīti asaṃbhavadvastusaṃbanvanibandhanā nidarśanā /
children.translated_text: Here, 'released' as a negation-word, through its otherwise-impossibility, implies the acquisition of the swan-gait for the feet. And since that [swan-gait] is impossible in them, it conveys similarity -- thus it is <s>nidarśanā</s> grounded in the connection of an impossible entity.
[Commentary on <s>Ruyyaka</s>'s <s>Alaṃkārasarvasva</s> 28/3:]

children.text:
ākṣitpāyā iti /
prātpipūrvakatvānniṣedhasya /
seti prātpiḥ sādṛśyamiti pādayorhasagatitulyāyā gateḥ pratīteḥ /
iyaṃ ca sāmānyasyānugāmitayā /
yathā- avyātma va ityādi /
atra nisargavakratākṣyadharmasyānugāmitvam /

children.translated_text: Through pure generic similarity, for example --
"With a necklace of pearls, large as <s>āmalaka</s> fruits, with hair unbound,
He attained the splendor of <s>Dhūrjaṭi</s> (<s>Śiva</s>) whose matted locks are bound with the serpent-king."

'Through implication' -- because negation presupposes [prior] acquisition. 'That' refers to: the perception, i.e. the similarity -- namely, the perception of a gait equal to that of swans for the feet. And this [occurs] through the following-along of the common property. For example: 'may he protect you' etc. Here, the property of natural crookedness has the quality of following along.
Through the relation of original and reflection, for example --
[Prakrit:] "Look! Having come to the image of the fresh, rounded cheek of the doe-eyed one,
At the end, the moon performs the act of applying vermilion to the conch-shell whorl."
Here, the properties of 'unbound' and 'bound' have pure generic similarity.
[Sanskrit reconstruction:] "Look! Having come to the image of the fresh, rounded cheek of the doe-eyed one,
At the end, the moon performs the act of applying vermilion to the conch-shell whorl."
Here, the properties of the tooth-circle and being vermilion-marked stand in the relation of original and reflection.
START <s>Sūtra</s> 29:

When difference is predominant, [and there is] superiority of the object of comparison over the standard, or the reverse, it is <s>vyatireka</s> (contrast). [<s>Ruyyaka</s>'s <s>Alaṃkārasarvasva</s> 29]

children.text:
adhunā bhedaprādhānyenālaṅkārakathanam /
bhedo vailakṣaṇyam /
sa ca dvidhā bhavati, upamānādupameyasyādhikaguṇatve viparyaye vā bhāvāt /
viparyayo nyūnaguṇatvam /
children.translated_text: Now, the discussion of figures with predominance of difference [begins]. Difference means dissimilarity. And it is twofold, because the object of comparison either has superior qualities to the standard, or the reverse. The reverse means having inferior qualities.
[Commentary on <s>Ruyyaka</s>'s <s>Alaṃkārasarvasva</s> 29:]

children.text:
bhedaprādhānya ityādi /
adhuneti prātpāvasaram /
bhedasya cātra prādhānyādabhedasya vastutaḥ sadbhāvaḥ /
sādṛśya eva paryavasānāt /
ata eva sādṛśyavyatirekeṇa saṃbhavannapi bhedo nāsya viṣayaḥ /

children.translated_text: For example --
"Let those of greedy minds fix their attachment upon the Supreme Lord who wears a divine upper garment and sports the <s>Kaustubha</s> gem.

children.text: rūpaṃ digambaramakhaṇṭanṛmuṇḍacūḍaṃ bhāvatkameva tu bateśa mama spṛhāyai' //
children.translated_text: But, O Lord, the form that is sky-clad, with an unbroken garland of skulls -- that alone indeed is to my desire!"

'Predominance of difference' etc. 'Now' means: at the appropriate occasion. And here, because of the predominance of difference, there is in reality the presence of non-difference. Because it ultimately resolves into similarity alone. Hence, difference that is possible without similarity is not the domain of this [figure].

children.text:
atra vaiṣṇavebhyaḥ svātmani viṣṇorvā parameśvare bhedamātraṃ vivakṣitaṃ na tu kenāpi kasyacidaupamyam /
sa iti bhedaḥ /
tasyādhikyaviparyayābhyāṃ vaividhyādvayatireko 'pi dvividhaḥ /
tadāśrayatvādasya /
children.translated_text: Here, what is intended is mere difference of oneself [i.e. the speaker, a <s>Śaiva</s>] from the <s>Vaiṣṇavas</s>, or of <s>Viṣṇu</s> from <s>Parameśvara</s> (<s>Śiva</s>) -- but no simile-relation of anyone with anyone. 'That' refers to this difference. Due to the variety [arising] from superiority and its reverse, <s>vyatireka</s> too is twofold -- because it [the figure] depends on that [distinction].
[<s>Ruyyaka</s>'s <s>Alaṃkārasarvasva</s> 29/1:]
Examples in order -- "Desirous of seeing the charming eyelash-play of your thousand eyes,
In pools where blue lotus beds are blooming, the swarms of bees do not delight."

children.text: 'kṣīṇaḥ kṣoṇo 'pi śaśī bhūyo bhūyo vivardhate satyam /
children.translated_text: "The moon, though waning, truly waxes again and again.

children.text: virama prasīda sundari yauvanamanivarti yātaṃ tu' //
children.translated_text: Desist! Be gracious, O beautiful one! Youth, once departed, does not return."

children.text:
atra vikasvaranīlotpalinyapekṣayā akṣisahasrasya pakṣmalatayā adhikaguṇatvam /
candrāpekṣayā ca yauvanasya nyūnaguṇatvam /
śaśivailakṣaṇyena tasyāpunarāgamāt /
children.translated_text: Here, the thousand eyes have superior qualities compared to the blooming blue-lotus pool through [their] eyelash-play. And youth has inferior qualities compared to the moon, because of its non-return, unlike the moon.
[Commentary on <s>Ruyyaka</s>'s <s>Alaṃkārasarvasva</s> 29/1:]

children.text:
candrāpekṣayeti /
śaśiyauvanayorhi samāne 'pi gatvaratve śaśinaḥ punarāgamanamapi saṃbhavati na tu yauvanasyeti tato 'sya nyūnaguṇavattvam /
nanvatra viparyayameveti sūtritaṃ bhedāntaramayuktam /
upamānādupameyasya nyūnaguṇatve vāstavatvāt,tattve cālaṅkāratvānupapatteḥ /
yauvanasya cātrāsthiratve pratipādye pratipādye candrāpekṣayādhikaguṇatvameva vivakṣitam /
yadetañcandravadyātaṃ sanna punapāyātīti /
asadetat /
yato 'tra candravad gataṃ sad yauvanaṃ yadi punarapyāgacchret tat priyaṃ prati ciramīrṣyānubandho yujyeta /
kālāntare 'pi hyasya tadavalokanādunā saphalīkāraḥ syāt /
idaṃ punarhatayauvanaṃ yātaṃ satprunarnāgacchratītīrṣyādyantarāyaparihāreṇa nirantaratayaiva priyeṇa saha saphalayitavyamiti dhigīrṣyām,tyaja priyaṃ prati manyum,kuru prasādamityāsmin priyavayasyopadeśe priyaṃ prati kopopaśamāya candrāpekṣayā yauvanasyāpunarāgamanaṃ nyūnaguṇatvenaiva vivakṣitamiti vākyārthavida eva pramāṇam /
na caitad vāstavamupameyasya nyūnaguṇatvam /
tasyaiva sātiśayatvenapratipādyatvāt /
prakṛtārthoparañjakatve hi sarvathā kaveḥ saṃrambhaḥ /
taccādhikaguṇamukhena bhavatu,itarathā vā ko viśeṣaḥ /
tasmādyuktameva viparyaye veti sūtritam /
pratyuta pratitpatvāt /

vataḥ 'svareṇa tasyā abhṛtastruteva' ityādāvanyaṣṭālāpasya pratikūlatvokteḥ karṇakaṭukatvādinā nyūnatvāvagaterupameyabhūtāyā bhagavatyāḥ saṃbandhinaḥ svarasyāmṛtastratevetyabhidhānādānandātiśayadātiśayadāyitvādeścādhikyamevāvagamyata ityalaṃ bahunā /
children.translated_text: For in 'as if nectar were streaming from her voice' and similar [passages], since the unpleasantness of another's speech is stated, through the understanding of inferiority by means of harshness to the ear etc., while for the goddess who is the object of comparison, her voice being described as 'as if streaming nectar' conveys a degree of joy-producing excellence -- thus superiority alone is understood. Enough of this elaboration.
Since this [<s>vyatireka</s>] too is based on similarity, the common property has three modes.

There, the 'following along' (<s>anugāmitā</s>) is illustrated as follows: The trunks of elephants, due to the roughness of their skin, and the distinctive banana plants, due to their absolute coldness,
even though they have attained a well-rounded form in this world, have become beyond comparison to those thighs.

'Compared to the moon' -- for though the moon and youth share equally the quality of going away, it is possible for the moon to return again, but not for youth -- hence youth's having inferior qualities. Now, [one may object:] the <s>sūtra</s> states only 'the reverse,' so another type of difference is inappropriate, because the inferiority of the object of comparison to the standard is real, and if real, the status of a figure of speech would be impossible. And here, since the instability of youth is to be conveyed, what is intended is precisely the superiority of qualities compared to the moon -- namely, 'like the moon, having departed, it [youth] does not come back again.' This is incorrect. For here, [the meaning is:] if youth, having departed like the moon, were to come back again, then prolonged jealousy toward the beloved would be justified, since even at a later time, the sight of it would make things fruitful. But this accursed youth, having departed, never returns -- therefore, removing obstacles such as jealousy, one should make [life] fruitful through uninterrupted [union] with the beloved alone. Hence, shame on jealousy! Abandon anger toward the beloved! Show grace! -- In this advice of the beloved's friend, for the purpose of calming anger toward the beloved, the non-return of youth compared to the moon is intended precisely as inferior quality. Those who know sentence-meaning alone are the authority [here]. And this inferiority of the object of comparison is not real, because that very [youth] is intended to be conveyed as possessing excellence. For the poet's effort is entirely toward embellishing the primary subject. Whether that occurs through the mode of superior quality or otherwise -- what difference does it make? Therefore, the formulation in the <s>sūtra</s> 'or the reverse' is entirely appropriate. On the contrary, because it is well-established [as a type].

children.text:
atra pariṇāhirūpatvasyātugāmitvam /
vastuprativastubhāve punargranthakṛtaivodāhṛtam - didṛkṣava ityādi /
atra manoharatvaramyatvayoḥ śuddhasāmānyarūpatvam /
pakṣyalatāvilāsavikasvarayośca bimbapratibimbabhāvaḥ /
children.translated_text: Here, the quality of having a well-rounded form is the 'following along' (<s>anugāmitā</s>). For <s>vastuprativastubhāva</s> (object-counterpart relation), the author himself has given the example beginning with 'didṛkṣavaḥ' etc. There, the qualities of being captivating and being beautiful are of the nature of pure generality (<s>śuddhasāmānya</s>). And between the graceful movement of the wing-creeper and the blossoming, there is the relation of image and reflection (<s>bimbapratibimba</s>).
START Sūtra 30:

When one of the <s>upamāna</s> (standard of comparison) and <s>upameya</s> (object of comparison) is indicated as primary, and the other is connected with the meaning of 'together' (<s>saha</s>), it is <s>sahokti</s> (co-expression). || 30 ||

children.text:
bhedaprādhānya ityeva /
guṇaprādhānabhāvanimittakamatra bhedaprādhānyam /
sahārthaprayuktaśca guṇaprādhānabhāvaḥ /
upamānopameyatvaṃ cātra vaivakṣikam, dvayorapi prākaraṇikatvādaprākaraṇikaraṇikatvādvā /
sahārthasāmarthyāddhi tayoḥ tulyakakṣatvam /
tatra tṛtīyāntasya niyamena guṇatvādupamānatvam /
arthācca pariśiṣṭasya pradhānatvādupameyatvam /
śabdaścātra guṇaprādhānabhāvaḥ /
vastutastu viparyayo 'pi syāt /
tatra niyamenātiśayoktimūlatvamasyāḥ /
sā ca kāryakāraṇapratiniyamaviparyayarūpā abhedādhyavasāyarūpā ca /
abhedādhyavasāyaśca śleṣabhittiko 'nyathā vā /
sāhityaṃ cātra katrādinānābhedaṃ jñeyam /
tatra ca -
'kāryakāraṇapratiniyamaviparyayarūpā yathā -
'bhavadaparādhaiḥ sārdhaṃ saṃtāpo vardhatetarāmasyāḥ' /
atrāparādhānāṃ saṃtāpaṃ prati hetutve 'pi tulyakālatvenopanibandhaḥ /
śleṣabhittikābhedādhyavasāyarūpā yathā -
'astaṃ bhāsvānprayātaḥ saha ripubhirayaṃ saṃhniyantāṃ balāni' /
atrāstaṃ gamanaṃ śliṣṭam /
astamityasyobhayārthatvāt //
children.translated_text: The predominance of distinction (<s>bhedaprādhānya</s>) is precisely this. The predominance of distinction here is caused by the relation of subordinate and principal (<s>guṇaprādhānabhāva</s>). And the relation of subordinate and principal is occasioned by the meaning of 'together' (<s>sahārtha</s>). The status of being <s>upamāna</s> and <s>upameya</s> here is intentional (<s>vaivakṣika</s>), since both can be either contextually relevant or contextually irrelevant. For by the force of the meaning of 'together,' the two are of equal status. In that case, the word in the instrumental case is necessarily subordinate, hence it is the <s>upamāna</s>. And by implication, the remaining word, being principal, is the <s>upameya</s>. This relation of subordinate and principal is verbal (<s>śābda</s>). But in reality, the reverse may also hold. In this [figure], there is necessarily a basis in <s>atiśayokti</s> (hyperbole). And that [hyperbole] takes the form of reversal of the fixed sequence of cause and effect, or the form of non-differentiation (<s>abhedādhyavasāya</s>). And non-differentiation may be based on <s>śleṣa</s> (paronomasia) or otherwise. The togetherness here should be understood as having various forms through the instrumental case and other [case-endings]. Among these: The form involving reversal of the fixed sequence of cause and effect is illustrated as follows: 'Along with your offenses, the anguish of this [woman] increases all the more.' Here, although the offenses are the cause with respect to anguish, they are presented as simultaneous. The form involving non-differentiation based on <s>śleṣa</s> is illustrated as follows: 'The sun has set along with the enemies; let the armies be withdrawn.' Here, the 'setting' is used with double meaning, since 'astam' has both senses.

anyatheti aśleṣarūpaḥ /
tadevamasyā atiśayoktibhedacatuṣṭayamanuprāṇakam /

tatreti nirdhāraṇe /
[kāryakāraṇapratiniyamaviparyayarūpeti] /

evamanyatra jñeyam /
'kṣayameti sā varākī snehaṃna samaṃ tvadīyena' ityasyārdham /
'kurvantvātpā hatānāṃ raṇaśirasi janā vahṇisād dehabhārānaśrūnmiśraṃ kathañcidvadatu jalamamī bāndhavā bāndhavā bāndhavebhyaḥ /
mārgantāṃ jñātidehān hatanaragahane khaṇḍitāngṛdhrakaṅkaiḥ' ityasyādyaṃ pādatrayam /
children.translated_text: '<s>upamāna</s>' etc. Anticipating the question 'What is the cause of the predominance of distinction here?' he says '<s>guṇa</s>' etc. To the question 'What causes the relation of subordinate and principal?' he says '<s>sahārtha</s>' etc. Because one is indicated with a case-ending denoting principality, and the other with a case-ending denoting subordination. 'Intentional' means not real. The status of <s>upamāna</s> and <s>upameya</s> arises when the two are of equal status; anticipating the question 'What is the basis for this here?' he says '<s>sahārtha</s>' etc. 'Of the remaining' means of the word in the nominative case. 'Verbal' means not real, since in reality the reverse is also possible. Thus the predominance of distinction caused by the subordinate-principal relation should also be understood as merely verbal here. For in reality, since the end-point is similarity itself, differentiation and non-differentiation are understood as equal. Therefore, relying merely on the verbal predominance of distinction, its definition is given here. 'Reverse' means: what is indicated by the principal case-ending may be non-principal, and what is indicated by the subordinate case-ending may be principal. 'Necessarily' implies that without being animated by <s>atiśayokti</s>, this does not even qualify as a figure of speech. 'That' refers to <s>atiśayokti</s>. The reversal of the fixed sequence of cause and effect means the expression of simultaneity instead of succession. 'Otherwise' means without <s>śleṣa</s>. Thus four varieties of <s>atiśayokti</s> animate this [figure]. '<s>Katra</s> etc.' — the word 'etc.' includes the accusative and other cases. 'Among these' is used in the partitive sense. [The form of reversal of the fixed sequence of cause and effect]: the completion is 'is established as the animating principle in this [example].' Here, the subordinate status of the offenses is verbal. But in reality, they are principal, being the subject of communication. The same should be understood elsewhere. [He cites] the half-verse 'That poor woman's affection (<s>sneha</s>) diminishes, not equally with yours.' [Then the verse] 'Let the people perform libations of water for the slain on the battlefield, shedding tears mixed with fire-like body-heat; let these kinsmen somehow speak water-words to their kinsmen; let them search for the bodies of relatives in the impenetrable [field] of slain men, [bodies] dismembered by vultures and herons' — [of this] the first three quarters [are cited].

atra vighaṭanaṃ saṃbandhibhedādbhinnaṃ na tu śliṣṭam /

yathā-

children.translated_text: 'With him I sport on the shores of the ocean, where the palm-groves rustle' — and so on, [this is not a figure].
These same [verses] are examples in the case of agent-accompaniment (<s>kartṛsāhitya</s>).

children.text: karmasāhitye yathā - 'dyujano mutyunā sārdhaṃ yasyājau tārakāmaye /
children.translated_text: In the case of object-accompaniment (<s>karmasāhitya</s>), the example is: 'The celestial host, along with Death, in the battle called <s>Tārakāmaya</s>,
fashioned with [the weapon] named <s>Cakra</s> (discus) the desire that was [fulfilled] by the servant.'

The form that is otherwise [i.e., without <s>śleṣa</s>] is illustrated as follows: 'Along with the lotus groves, the <s>cakravāka</s> (ruddy sheldrake) couples are now separating.' Here the separation differs due to the difference in the related entities, and is not used with double meaning. Without the distinguishing feature [of hyperbole], mere co-expression is not a figure of speech. For example:

children.text:
atra karotikriyāpekṣayā dyujanasya mṛtyośca karmatvam /
eṣā ca māsayāpi bhavantī dṛśyate /
yathā-
'utkṣitpaṃ saha kauśikasya pulakaiḥ sārdhaṃ mukhairnāmitaṃ bhūpānāṃ janakasya saṃśayadhiyā sākaṃ samāsphālitam /
vaidehyā manasā samaṃ ca sahasākṛṣṭaṃ tato bhārgava- prauḍhāhaṅkṛtikandalena ca samaṃ tad bhagnamaiśaṃ dhanuḥ' //
children.translated_text: Here, with respect to the action of 'making,' both the celestial host and Death have the status of object. This [figure] is also seen occurring with multiple [accompaniments]. For example: 'That bow of <s>Īśa</s> (Śiva) was — lifted along with the bristling of <s>Kauśika</s>'s (Viśvāmitra's) [hair]; bowed over along with the faces of the kings through <s>Janaka</s>'s doubtful thought; struck along with the mind of <s>Vaidehī</s> (Sītā); and then broken along with the swelling arrogance of the son of <s>Bhārgava</s> (Paraśurāma).'

etadviśeṣaparihāreṇeti atiśayoktyanuprāṇanamantareṇa /
'dvīpāntarānītavaṅgapuṣpairapākṛtasvedalavā marudbhiḥ' iti dvitīyamardham /
